Mathieu Andreux and fifty-two co-authors introduce Surfer 2, a computer-use agent that operates software purely by looking at the screen, across web, desktop, and mobile. Earlier agents leaned on platform-specific interfaces, blocking cross-platform use. Surfer 2 combines hierarchical context management, separate planning and execution, and self-verification with adaptive recovery to survive long tasks.

The system set state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks, all without task-specific fine-tuning. It scored about ninety-seven percent on WebVoyager and about eighty-seven percent on AndroidWorld. It reached about seventy percent on WebArena and about sixty percent on OSWorld. Given multiple attempts it exceeded human performance on each benchmark. The authors credit careful orchestration of foundation models, while calling for better vision-language models to cut costs.
arxiv-2510-20349:
Estelle Chigot and four co-authors train sight models to spot runways with fake images made in a flight sim. Real image sets are dear to build and tag. For key jobs like auto land, rare states must be in the set as well. Their sim set joins a small set of tagged real shots to fill those gaps.

Tight grip on how shots are made, and on how fake and real sets mix, lets stock sight models score well. The team checks strength on night shots, a state not in the real set. A tuned domain shift step helps the models hold up there. The work backs fake data as a cheap route to full state cover.
arxiv-2510-20649:
Francesco Di Filippo questions a widely held belief that every black hole must hide a point where the rules of general relativity break down. Working alone, he studies a charged round black hole that forms from collapse and then slowly loses mass through Hawking radiation.

Di Filippo shows that electric repulsion and the odd energy effects of the radiation can together block both a central crunch point and an inner horizon from forming. He also argues that spin may play the same saving role for real black holes in space. If the claim holds, the inside of an evaporating black hole may stay far less extreme than textbooks suggest.
arxiv-2510-20849:
Alejandro H. Artiles and eight co-authors present a method for making art ideas. Open ended art needs ideas that are fresh yet still hang together. Large language models tend to fall back on familiar cultural patterns. When pushed for novelty, they often lose inner coherence. Coherence here means the parts of an idea fit together.

Their method, the Cultural Alien Sampler, splits fit from typicality. Typicality means how common an idea is in a culture. One small model scores whether concepts plausibly occur together in art. A second scores how typical those mixes are for one artist. The sampler picks mixes that fit well but seem uncommon. In a human test with one hundred people, it did well. It beat random choice and a GPT-4o baseline. It matched art students on freshness and harmony. A second study found its outputs more varied and broader.
arxiv-2510-20949:
Yuncheng You, working alone, studies robust synchronization of time fractional Hopfield networks with memristive couplings and Hebbian learning rules. Fractional time gives the network strong memory and long range dependence on its past, closer to some biological learning than standard models.

Scaled group estimates show the dynamics stay globally dissipative under broad assumptions, so activity cannot blow up. A threshold on the coupling strength between neurons guarantees robust synchronization, and the threshold can be computed from the raw parameters. The threshold falls as the fractional order changes in a stated direction, giving designers a clear tuning rule for memory rich networks.
arxiv-2510-21249:
Daniele Girolimetto, Anastasios Panagiotelis, Tommaso Di Fonzo, and Han Li work on forecast reconciliation, where related forecasts are adjusted so they agree with each other. Known methods handle straight-line constraints, but some series are linked by ratios, such as death rates or jobless rates.

Their method adjusts any forecast that breaks a ratio constraint by projecting it onto the curved surface the constraint defines, set up as an optimization problem. They also derive conditions that guarantee the adjustment improves accuracy. Applied to population and economic data sets, the method clearly beats standard comparison methods, showing that reconciliation can extend beyond straight-line relationships between series.
arxiv-2510-21349:
Dmitry Kudryavtsev studies semigroups, algebraic systems with one combining operation, and asks a preservation question about local embeddability. A semigroup is locally embeddable into finite ones when every finite piece of its multiplication table can be copied inside some finite semigroup. He asks whether a shared extra property survives that copying.

The answer depends on the property. For completely simple semigroups and for Clifford semigroups, the copying can always keep the property, matching earlier findings for groups and inverse semigroups. For J-trivial semigroups the answer is no, matching the earlier negative case of cancellative semigroups. He also settles a standing question separating local embeddability from the weaker notion of local wrappability, by building J-trivial examples that satisfy the second but not the first.
arxiv-2510-21849:
André G. Viveiros leads a ten-author team studying why vision-language models work well in English but lag in other languages. The group examines the design choices behind that gap, including what training data is mixed in, which image encoder is chosen, and which text model forms the backbone.

The result is TowerVision, a family of open models for image and video tasks built on a multilingual text model. Adding visual and cultural context during fine-tuning gave strong results on translation and culturally grounded benchmarks, beating systems trained on far more data. The team also releases a curated dataset called VisionBlocks plus all models and recipes. A key finding is that multilingual training data improves transfer in both directions between rich and scarce languages.
arxiv-2510-22149:
Mohammadsajad Alipour and Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri imagine the worst coworker in federated learning, the scheme where many clients train one shared model without pooling their private data. Their invention is the dictator client: a malicious participant who can wipe every other client's contribution out of the server model while keeping its own fully intact.

The pair design concrete attacks that grant that power and analyze what happens to training in each case. They then complicate the picture with several dictators at once, cooperating, ignoring each other, or banding together with plans to betray the alliance later. For every arrangement they track the effect on whether the global model still converges. The exercise maps a sharp vulnerability class so that defenses can be designed against defined attacks rather than vague fears.
arxiv-2510-22249:
Ibuki Nakamura, Yutaro Kashiwa, Bin Lin, and Hajimu Iida read the confessions developers leave in test code. Programmers under deadline take shortcuts and sometimes admit it in comments, a practice called self-admitted technical debt. Research has cataloged such admissions in production code for years while mostly assuming test code behaves the same.

Mining more than seventeen thousand admitted-debt comments, most of them from test files, the team maps how the debt is distributed and what kinds appear, finding plenty that fit no production-code category. They also test whether the presence of admitted debt in a test suite tracks with the quality of the tests themselves. The study gives test debt its own profile, a first step toward paying it down deliberately instead of discovering it during a failure.
arxiv-2510-22349:
William Barker, Le Xuan Dong, Vu Trong Luong, and Nguyen Duong Toan prove that certain diffusion equations support waves that travel without changing shape. The equations are nonclassical. Alongside ordinary diffusion, they carry a higher-order term mixing space and time derivatives. That term models memory in the spreading process. The reaction term obeys only general structural conditions.

The team seeks monotone traveling waves. These are fronts that climb steadily from one state to another. The method builds the wave between an upper and a lower trial solution. Those guides may be less smooth than classical proofs demand. Iteration proceeds monotonically inside a convex set. Schauder's fixed point theorem guarantees convergence to a true solution. Explicit constructions of the guides are included. The existence proof doubles as a recipe others can adapt.
arxiv-2510-22849:
Hard reasoning tasks may suit a custom program better than prose. Adam Stein, Neelay Velingker, Mayur Naik, and Eric Wong propose such a route in 2025. It is called Per-Instance Program Synthesis, or PIPS. For each input, it writes and refines a program. Structural feedback guides the refinement.

No task specific guidance is needed. No explicit test cases are needed either. A confidence score picks a strategy per instance. It chooses direct inference or program synthesis. Tests span thirty benchmarks and three frontier models. PIPS raised accuracy over chain and program baselines. It also cut undesirable program outputs sharply. Algorithmic tasks showed the clearest gains.
arxiv-2510-22949:
Benedictus C G Cinun and five co-authors built a low-cost Stewart platform, a table held by six moving legs that can tilt and shift in six ways. Such platforms serve as test beds for control research, but good ones are often costly. Their build mixes shelf parts with printed and custom pieces.

Software on the platform handles modeling, data capture, and real-time control in one frame. A feedback-based controller with an added optimal scheme tracks paths despite nonlinear motion, while a Kalman filter merges sensor and encoder data. Tests confirm the cheap build can still move with care and steadiness.
arxiv-2510-23049:
Christos Thrampoulidis, Sadegh Mahdavi, and Wenlong Deng show that two rival ways to train for the Pass-at-K goal are in fact the same. That goal rewards a model if any of K tries solves a task with a checkable answer. One camp uses direct policy gradients, the other reshapes advantages inside GRPO.

By reverse-engineering the shaping methods, the authors reveal hidden surrogate rewards they optimize. Popular tricks that up-weight hard examples act as reward-level regularizers. Starting from surrogate rewards, they derive the matching gradients. The unified view helps trainers pick settings with clear intent instead of folklore.
arxiv-2510-23549:
Nikolaj B. Sillassen and thirteen co-authors give a portrait of the Cosmic Vine, a forming galaxy cluster at redshift 3.44 in the CEERS field. Such protoclusters show how the largest structures in space began to assemble. Drawing on James Webb Space Telescope archive data, the team maps the structure, its galaxies, and the dark matter halos that hold them.

They confirm 136 galaxies in the Vine and 47 more in a nearer diffuse structure they call the Leaf. Eleven members have already stopped forming stars, the largest such group yet found in a dense region that early, and they line up on a tight red sequence. Both star-forming and quiet galaxies skew heavier than field galaxies of the same era. With three subgroups apparently falling toward the core, the Vine shows massive galaxies assembling fast when the universe was under two billion years old.
arxiv-2510-23649:
Tenghui Li and four co-authors present LRQK, a method that lets large language models handle long inputs without the memory blowup of the key-value cache. As text grows, storing keys and values for every token eats GPU memory and blocks long-context work. Older fixes quantize or prune the cache, losing precision or dropping the wrong entries.

LRQK instead splits the query and key matrices into low-rank factors during the first pass over the text. At each decoding step it uses those small factors to score tokens cheaply, then attends exactly to only the top-scoring tokens plus a few recent ones. A mixed GPU-CPU cache fetches full-precision pairs only when missing, cutting data movement while keeping outputs exact. On the RULER and LongBench tests with two mid-size models, LRQK matched or beat sparse-attention methods and saved much memory.
arxiv-2510-23949:
Kyomin Hwang and four co-authors expose a blind spot in machine unlearning for multilingual language models: erasing knowledge with English data alone can scramble the model's languages. Prior studies showed English-only unlearning under-erases other languages, but judged success by performance scores. This study looks at the evaluation itself, in models fully fine-tuned on parallel multilingual data before unlearning.

After unlearning, the models suffer language confusion, answering in a different language than the prompt used. The authors introduce an n-gram-based score, N-Mix, showing the confusion is widespread and consistent. Worse, standard reference-based metrics misread confused output and report false negatives — they claim knowledge survives or vanished for the wrong reasons. The team argues for semantic metrics that judge the content of what the model actually says. Evaluators, they warn, must check the answer's language before trusting any unlearning score.
arxiv-2510-24049:
Hao Jia and five co-authors present a method for predicting how complex physical systems change over space and time. Deep learning models can do this task well at first, but errors build up over long runs. The result can look wrong for the real system and break basic physical rules.

Their method, called RAP, pairs a neural network with real past cases from history. For each new state, it looks up past patterns that show how the system moved before. That history acts as a check on the network's guess. The authors report more stable long term forecasts and fewer false patterns than models that rely on learned rules alone.
arxiv-2510-24849:
Jack T Warfield leads a team with fifteen co-authors who track the slow drift of Draco II, a very faint dwarf galaxy near our own. Two rounds of shots from the Hubble scope, seven years apart, give the base for their read. Such faint systems have few member stars, so the fixed frame behind them must be built with care.

The team built that frame three ways: from stars with known drift, from far still galaxies, and from a mix of both. All three frames gave the same drift for Draco II. The galaxy frame, with about three hundred far galaxies, cut the error by up to two fold. The result is their most tight drift read yet.
arxiv-2510-25149:
Justin Lawrence, Nicholas Rouse, and Ben Williams set tests for when a small algebra with a flip act can grow from part of a curve to the whole curve. The algebra is of degree two, and the flip act is of order two. Both the algebra and its flip act must grow, and the pair is the point.

Tests for the algebra part were known; the new part is a test for the act, which code algebra tools can run. The work is tied to marked parts of trait webs for knot groups with flip traits. Last, the team runs the math for a few flip traits of the known figure eight knot. That case shows the tests at work.
arxiv-2510-25449:
Lucas Q Galvao, Anna Beatriz M de Souza, Marcelo A Moret, and Clebson Cruz review variational computing. Their 2025 review covers quantum run uses specifically. Variational quantum computing plays a key role there. It differs from methods centered on classic data. Quantum data are critical in variational methods here. Quantum machine learning also uses such data heavily.

The review delineates foundational principles of variational computing. It sets motivation within the noisy intermediate-scale era. Current quantum devices are noisy and medium sized. Hybrid quantum-classic approaches run these methods in practice. Their practicality depends on trainability and scalability issues. Noise and barren plateau constraints limit results strongly. The authors study prototypical quantum run problems critically. Recent advancements in the field are synthesized jointly. Persistent challenges and emerging opportunities are highlighted. The review complements current literature with focused perspective. It maps the current landscape for quantum run scholars.
arxiv-2510-25549:
Andre H A Malavazi, Borhan Ahmadi, Pawel Horodecki, and Pedro R Dieguez study quantum batteries. It also measures maximal useful stored energy. Their concepts reorganize internal form without changing total.

Those operations keep total ergotropy value unchanged throughout. Ideas are illustrated for two system types. Discrete two-level systems form the first case. Continuous-variable single-mode Gaussian states form the second. Displacement and squeezing parts are redistributed for Gaussians. Energy and entropy variations are tracked during transformations. Beam-splitter effects with auxiliary systems implement them dynamically. Useful implications include tuning charging protocols for batteries. Mitigating charge loss in open quantum batteries matters too.
arxiv-2510-25749: Boris Y Rubinstein gives a new class of ties for same-form symmetric polynomials, in a 2025 math paper. Ties he gave first for Bernoulli type polynomials are shown to hold for all such polynomials of one degree. Study of those ties leads him to a new kind of non-linear tie for the Bernoulli numbers. The note is short and dense, for readers who work with symmetric polynomials.
arxiv-2510-25849:
Elisa Damiani, Margherita Marsili, and Maria Clelia Righi study why carbon films sometimes peel from metal surfaces. Diamond and diamond like carbon coatings are hard and useful, but weak sticking to a metal base limits their use. The team use first principles calculations, which start from basic physics rather than fitted data, to test many metal and carbon surface pairs at once.

Damiani and her co-authors cover fifteen metals and four carbon surfaces and look for clear trends. They find that sticking strength follows a simple rule tied to the surface energies of the two sides. Comparing break strength with the metal cohesion also predicts where a joint will split under pull.
arxiv-2510-25949:
Sahin Kocak, working alone, gives a new way to view the attractor of an iterated function system as a sculpture like intersection. An iterated function system is a set of shrinking maps whose repeated use builds a fractal, a shape with fine detail at every scale. Usually the attractor is defined as the limit, in the Hausdorff sense, of any nonempty compact set under repeated iteration.

Kocak shows that on a boundedly compact metric space, such a system has compact, invariant subspaces with a special property. The attractor can then be written as the intersection of a decreasing chain of compact spaces. The note offers a clean alternative picture of a standard fractal construction.
arxiv-2510-26249:
Oleg Aristov, working alone, computes the homology dimensions of algebras built from analytic functionals. A functional is a dual object to a function, used in complex analysis and in representation theory. Homology dimensions measure how complex an algebra is. They gauge how long the step by step builds of its modules must be.

Aristov shows that the main dimensions of this algebra all take one value. The same holds for some completed forms of the algebra. That value is the dimension of the simply connected solvable factor of the group. The factor comes from the standard split of the linear form of the group. A striking point follows. A nonzero reductive factor might be expected to muddy the algebra. It has no effect on these homology traits.
arxiv-2510-26449:
A Empey, with six co-authors, studies young stars whose light dips often and sharply. These dipper stars sit inside disks of gas and dust, and their dips likely come from dust near the inner disk crossing the line of sight. Irregular dippers show no steady rhythm, so their cause is less clear than for steady ones.

Empey and the team take a first multi-epoch look at sixteen irregular dippers with the X-Shooter instrument. They build each star's true face by mixing standard templates with Gaia data, then measure dip depth, infrared excess, and how deep dips look at each colour. Twenty clear dips showed no shared pattern. Most had low depth and small excess, and grain models point to clumps of processed dust, some grains as large as twenty micrometres across, lifted above the disk.
arxiv-2510-26649:
Zhicheng Jiang, Hengne Li, and Jin-Han Liang propose a new way to hunt long-lived particles at future Higgs factories. Such particles travel some distance before decaying, and a common search looks for a lone photon. At these colliders, though, a background process that yields the same lone photon grows overwhelming.

Jiang and his two co-authors instead look for displaced photons, photons born away from the collision point, inside the barrel of the hadronic calorimeter, the detector layer that measures hadron energy. The detector's own shielding makes that region nearly background-free. Their analysis is sensitive to particles with decay lengths from about one metre up to a million metres in scale. For standard test models, it improves on conventional searches by up to a factor of ten.
arxiv-2510-26749:
Fahad Aziz, with fourteen co-authors, builds a superconducting artificial atom that converts and combs frequencies. An artificial atom is a circuit that behaves like a single atom for microwaves. Theirs sits at the end of a semi-infinite transmission line and is driven by two continuous radio-frequency fields.

Aziz and the team observe many frequency peaks in the emitted spectrum, forming combs with equal spacing. The peaks come from wave mixing of the two drives, mediated by the atom. Control is precise across a range of tens of megahertz, wider than the atom's own linewidth, and matches theory well. The device is small and broadly tunable. The authors pitch it for quantum optics on chips and other quantum technology uses.
arxiv-2510-26949:
Taylor Schaffner and Benjamin Machta model how proteins that meet in the cell membrane may react to changes in that membrane. The membrane is a fluid sheet where patches rich in certain fats, often called rafts, can form. Near a phase change, meaning a shift in how the fats order themselves, patch sizes can swing with small changes in heat or mix.

Using a model and Monte Carlo simulations, which test many random arrangements, the pair show reaction rates can shift sharply near that critical point. In some runs, proteins pull partners into small held pockets that stay out of balance. The work warns that many membrane networks may be far more sensitive near the transition than expected.
arxiv-2510-27049:
Ponrawee Prasertsom works with Andrea Silvi, Jennifer Culbertson, Moa Johansson, Devdatt Dubhashi, and Kenny Smith to explain why number-word systems look so regular across languages. Recursive numeral systems build large numbers from small parts by fixed rules. Past accounts credited a trade-off between vocabulary size and average form complexity, but ruling out unnatural systems took extra ad hoc constraints.

Using minimum description length, a measure of how compactly a system can be described, the team scores regularity and processing cost directly. Those scores separate real language systems from merely possible ones better than the older trade-off, including systems once called optimal. The extra constraints also follow naturally from regularity itself. The study argues efficiency research must weigh regularity across whole sets of forms.
arxiv-2510-27149:
Olena Podladchikova proposes that coronal streamers act as resonators that set the rhythm of solar wind density patterns. Periodic density structures seen in coronagraph images repeat roughly every forty-five, eighty, and one hundred twenty minutes. Earlier candidate cavities give periods that clash badly with those values, from minutes to years.

Streamers, the bright helmet-like structures above the Sun limb, instead ring as magnetohydrodynamic resonators with harmonic periods matching observations closely. Slow standing waves compress plasma into density bumps, amplified because the resonator quality is fairly high. At streamer tips the bumps trigger reconnection and release plasma blobs at the resonant periods. Energy budgets and amplitude estimates complete a model linking remote images to in-situ solar wind measurements.
arxiv-2510-27249:
Suklav Ghosh, Sonal Kumar, and Arijit Sur test a fresh shield for image AI in this 2025 paper. Attackers can flip a network's answer with changes too small for eyes to see. Most shields train on attacked images alone. Their method, C-LEAD, adds contrastive learning, a style that pulls like images close and pushes unlike ones apart.

The network trains on both clean and attacked images at once. The setup adjusts the model and the attack tweaks side by side. The aim is features, the traits the network reads, that stay steady under attack. In tests, the shield held up well against many attack kinds. The authors say the contrastive loss draws out stronger, more telling traits. Code is shared on GitHub for others to check.
arxiv-2510-27549:
Steven Cunnington leads a team with ten co-authors who report on MeerKLASS, a sky survey with the MeerKAT radio array in 2025. The survey maps a faint radio line from hydrogen gas, which traces dark matter, the unseen mass that shapes space. By scanning wide areas, the team aims to chart how matter clumps across a large span of cosmic time.

Early maps are cleaned of bright foreground noise and checked for lost signal. The team then matches the maps with known galaxy surveys to confirm a real cosmic signal. Code for the work is shared in public, and the results point to what wider MeerKLASS scans could reveal about the growth of structure in space.
arxiv-2511-00349:
Weiyou Kong, Weijia Kong, Lukas Chrostowski, and Xin Xin chase a fabrication failure in photonic devices built on barium titanate films. A routine oxygen plasma clean, meant to prepare the surface, caused photoresist to lift off during gentle rinsing and ultrasound. Optical microscopy and two spectroscopy methods let them separate bulk changes from surface changes in the film.

The bulk stayed the same, but the surface did not: plasma created a nanometer-thin layer rich in barium carbonate that weakened the resist bond. Each plasma step recreated the weak layer, while simple solvent cleaning removed it. The practical guidance is direct: avoid routine oxygen plasma on this material, use gentler cleans such as UV-ozone, or tune the plasma with care.
arxiv-2511-00749:
Tanvi Dinkar, Aiqi Jiang, Gavin Abercrombie, and Ioannis Konstas audit how image generators encode beauty and erase its opposite. Social media already promotes Western beauty norms with documented harms, and AI-generated content now floods the same feeds. The team prompts three language models and two image models through two generation pipelines, structured by a beauty taxonomy they built, producing nearly six thousand images.

Women and non-binary social media users then rated twelve hundred of the images in a within-subjects study, with high agreement. More than eighty-six percent of generated people had lighter skin tones, and about three quarters read as young. Explicit content appeared in over a fifth of images despite safe-for-work training. Non-binary figures were rated younger and more sexualized, and prompts with so-called negative traits drew higher unsafe ratings across genders.
arxiv-2511-00849:
Zhexiao Huang and colleagues propose P-OCS, a method for flagging out of distribution inputs, data unlike anything a model was trained on. Spotting such inputs matters when deep learning systems run in open environments, where strange cases appear without warning.

The method works in the space left over after the main feature directions of normal data are removed. A single small nudge applied only inside that leftover space sharpens the faint differences between normal and foreign samples, without disturbing the geometry of the normal ones. The authors prove a one step update suffices in the small nudge regime and give convergence guarantees. Across designs and data sets, they report top detection scores at almost no extra computing cost and with no retraining.
arxiv-2511-01049:
Andrei Lebed predicts an unusual magnetic effect in quasi one dimensional conductors, materials where electrons move far more easily along one direction than across it. Under magnetic breakdown, electrons tunnel between two open orbits. He finds that the electron scattering time can then oscillate in a way that Fermi liquid theory, the standard picture of metals, cannot explain.

The oscillations come from electron electron interactions in the metallic phase under that breakdown condition. Lebed works the effect out in formulas and in numbers for the known electron spectrum of the organic conductor (TMTSF)2ClO4. He also argues that similar resistivity oscillations should appear in another quasi one dimensional organic conductor, giving labs a concrete place to look for non Fermi liquid behavior.
arxiv-2511-01449:
Riddhi Jain and colleagues judge fruit freshness from photographs, a non-invasive way to cut waste of perishable produce. Fine grained freshness labels from experts are costly, so training data are scarce. Proprietary vision language models do well at the task, but food retailers cannot send their data to closed services, and open models lag behind.

Their algorithm, model agnostic ordinal meta learning, trains smaller vision language models by meta learning across tasks while exploiting the ordered nature of freshness grades. It is designed for both zero shot and few shot use under data sparsity. The reported accuracy, averaged across fruits, is about ninety two point seven percent, which the authors describe as industry standard, with state of the art results for this classification task.
arxiv-2511-01749:
Hong-Fei Huang, Houssam Sabri, Jiadong Zang, and Jie-Xiang Yu explain a rare mix of traits in one oxide. The compound Sr3Co2O7 is a metal. It is also a magnet, and it is ferroelectric, with a built-in electric polarization. Polar order and free conduction rarely coexist. Their coupling could serve spintronic uses.

First-principles calculations trace both traits to one cause: charge disproportionation. Cobalt ions split into unequal charge states. At one site, an inverted ligand-field splitting drives the shift that breaks symmetry. Orbitals at both sites keep the material conducting. The on-site Hubbard interaction holds the split in place. The authors propose this route as a design rule: split charges within chosen orbitals, and a metal can turn polar and stay magnetic at once.
arxiv-2511-01949:
U. Vijaya Chandra Kumar, H. M. Nagesh, and Narahari N promote a graph invariant from pure mathematics into chemistry's predictive toolbox. Drug and materials research leans on topological indices. These are numbers computed from a molecule's structure. They correlate with its physical and biological behavior, in structure-property and structure-activity studies.

Edge irregularity strength is a labeling measure. Assign numbers to a graph's edges, under rules that make every vertex's total distinct. Then find the smallest largest label needed. The authors explore its chemical uses. They show it can predict physical and chemical properties, in the same spirit as topological indices. It captures structural features those indices use. They present the invariant as a companion descriptor. It adds a new angle on a molecule's structure to the standard QSPR and QSAR workflow. It does not take their place.
arxiv-2511-02149:
Yovna Junglee, Vianey Leos Barajas, and Meredith Franklin build a statistical method for estimating pollution exposure when the data refuse to line up. Public health studies combine satellite readings with ground monitors, but the two sources observe different places at different times, and gaps are common. Standard fixes fill gaps or force alignment first, which adds error before the real modelling starts.

Their Bayesian framework folds the mismatch into the model itself: a space-time kernel averages each predictor over its local neighbourhood, directly inside the likelihood. A Voronoi-based approximation handles the irregular sampling. Simulations showed that careless choices of spatial and temporal lag bias the results, while careful tuning kept predictions accurate even under severe missingness. Applied to fine particulate pollution in northern California, the method beat a traditional model on out-of-sample prediction.
arxiv-2511-02349:
Jiankai Tang and twelve co-authors release a dataset for measuring heart signals with an ordinary smartphone. Photoplethysmography reads pulse from tiny colour changes in skin, and phones can do it through their cameras, avoiding special equipment and awkward postures. Single-camera methods, though, wobble under movement and changing light, and almost no open data existed for checking accuracy across devices, especially in real patients.

The M3PD dataset is the first public collection to record face and fingertip videos at the same time, using a phone's front and rear cameras together. Its sixty participants included forty-seven cardiovascular patients, recorded in laboratory and clinical settings. A companion model that fuses the two views with temporal modelling cut heart-rate error by roughly twenty-two to thirty percent compared with single-view baselines, and held up better in difficult real-world conditions.
arxiv-2511-02449:
Ching Yan Timothy Yau, a mathematician, computes the sizes of layers inside a space that algebraic geometers use to organise representations of a quiver. A quiver is a directed graph whose representations assign vector spaces to vertices and maps to arrows. The Harder-Narasimhan filtration sorts representations by stability. Its strata inside the zero set of the moment map have dimensions that were earlier accessible through methods of Kac, Crawley-Boevey, and Reineke for simpler quivers.

Yau generalises those methods to quivers without loops but with many edges, and computes the dimension of the Harder-Narasimhan strata of the moment map's zero set in that broader setting. A noticed link ties this dimension to the terms of Kac's polynomial. That invariant counts absolutely indecomposable representations over finite fields and is computed by the equivariant cohomology of the same zero set. The two quantities illuminate each other.
arxiv-2511-02649:
Alvaro Gutierrez, Rosa Orellana, Franco Saliola, Anne Schilling, and Mike Zabrocki study plethysm coefficients, numbers that govern how Schur functions combine. These coefficients are basic in algebra but notoriously hard to compute. Their 2025 paper looks at a generating function that packages the coefficients when one index has bounded length.

The team proves that this bivariate generating function is a rational function, using MacMahon's combinatory analysis as a key step. When the length bound is two, they give an explicit geometric recipe based on q-Ehrhart theory, which counts lattice points in shapes. They present evidence that the function is a quantum Ehrhart series of certain half-open polytopes, and they prove a reciprocity law in the spirit of Ehrhart's. Recursions for the smallest case complete the picture.
arxiv-2511-03249:
Power engineers J Gutierrez-Florensa, F Sanniti, D Tedeschi, L Sigrist, A Ortega, and F Milano tackle a timing problem in electric grids. They focus on how fast grid frequency changes after a fault, a measure tied to stored spinning energy and to the size of the shock. Protection gear relies on that measure to shed load or stop unwanted islanding.

Modern grids carry less spinning mass and more converter-based power, so old meters read the change less well. The team offers a sturdier method drawn from geometry and fluid ideas, then checks it against fast real measurements. The method also tells protection gear more about what kind of fault happened. A quicker control scheme built on it can react sooner and more wisely.
arxiv-2511-03549:
Ziv Nevo, Orna Raz, and Karen Yorav ground code explanations in the human chatter that surrounds the code on GitHub. Language models explain code well in isolation but miss why it was written that way. Pull request notes, issue threads, and commit messages hold that missing engineering context.

Their system first extracts and structures the relevant GitHub artifacts for a code area. A generator then writes a high-level account of the code's purpose from that context, and a validator checks the account. The tool runs standalone or as a server inside a standard model protocol, easing adoption. Maintenance, onboarding, and modernization all depend on purpose, so richer explanations can save teams real time.
arxiv-2511-03949:
B P Pandey and Mark Wardle compute transport values for a partly ionized plasma like the solar atmosphere, about ninety percent hydrogen and ten percent helium, under an assumed magnetic field profile. Catalog evidence carried a doubled long title; the arXiv record gives the shorter title used here.

Resonance charge exchange dominates the ion Hall work, with weaker nonresonant collisions included. Neutral particles rule thermal conductivity both along and across the field, and the cross-field parts stay close to the parallel ones with weak Hall dependence. Wave damping through neutral conductivity may aid solar heating. Cross-field terms, the authors stress, must stay in models of the photosphere-chromosphere transition, spicules, and prominences.
arxiv-2511-04649:
Krinio Marouda leads five authors probing gravitational collapse with twist and higher modes. A massless complex scalar field collapses in an axisymmetric spacetime here. The setup follows Choptuik and co-authors from 2004, with symmetry set by an azimuthal number.

That choice allows both twist and angular momentum in the field. The team extends earlier work to higher angular modes using the bamps code. A new symmetry reduction, called m-cartoon, plus a twist-aware horizon finder support the runs. For the first mode, they recover discrete self-similarity and known scaling, confirming the machinery before pushing further.
arxiv-2511-05149:
Cristina Olmedilla and co-authors work on injection throttling, a way to hold back traffic and ease congestion in the fast nets that link supercomputers and data centers. Those nets face huge loads from science, AI, and cloud work, and a slow net can stall the whole machine.

The study reviews how such systems have grown, from faster links to added accelerators, and why the net is now a key bottleneck. It then improves throttling rules so senders pause in a smarter way. The aim is higher total throughput with less jam at peak load.
arxiv-2511-05449:
Tuan Anh Tran and co-authors ask how many tokens 3D point cloud transformers truly need, and find the answer is far fewer than used today. Such models lead on tasks like semantic segmentation, but dense token sets make training and use slow and costly.

gitmerge3D, their graph-based merging method, cuts token counts by up to about nine tenths or more while scores stay competitive. Global data guides which points to merge. The result challenges the habit of feeding every point to the model, and could cut the cost of 3D AI by a wide margin.
arxiv-2511-05549:
Yubo Wang, Haoyang Li, Fei Teng, and Lei Chen present AGRAG, a system that gives language models access to knowledge stored as a graph. Graph-based retrieval can help, but it suffers three flaws. Graphs carry errors from the model itself, reasoning about why passages were picked is weak, and answers cover only part of a question.

AGRAG builds its graph with a statistics-based method instead of model extraction, cutting error spread. For retrieval it searches for a subgraph that packs high influence at low cost, a problem the authors prove is hard and solve with a greedy method. Those subgraphs act as clear reasoning paths, helping the model focus on the right text.
arxiv-2511-05649:
Jung-Wook Kim, Raj Patil, Trevor Scheopner, and Jan Steinhoff clear up a naming clash in scattering physics. Two different quantities both go by the name eikonal. One is a generator, an operator whose classical limit produces every scattering observable. The other is a phase, equal to a classical action computed along the scattering path.

The authors show the two are not the same thing and derive the exact general relation between them. In the special case of integrable scattering, the two agree up to a known transformation, which explains older confusion. With spin or radiation involved, that neat match fails. The result gives amplitude researchers a sharper shared language.
arxiv-2511-05749:
P Oliveira Silva and co-authors characterize a disordered magnetic material, Ho2Zr2O7, and explain why it stays magnetic without ever ordering. In this defect-fluorite crystal, holmium and zirconium atoms share one site at random, and oxygen spots sit empty. Frustration and disorder mix, making its magnetism hard to read.

Cooling powder samples toward absolute zero, the team found spin motion slowing near one kelvin but no glassy freeze, and no long-range order in heat data down to very low temperature. Neutron scattering revealed the crystal-field energy levels of the holmium ions. Their model says the clean ground state would carry no magnetic moment at all. Disorder itself guarantees the magnetism, by mixing low-lying states at finite temperature.
arxiv-2511-05849:
Nan Jiang, Ziyi Wang, and Yexiang Xue speed up symbolic regression, the search for a formula that fits data, by teaching the search that different formulas can mean the same thing. Many expressions differ in writing yet define one function, and standard tools waste time treating each as new.

Their framework, EGG-SR, groups equivalent expressions in an equality graph. That grouping prunes repeated branches in tree search, pools rewards across equivalents in deep reinforcement learning, and enriches the feedback given to language models. Theory shows the grouping tightens search regret and steadies the learning gradient. In practice it improved every model family tested. The authors frame symbolic equivalence as an untapped lever for scientific discovery tools.
arxiv-2511-06049:
Nabil Baouche and Amine Ahriche map what a two-Higgs-doublet model with scale invariance predicts for particle physics. In this framework no mass scale is put in by hand. Electroweak symmetry breaking happens through quantum corrections, and the whole scalar spectrum, including the known Higgs boson's mass, is generated at one loop.

After applying strict theory and experiment constraints, only a narrow slice of parameter space survives. In that slice the Higgs-like mass is purely radiative, a sharp claim. The model's triple Higgs couplings are strongly suppressed, and double-Higgs production at the LHC could fall by nearly half versus the Standard Model. Those signatures give experimenters a clear target: find the suppression, or rule the model out.
arxiv-2511-06149:
Dominique Briechle and co-authors build a workbench to make product repair and maintenance services trustworthy enough to use. Electric goods are produced at record levels, straining resources and health. Circular economy ideas prolong product life based on each item's condition, yet customers shy away from such services.

One blocker is price uncertainty: clients cannot know a service's cost in advance. Providers face the mirror problem, since they cannot judge an item's condition before taking the job, and a bad surprise can mean real losses. The Lifecycle Workbench is a configurable framework for digitized maintenance services meant to close that knowledge gap. The authors frame reliable condition and cost knowledge as the precondition for circular services to scale.
arxiv-2511-07249:
Tsz Wai Ko and five co-authors build a foundation potential for atomistic simulation that takes electric charge seriously. Machine-learned potentials that mimic quantum mechanics now drive large materials simulations, but most ignore electrostatics outright or pay a prohibitive cost for it. Their charge-equilibrated TensorNet design is equivariant and charge-aware, with a solvable equilibration scheme that can be worked out in closed form that keeps the cost growing only linearly with system size.

Trained once, the potential matches leading rival potentials on standard materials benchmarks yet disagrees qualitatively where electrostatics dominate. There it is right: it reproduces the structure and density of a sodium-calcium chloride ionic liquid and the crystallization of a phase-change memory alloy that charge-blind models miss. Fine-tuned, it also captures reactions at a lithium battery interface under applied voltage.
arxiv-2511-07549:
Soumavo Ghosh, Paola Di Matteo, and Chanda Jog dissect why galaxies like ours lean to one side. The Milky Way shows a one-sided lopsided pattern in both stars and gas. Minor mergers can excite such patterns, and chemistry offers a way to trace which stars take part.

Seven detailed merger simulations vary orbit direction and tilt between a Milky Way-like host and a satellite. A tidal pass reliably triggers the lopsided mode. Splitting stars by chemical makeup then shows how different populations carry the distortion over time. The results help observers read our Galaxy lopsided shape as a record of past encounters.
arxiv-2511-07849:
Chen-Bo Zhu lectures on the local theta correspondence, a bridge between representations of paired groups. These notes record a March 2025 mini-course at the Institut Henri Poincaré in Paris, within a program on representation theory and noncommutative geometry. The emphasis falls on the Archimedean theory for classical Lie groups.

Early sections build the basic theory, including Howe duality theorem and conservation relations, with an invariant-theoretic proof highlighted. Later sections track how two fundamental representation invariants behave under the correspondence. A closing section points onward. As lecture notes, the text offers newcomers a guided entry into a correspondence that organizes much of modern representation theory.
arxiv-2511-07949:
Weichao Liang and Daoyi Dong propose a lighter filter for stabilizing uncertain quantum systems through feedback. Real quantum devices face unknown starting states, imprecise parameters, and extra environmental noise. Full filters track a number of variables that grows with the square of the system size, which gets costly fast.

The reduced filter tracks only diagonal density matrix entries in a chosen measurement basis, a count growing just linearly with size. That cut makes real time computation and feedback much simpler. Analysis still gives global exponential stability of the target subspace, plus robustness against time varying changes and dissipative effects.
arxiv-2511-08049:
Weixu Wang and co-authors propose CometNet for long term time series forecasting guided by recurring contextual motifs. Forecasters that only look back over a fixed window miss dependencies stretching much farther into the past. Widening the window adds heavy cost and buries useful long patterns under historical noise, so a smarter summary is needed.

A motif extraction module first finds repeated, dominant patterns in complex past sequences. The forecasting module then maps the recent window to its relevant motifs and uses their context to predict ahead. On eight real world data sets, CometNet beats leading methods by a clear margin, especially at longer forecast horizons.
arxiv-2511-08349:
Amin Ebrahimi and Farzan Haddadi propose a hybrid quantum classic choice device for the Mamba sequence design, aimed at time sorting. Large language models spend heavily on matrix multiplication and high dimensional tuning. Quantum circuits work in huge Hilbert spaces and may offer richer pictures plus speed, which drives inserting them where Mamba selects which information to keep or discard.

Variational quantum circuits act as gating modules, sharpening feature extraction and suppressing irrelevant content. The manuscript analyzes how such quantum subroutines affect generalization, expressivity, and parameter efficiency in the combined model. The authors present quantum enhanced gating as a route toward scalable, resource lean language models for sequence tasks.
arxiv-2511-08549:
Parshwa Shah and four co-authors tackle the problem of locating user devices in wireless networks from channel measurements alone. Standard deep learning models spread attention evenly over the input and handle single snapshots of channel data poorly, so the team builds a vision transformer tuned for this task.

Their model focuses on the angle delay profile drawn from the channel state information matrix. Tested on the DeepMIMO and ViWi ray-tracing datasets, it errs by about half a meter indoors. Outdoor errors are larger, near thirteen meters in one dataset and about three meters in a blockage scenario in the other. The authors report accuracy about thirty-eight percent better than leading prior schemes.
arxiv-2511-08749:
Mehrdad Zakershahrak redesigns reinforcement learning agents as queryable knowledge bases rather than pure control machines. A trained agent silently learns a great deal about its world, including reachability, distances, and dynamics, but standard architectures bury that knowledge where nobody can ask for it.

The proposed architecture, QDIN, gives each query type its own specialized neural module: one for policy questions, others for reachability, paths, and comparisons. The striking finding is a decoupling between knowing and doing. Inference accuracy can reach near perfection, with reachability scores around ninety-nine percent, while control returns stay near thirty-one percent. Query-specialized designs beat both unified models and after-the-fact extraction, while keeping competitive control. The author frames this as a research agenda for interpretable, verifiable agents.
arxiv-2511-09249:
Rustam Ibragimov, Jihyun Kim, and Anton Skrobotov build sturdier tests for predictive regressions. These workhorse models forecast returns from valuation ratios. Standard tests distort badly when predictors are persistent, heavy-tailed, or endogenous, and when error volatility lingers. Their paper extends the Cauchy estimation approach to handle exactly those problems.

They propose two tests: one using group inference on t-statistics, and a hybrid combining Cauchy with ordinary least squares estimation. Both are simple to implement and work in continuous- and discrete-time models. Simulated runs show good finite-sample behavior across realistic settings. Applied to excess stock returns, the tests find the dividend-price ratio has predictive power, while the earnings-price ratio does not forecast significantly.
arxiv-2511-09349:
Dhananjaya Mahapatra and three co-authors measure how orbital currents in light metals exert torque on a neighboring magnet. The orbital Hall effect generates flows of orbital angular momentum, a younger cousin of the spin Hall effect. Their samples pair titanium films with nickel, measured through second-harmonic voltages under alternating current.

Inserting a copper layer between the nickel and titanium boosts both the orbital torque efficiency and a related magnetoresistance signal. Both effects also grow with titanium thickness, pointing to a bulk origin in the titanium layer rather than the interface alone. Cooling the samples clearly reduces both quantities, with a nearly linear, correlated temperature dependence. That shared behavior ties both effects to the orbital Hall effect.
arxiv-2511-09449:
Remi Luschei and Werner Brannath examine error control in clinical trials that test tailored treatments across overlapping patient populations. When several populations and treatment policies are involved, one false claim can affect many groups. Trials therefore control the family-wise error rate, the chance of rejecting at least one true null hypothesis.

Standard adjustments exploit the joint distribution of test statistics under analysis-of-variance assumptions. The authors show those procedures are valid only when null effects are homogeneous across every subpopulation and intersection. When heterogeneous effects cancel out, the usual procedure fails to control the error rate, they demonstrate. They propose alternative procedures and compare them on both error control and statistical power.
arxiv-2511-09549:
Daniel Platnick and four co-authors compare two ways for greedy planners to escape regions where the heuristic gives no guidance. Plateaus and local minima trap methods like Greedy Best-First Search and Enforced Hill-Climbing. The standard escape is breadth-first search; the challenger restarts random walks until one finds an exit.

The team derives expected escape runtimes for both strategies from properties of the trapped region and the walk procedure. Those formulas identify when random walks win in expectation. Experiments on PDDL planning benchmarks compare standard Enforced Hill-Climbing against walk-based variants. The walk variant keeps strong runtime guarantees where the classical method was already known to work. That clarifies when each escape strategy deserves use.
arxiv-2511-09649:
Joey Braspenning, Joop Schaye, Annalisa Pillepich, and Dylan Nelson hunt for what makes galaxy clusters scatter around their X-ray luminosity-halo mass relation. Clusters trace large-scale structure, and the relation is tight, but its scatter's origin was hard to pin down statistically. Two huge simulation suites, FLAMINGO and TNG, finally provide the volume.

The models agree qualitatively but differ in detail, the authors find. Among twenty-three extra properties tested, two correlate most strongly with the scatter. The gas fraction and the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich signal cut it by over half when included. Galaxy and halo properties help only modestly. The team provides fitting formulas so observers can correct the scatter in cosmological analyses directly.
arxiv-2511-10049:
Divyanshu Saxena and nine co-authors argue that benchmarks for enterprise AI agents must be generated continuously rather than fixed once. Fixed test sets suit simple coding tasks, but enterprise agents face evolving services, shifting requirements, and sparse ground truth. Their process builds fresh benchmarks as requirements change, starting from semi-structured documents where developers state high-level intent for a migration or service.

State-of-the-art language models turn a small number of such documents into evaluation cases. The authors demonstrate the approach on a real case: migrating a service between deployment platforms at a large public enterprise. The result is a maintainable evaluation framework that gives rapid feedback on agent performance and points improvements at the right targets as the underlying platform keeps moving.
arxiv-2511-10149:
Arani Maiti and five co-authors study how light beams shift sideways when they reflect off a corrugated silver surface near surface plasmon resonance. These tiny displacements, the Goos-Hänchen and Imbert-Fedorov shifts, grow large near resonance because the reflection coefficient changes rapidly there, an effect the authors frame through weak value amplification. Corrugation lets incoming light couple naturally to surface excitations.

By choosing the incoming and projected polarization states carefully, they produced a pronounced spatial spin Hall effect of light. Vortex beams showed their own distinctive shift signatures tied to angular momentum, and the analysis also covers conical diffraction with full mixing between polarization states. The work ties spin-orbit interaction of light to plasmonics for nanoscale light control.
arxiv-2511-10249:
Fabian Ihle, Moritz Flüchter, and Michael Menth implement the time-aware shaper of time-sensitive networking on a programmable switch chip. The shaper opens and closes output queues on a schedule to protect time-critical traffic, but commercial switches hide the internal delays of that mechanism, which quietly degrade scheduling precision. Their P4-TAS runs on an Intel Tofino 2 processor and adds per-stream filtering, policing, and precision time synchronization.

A stream of internally generated control frames drives the periodic queue updates. This enables the shaper on a P4 device for the first time, at line rates up to four hundred gigabits per port. The team measured three internal delay sources, totaling a worst case of eighty-six nanoseconds between slices, well below commercial reports, and proposed measurement methods plus guard intervals for designers.
arxiv-2511-10749:
Inés García-Redondo and five co-authors generalize effective resistance, a concept born in electrical circuit theory, from graphs to the richer setting of simplicial complexes. On a graph, effective resistance between two vertices measures the opposition to a unit current and quietly encodes the graph's structure, its geometry, and even spanning tree probabilities.

Earlier generalizations to complexes were written as matrix products that depend on a chosen basis. This paper instead defines a basis-independent bilinear form from an algebraic reading of circuit theory. It then extends the form to simplices, chains, and cochains, unifying all the existing matrix formulations. The authors prove higher-order versions of the classic properties, including that resistance induces a metric on cycles, and a generalization of Foster's theorem to simplicial complexes.
arxiv-2511-11149:
Christopher Thorpe and Elena Gramellini introduce a new way to estimate neutrino energy in liquid-argon detectors, where pinning down that energy is central to precise oscillation studies. Their estimator rests on the measured mass of the hadronic debris left after a neutrino hits. It is aimed at broad beams that cross the hard zone between shallow and deep scattering regimes.

Against four common estimators, theirs showed the smallest bias across true energies in a toy long-baseline study. It also stayed steady when key inputs such as lepton angle, missing energy, and final-state effects were modeled wrong. The trade-off is somewhat worse resolution when modeling is perfect.
arxiv-2511-11749:
Almond Kiruthu Murimi reviews how machine learning can make data copying in large systems adaptive. Copies keep data safe when machines fail. Static plans fix copy counts and places in advance. They waste resources in quiet times. They can still leave data exposed when loads shift or machines die.

The proposed path uses predictive analytics and reinforcement learning. Failures are forecast ahead of time. Copies are moved or added in real time where risk is rising. A literature review weighs this path against older strategies. Their limits are listed in detail. For cloud operators, learning-based copying promises less downtime and better storage use.
arxiv-2511-11849:
Junyang He and four co-authors test which extra information actually helps forecast river flow from rainfall, using the CAMELS-US dataset covering six hundred seventy-one American catchments. Time series foundation models promise general skill, but hydrology is a physical downstream task where domain knowledge may beat generality.

Models given comprehensive known exogenous inputs, including natural annual periodic series, beat more limited approaches and the foundation models themselves. Six data streams and thirty static catchment features frame the comparison. For water managers, the message is practical: carefully chosen physical inputs still outperform fashionable general models, and forecasting studies should test foundation models on real downstream tasks, not only benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-12249:
Khang T. Huynh, Dung H. Nguyen and Binh T. Nguyen present ViConBERT, a model for Vietnamese word meanings in context. Most progress on sense-aware embeddings has come in English, while Vietnamese lacks strong models and test resources. Words with several senses are a hard case, since the right meaning depends on the sentence around them.

ViConBERT learns embeddings with contrastive training and with distillation from dictionary glosses, so senses are tied to definitions. The team also builds ViConWSD, a large synthetic dataset for word sense and similarity tests in Vietnamese. Results beat strong baselines on sense disambiguation and stay competitive on graded similarity measures.
arxiv-2511-12349:
Divya Kiran Kadiyala and Alexandros Daglis propose SURGE, a technique to ease the memory bandwidth wall in server processors. As core counts rise, the pins that carry data off the chip do not keep pace, so each core gets less memory bandwidth. In typical designs about half the off-chip bandwidth is reserved for input-output traffic, whether or not it is busy.

SURGE harvests that idle input-output bandwidth for memory traffic, using a flexible interconnect technology known as CXL that can reroute links dynamically. Software support helps decide when to shift capacity. The goal is bandwidth that can be spent in whichever form, memory or input-output, a workload actually needs.
arxiv-2511-12649:
Georgy L. Alfimov, Pavel A. Korchagin, and Dmitry E. Pelinovsky examine localized waves that sit still on a lattice, known as intrinsic localized modes. Their model is the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation with two competing power nonlinearities, a focusing one and a defocusing one at higher power. They focus on three physically relevant pairs of powers. In a limiting case where sites decouple, every localized mode can be labeled by a code that records its pattern of states and signs.

Using spectral stability analysis, the authors prove that codes built from the larger states with one sign are both spectrally and nonlinearly stable. Codes from the smaller, sign-alternating states are spectrally stable but carry eigenvalues of negative Krein signature, a warning sign for stability. Computer work then identifies which stacked mixtures of the two kinds remain spectrally stable.
arxiv-2511-12749:
Zong-Han Bai and Po-Yen Chu ask when pooling information across many sparse demand series actually helps a forecast. Retailers must predict intermittent demand, where most periods sell nothing. A forecaster decides how much of each item's past to keep and how much to borrow from related items. In their hierarchical Bayesian hurdle model, one forgetting rule applied at both levels turns those two choices into a single decision with two opposing effects.

Forgetting keeps a shared prior influential, but raises the noise that fine differences must rise above. The authors turn that trade-off into a diagnostic that screens, in advance, for cases where refining pools cannot pay. On five public panels with over nineteen thousand series, the diagnostic was right both ways. One panel with room to improve resisted, which they flag as an open problem.
arxiv-2511-13049:
Antoine Ledent, Mun Chong Soo, and Nong Minh Hieu bound the error of recommender systems that learn from clicks as well as ratings. In their matrix completion setting, both the true preference matrix and the distribution deciding which entries get observed are low rank and share a subspace. Abundant unlabeled data, the implicit feedback of clicks and purchases, comes from that distribution, while labeled explicit ratings are scarce and noisy. Combining low-rank subspace recovery with classic generalization theory, they prove an error bound with two terms, one shrinking with the unlabeled sample size and one with the labeled.

Synthetic experiments confirm the error really splits that way, and on Douban and MovieLens, with most ratings removed, their method beat baselines using explicit ratings alone. The theory formalizes the intuition that implicit feedback carries real information about preferences.
arxiv-2511-13549:
Rayirth Bhat, Justin R. David, and Semanti Dutta test holographic entanglement formulas with vector excitations in three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. They quantize a massive Chern-Simons field and compute its single-particle states' effect on entanglement entropy across a Ryu-Takayanagi surface. The correction is evaluated at the first sub-leading order in Newton's constant.

The lowest state matches a spin-one primary operator in the dual field theory, with the rest forming its descendant tower. Their entropy from the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula agrees exactly with a replica-trick calculation in the dual theory at leading and sub-leading order. A careful check shows the edge mode adds nothing after vacuum subtraction, which the match requires.
arxiv-2511-13849:
Duncan Farrah and 25 co-authors ask how well astronomers can measure the brightness of dusty, infrared-bright galaxies. Such galaxies build stars and black holes, but their power is usually estimated by fitting model curves to infrared data points. The team used simulated observations of a well-studied nearby sample to test how each choice in the data affects the answer.

They find that covering the peak of a galaxy's infrared output, with dense sampling, matters most, keeping bias under about twenty percent for starburst and active nucleus power. Host galaxy light is harder and usually comes out too low. Their tables of bias and error can guide work with JWST and future far-infrared missions.
arxiv-2511-14249:
Rui Liu, Yuan Zhao, and Zhenqi Jia argue that automatic movie dubbing sounds fake because it skips the director. Real dubbing starts with directors feeding actors reference footage so they absorb a scene's emotion before performing. Their system, Authentic-Dubber, rebuilds that director-actor loop around a multimodal reference footage library.

Language models help the system grasp emotional content across the library's signals. At dub time, an emotion-similarity retrieval step pulls the reference material closest to the target silent clip. The generated voice then matches both the speaker's timbre and the intended feeling, while keeping lip sync. A progressive learning scheme ties the pieces together toward more authentic dubbed performances.
arxiv-2511-14349:
Junfu Pu, Teng Wang, Yixiao Ge, and three co-authors cut hour-long videos into navigable chapters with summaries at several levels. Lectures, podcasts, and documentaries are hard to browse, and earlier chaptering tools trained on small sets with short, coarse labels that missed subtle transitions. ARC-Chapter is a model trained on more than a million long-video chapters with bilingual, time-grounded, hierarchical annotations.

The training data were built by unifying speech transcripts, on-screen text, and visual captions into multi-level labels from short titles to long summaries. A new metric, GRACE, rewards flexible many-to-one segment matching plus semantic similarity. Experiments show large gains over the previous best and strong transfer to new domains.
arxiv-2511-14549:
Su Yang, Sathyanarayanan Chandramouli, and Panayotis Kevrekidis study dispersive shock waves in periodic lattices. Such waves appear in optical waveguide arrays and in superfluids held in optical lattices. The model is a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a periodic potential. Initial data join two distinct nonlinear periodic modes in a piecewise smooth way.

A tight binding approximation reduces the system to a discrete model with a Riemann problem. Each constant state stands for a Floquet-Bloch mode of the full system. The reduction works best for deeper potentials. The authors then apply Whitham modulation theory to interpret the wave dynamics. The framework links lattice physics to classic shock wave analysis.
arxiv-2511-14749:
Alexander Vedernikov, Puneet Kumar, and three co-authors use vision-language models to clean up noisy labels in student engagement videos. Judging engagement from video is subjective, so training labels often disagree, and that noise caps how well detectors can learn. The team lets a large vision model do the first pass at quality control.

A questionnaire draws behavioral cues from each clip, and clips are split into high- and low-reliability groups. Training then follows a curriculum: clean clips first, doubtful clips later with softened labels that reflect the doubt. Classic vision models trained this way improve on the raw data. The lesson is that strong models can serve as noise handlers for weaker ones.
arxiv-2511-14849:
Adeel Mahmood and Aaron B. Wagner refine the theory of sending information over a noisy Gaussian channel under detailed power limits. Real transmitters face more than a simple average power cap: peaks and other traits of the power pattern can each be limited. The authors model this with a general setup where any finite set of power statistics can be constrained at once.

Through a careful higher-order analysis, they characterize the best possible error rate as a function of the main coding rates. Older limits, from the plain maximum power rule to recent mean-and-variance rules, fall out as special cases. Sharper limits tell engineers how close practical codes can come to perfect on power-limited links.
arxiv-2511-15049:
Antonio Enea Romano shows how dark energy perturbations can be encoded as an effective coupling between matter and gravity. Dark energy is expected to perturb and thus alter how cosmic structures evolve. Romano finds that effect can be written as a coupling that depends on momentum, position, and polarization. That compact encoding clarifies several observational consequences at once.

For scalar perturbations the effective coupling can turn locally negative where dark energy is underdense. With phantom dark energy it can also explain suppressed structure growth at low redshift. For gravitational waves the coupling makes emitted radiation depend on polarization and frequency. The framework ties evolving dark energy hints to concrete, testable signatures in structure and wave data.
arxiv-2511-15749:
S. Preethi, Ankush Kamboj, Ramkarn Patne, P. A. L. Narayana, and Kirti Chandra Sahu find a new instability in a thin liquid layer driven by wind at its top and rotation at its base. The setup mimics ocean surface flows shaped by wind stress and Earth rotation. Stability analysis asks which small disturbances grow instead of fading, and the linearized problem is solved both numerically and with a long-wave approximation.

New long-wave unstable modes appear whenever the rotation measure is nonzero. The most unstable mode uses disturbances that vary across the flow but not along it, and it becomes unstable at the lowest parameter values. The approximation matches the numerics well and confirms the mode analytically, showing a combined wind and rotation effect not reported before.
arxiv-2511-15849:
Batya Kenig extends a key tool of parameterized algorithms to problems that must cut some links while keeping others intact. Important separators are minimal vertex cuts with a maximality property that keeps the set of useful cuts small enough to list. Cut-uncut problems add a demand: a chosen terminal set must stay linked to the source side. Standard separators ignore that demand.

Kenig defines connectivity-preserving important separators and bounds how many of bounded size can exist. A listing algorithm enumerates them in terms of a min-cut subroutine. Uses include better bounds for mixed multiway cut-uncut problems and a faster method for an annotated odd cycle problem with protected terminals.
arxiv-2511-16249:
Zihao Liu and six co-authors present controllable layer decomposition for reversible multi layer image creation. Designers build images layer by layer, but once layers are flattened into one raster, layer level editing is lost. Matting and inpainting methods recover layers only with limited control and precision. Their method separates a raster image into distinct editable layers with fine grained control.

A dedicated decomposition transformer decouples elements into layers. A multi layer conditional adapter injects target image information into layer tokens for precise conditional creation. A new benchmark and tailored metrics support comprehensive evaluation. Reversible decomposition would let editors revise finished artwork structurally. The work targets design workflows where layer structure is creative capital, not disposable metadata.
arxiv-2511-16749:
Shivani Harer and a large LISA test-bench team report validation of an optical interferometer demonstrator built for the LISA gravitational wave observatory. LISA is a European Space Agency mission set to launch in the mid-2030s with arms millions of kilometers long. The space detector needs picometer path length stability, and ground demonstrators must prove the technology first.

The Zerodur interferometer, called ZIFO, reduced bench noise enough to hold the needed stability specification across the millihertz to one hertz band. The team also identified and characterized the dominant remaining noise sources, including phasemeter noise and beam tilt leaking into the path length readout. The results validate critical technology for the test setup of LISA's interferometric core.
arxiv-2511-17149:
Marius Ghergu and Zhe Yu analyze what can happen at a single singular point of an elliptic equation set in a punctured ball, a domain with its center removed. Their first question is integrability. For a differential inequality with a nonnegative, radially symmetric potential, they find optimal conditions under which any smooth solution, and the terms built from it, remain integrable up to the missing point. That extends a 1982 result of Brezis and Lions, which covered only constant potentials.

Their second question concerns a nonlinear equation whose right-hand side involves a convolution, a weighted average of the solution's powers with a singular kernel. For dimensions three and up, they give sharp conditions on the exponents for singular solutions to exist, and describe exactly how those solutions blow up near the origin. The two-dimensional case is classified separately.
arxiv-2511-17249:
Riccardo Tedoldi and five co-authors present FlexiFlow, a generative model for drug discovery that designs a molecule and its shapes together. A molecule's three-dimensional conformations govern its properties and how tightly it can bind a protein target, yet leading design models produce only a single conformation. FlexiFlow extends flow matching so it samples a molecule jointly with an ensemble of its low-energy shapes, while respecting the symmetries the physics demands.

On the QM9 and GEOM Drugs benchmarks, the model generated valid, unstrained, novel molecules that matched the training distribution closely. Its conformational ensembles covered the relevant shapes about as well as established physics-based methods, at a fraction of the computing time. The model also transferred to designing ligands for a given protein pocket, even when training data lacked conformations for that task.
arxiv-2511-17349:
Christoph L. Schröder and Harvey B. Meyer develop coordinate-space perturbation theory for quantum field theories that contain a single mass scale. Working in Euclidean space of general dimension, they expand in Gegenbauer polynomials and derive analytic expressions for several three-point correlation functions in theories mixing one massive and one massless field. The technical core is a systematic study of antiderivatives of products of Bessel functions times powers of their argument.

Such results serve calculations with high-degree vertices, at finite temperature or in finite volume, and auxiliary computations for lattice treatments of hadronic effects in precision observables. As an illustration, the authors compute the one-loop propagator of a massive particle coupled to a massless one, in vacuum and at finite temperature. The paper is a toolkit contribution for perturbative quantum field theory.
arxiv-2511-17449:
Machine-learned interatomic potentials have become the default tool for atomistic simulations that do not track electrons explicitly. Standard guidance warns that these models need exhaustive training sets and must not be used beyond the training space. That confines them to interpolation and rules out finding new phenomena by luck. Iñigo Robredo-Magro and three co-authors take a more sanguine view and test two widely used approaches with minimalist training sets.

Their training sets rest on little prior knowledge of the materials, and the models use modest default settings. Even so, the models predict non-trivial structural effects correctly, in quality and nearly in quantity. The effects include competing polymorphs, energy barriers for structural changes, and non-trivial topologies. The authors argue that such cheap, easy models can serve as tools for finding novel and complex physical phenomena, not just for filling in known ground.
arxiv-2511-17649:
Juntao Cheng and nine co-authors introduce SWITCH, a benchmark for agents that must operate physical control panels over long stretches. Panels, remotes, lifts, and built-in screens fill daily life, and using them takes more than spotting a button: an agent must act. Watch the state change, and check whether the goal was reached. Older tests mostly grade single steps or passive looking, missing that loop.

SWITCH holds over a thousand interactive videos shot from a first-person view across many kinds of device. Each is labelled with instructions, actions, state changes, outcomes, and recovery moves when things go wrong. The set also probes whether models can picture how a scene evolves. For builders of household and workplace agents, it offers a far sterner test than one-step benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-17849:
Shuyuan Fan and Zhao Zhang present Pier, a training method that cuts the global communication slowing down pretraining of large language models. Synchronizing many processors often dominates cost, so Pier builds on an approach that syncs less often, with local training steps in between.

Two fixes to the outer update, warming up its momentum and then decaying it, keep training stable and preserve model quality. Across GPT models of several sizes, Pier speeds training several fold on large graphics clusters, with no loss on validation or on a suite of downstream tasks. The design also supports mixing data and tensor parallelism.
arxiv-2511-17949:
Ali Jafari, Mohamed Mousa, and Mostafa Nouh build logic gates out of sound waves traveling in a solid, so computation happens mechanically without converting signals to electronics. Earlier mechanical logic relied on slow shape changes or active materials, limiting speed.

Using topology optimization to search a huge design space, they carve voids into a uniform plate so waves interfere and concentrate energy at readouts that encode a logic function. Experiments confirm the gates work and tolerate uneven loading. By combining gates into a mechanical adder, they show the approach can scale toward larger signal processing circuits with very low power needs.
arxiv-2511-18149:
Kingshuk Adhikary, Darren Moore, and Radim Filip show how to create quantum states of an oscillator that carry coherence, a genuinely quantum feature, using only absorption of single quanta. Linear absorption through a saturable system can make non Gaussian states, but they merely approach simple number states and show no coherence.

Adding a minimal nonlinear absorption process changes the picture.
