It would also help teams guess sensor life in hard ray fields. The work serves groups who build tools for big test halls.
arxiv-2601-16349:
Gopinadh and coauthors test for place bias in large language models. Their 2026 preprint deals with fair acts of such models. Place bias means a model treats folk or facts by place in a slanted way. Slants can stem from the text hoards the model learned from. The team probes model replies for place tied slants.

Probes span prompts that vary place cues in set ways. Slants found in replies mark where guards are needed. Fair tools must serve users of all places with same care. The study gives a check list for place bias in new models. It comes from a team based in Andhra Pradesh, India.
arxiv-2601-16549:
Meet Raval, Tejul Pandit and Dhvani Upadhyay weigh ML and base models for med sorts. Their 2026 preprint deals with sorts that join pics and text. New vision and language tools open fresh paths for such sorts. Past tests oft span few sets or one data type. A fair test must span both text and pic sets at once.

The team runs one strict test on four open med sets. Sets span both types and both two class and more class sorts. Joint scores show where each tool type leads or lags. That map guides teams to the right tool per task. The work is a shared bench for med sorts.
arxiv-2601-16649:
Amin Rakhsha and a team at Qualcomm AI Research study AI agents that act over long spans. Large language models do well on short, single tasks. They still fail on jobs that run through many turns. Such jobs need plans, memory of state, and long text in mind. The team's 2026 preprint probes why these jobs stay hard.

The study asks which skill counts most for success. It weighs the worth of plans, state tracking, and long context use. The aim is to learn where gains will help most. That guide can shape how labs train the next agents. It also helps buyers judge what agents can truly do.
arxiv-2601-16749:
Pedro Picchetti builds a clean frame for cause work in two hard trial types. Some trials give each unit a mix of more than one cure. Others track the same units through time in steps. In both, some units skip their set cure. Their 2026 preprint sets out cause marks for such trials as fixed pools.

Fixed-pool marks treat the test crowd as the whole world. No vast unseen crowd sits in the back. The marks gauge how cure chains stack up. Which chain works best is the core ask. Clean marks help drug and policy trials read right. They curb claims that reach past the test crowd.
arxiv-2601-17049:
Christina Garcia and a team of six co-authors sum a contest on spot-the-odd-act tools. The contest ran at ISAS 2025 with pose data as its base. Pose data tracks body joints with no face shots. Care homes for folks with growth traits need such tools. Odd acts there can flag harm or pain fast. Their 2026 preprint sums how teams fared on the task.

Teams had to split plain acts from odd ones. Plain acts span meals, play, and rest moves. No-touch pose reads guard the privacy of those in care. Contest sums show what works and what fails. Homes gain a guide to tools that truly help.
arxiv-2601-17549:
Narek Maloyan and Dmitry Namiot give the first formal security analysis of the Model Context Protocol. MCP is now a common standard. It links language models to outside tools. No one had checked its design for flaws in a rigorous way. The authors find three protocol-level vulnerabilities. They call them fundamental, tied to the design itself.

Design flaws are worse than code bugs. Every tool built on the spec may share them. Prompt injection is a key concern in the study. Tool-linked models act on files and apps, so stakes are high. The analysis gives vendors a fix list. It also warns users to guard MCP links today.
arxiv-2601-17649:
Xiaoli Han and Yang Wen prove that weakly stable Yang-Mills fields cannot exist near the round sphere metric. Yang-Mills fields model gauge forces in physics and geometry. Weak stability is a mild calm trait for such fields. The authors look at the Euclidean sphere in five or more dimensions. Near its usual metric, in the C2 topology, no nontrivial weakly stable connections exist for any nearby metric.

A nonexistence result is a strong guide. It tells geometers not to hunt where nothing lives. It also sharpens what makes the sphere special. Stability questions drive much of gauge theory. This proof trims the search space in a clean way. Nearby metrics inherit the ban, which adds force.
arxiv-2601-17749:
Kyriakos Stylianopoulos and co-authors build over-the-air extreme learning machines with metasurfaces. Goal-oriented communication sends data for a task, not for its own sake. Inference can run right in the physical layer of MIMO systems. That in-air computing faces hard practical challenges. Their design uses nonlinear cascaded metasurfaces with extra-large reception.

Metasurfaces shape radio waves as they pass. Cascades can act like layers of a neural network. If inference rides the wave itself, delay and energy can drop. The work joins antenna design with machine learning. It points to radios that compute while they listen. Such fusion could serve dense 6G networks.
arxiv-2601-17949: Wenjie Fang studies a new statistic on Dyck paths called 0pt. His 2026 preprint places the statistic among the q,t-Catalan statistics, a family tied to counting path shapes. The 0pt statistic was proposed by Pappe, Paul, and Schilling in 2022. It was shown to share its joint distribution with the well-known area statistic. Fang extends the study to Łukasiewicz paths, a broader class of lattice paths.
arxiv-2601-18149:
Tomokazu Kiyota and a large team catalog faint dusty galaxies with the JWST telescope. Their 2026 preprint reports a spectroscopic census in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field. The targets are sources first seen at one millimeter by the ALMA telescope under deep survey programs. The team took rest-frame optical spectra of a flux-limited sample with JWST's NIRSpec instrument. Such spectra reveal star birth, gas state, and black hole activity in galaxies too faint for older tools.

A census ties the dusty, far-off population into the wider story of galaxy growth. Many of these galaxies hide behind dust that blocks normal light. Pairing ALMA's finds with JWST's spectra opens them up. The sample sets a base for studies of early, hidden star formation.
arxiv-2601-18349:
Piotr Bacik and Anton Varonka take on two linked asks in the maths of change and reach. The first ask is old: start with a point, apply a fixed rule again and again, and ask if the path ever hits a set mark. When the mark is one point, past work showed the ask can be solved, and fast. Later work stretched that proof to wider marks.

The pair look at a harder form in which the space is cut by a rule at the same time. They also take on a twin ask about paths that must hit more than one mark in step. These asks sit at the base of checks on code and on plans that must be safe. A firm yes or no here helps prove that a design can or cannot reach a bad state.
arxiv-2601-18449:
Mrinmoy Basak and three colleagues set up a fresh frame to study a classic toy world of quantum fields. The toy world has one space dim and one kind of field that pulls on it-self. Staff have long used it to test tricks that fail on the full world of bits and force. The team build the frame from small wave bits that live in push space, not in plain space.

Each wave bit is tagged by how fine it is and by where it sits. That double tag gives a built-in way to trim both the fine end and the broad end of the field. A trim that maths can trust is key for work that skips small-step tricks. The frame could let teams study strong pulls with less guess work. It may also serve as a test bed for new quantum kit.
arxiv-2601-18549:
Elvise Berchio and three colleagues study how heat-like spread runs on webs that go on for ever. The webs are sets of points with links, like road nets or power grids stretched with no end. On such a web, a value at each point can spread to its linked points and can grow or fade by a rule that leans on the value it-self. The team take on two kinds of rule.

One kind of rule is tame in a set way, and the next is tame in a rate way. For both, they prove that a start state leads to one sound path, and they chart how smooth that path is. The start can be quite rough and still give a good path. Such proofs back the use of web maths for heat, crowds, and spread on huge nets.
arxiv-2601-18749:
Haruhiko Yoshioka and six colleagues study what makes a code change count, for both human hands and smart agents. Code hosts now fill with change asks made by agents. Those asks are fast and cheap to make, but they are merged at a lower rate than asks by human hands. The team ask why, in a large study of past asks from a shared data set.

Their set holds tens of thousands of asks, by both kinds of maker. They weigh traits such as size, tests, and the words that go with each ask. Traits that track with a merge for one kind may not track for the next. A clear map could help agent teams write asks that land. It could also help hosts set fair bars for all makers.
arxiv-2601-18949:
Cole Granger and three co-authors build a test set where human bugs and model bugs mix. Large language models now help write code, but they add sly logic slips that differ from the slips people make. To study how the two kinds of error play off each other, the team made a hybrid set.

The new set, Tricky squared, grows an older corpus of human written defects. Two large models then inject fresh errors into code in three languages. The mix lets researchers see when model bugs hide near human ones, and when each kind is caught or missed by checks.
arxiv-2601-19249:
Xingkun Yin and Hongyang Du check the memories of language model agents against a changing world. Memory boosted models store notes to guide later acts. Most systems assume those notes can be validated, either by outside scores tied to one task or by the model's own reflection.

In live settings with drifting facts, both assumptions often break. Their verifier, GLOVE, realigns stored memory with the environment as it now stands. Stale memory is a quiet failure mode for agents: they act with confidence on facts that used to be true.
arxiv-2601-19449:
Celia Rubio-Madrigal and Rebekka Burkholz show that fixed features can match graph neural networks at their own game. Graph networks are prized for learning how to pool each node's neighborhood. The team challenges that belief with fixed aggregation features: set summaries of a neighborhood that need no training at all.

Their approach turns graph tasks into table tasks, where classic classifiers take over. The gains are strong interpretability and free choice of classifier. If much of a graph network's power sits in the features, simpler and clearer tools may serve many graph jobs just as well.
arxiv-2601-19549:
Fengling Li, Andrei Vesnin, and Xuan Yang work in knotoid theory, a young branch of knot theory. Knotoids are like knots drawn with open ends, a generalisation proposed by Turaev in 2012. Researchers have since built many ways to measure and classify them. This paper focuses on how hard a knotoid is to undo.

The measure is the unknotting number: the fewest unknotting moves needed to simplify the knotoid fully. The authors study this count for a class called plus-welded knotoids. Knowing the count tells us how tangled an object truly is, beyond how tangled it looks. Such numbers are basic data for any classification effort. The work adds to the slow build of knotoid theory's core tables.
arxiv-2601-19849:
Haya Alyoussef and five colleagues build a vision transformer that lives in curved space. Much real data is hierarchical: images, text, and graphs all contain tree-like structure. Flat Euclidean geometry represents such structure poorly. Hyperbolic geometry, which expands exponentially, fits trees naturally.

Their model, HexFormer, is a hyperbolic vision transformer for image classification. Its key novelty is aggregation using the exponential map inside the attention mechanism. Attention decides which parts of an image inform each other. Doing that step in hyperbolic space should respect hierarchical relations among features. The work tests whether curved geometry earns its keep on vision benchmarks. The tests are plain image tasks. They sort cats, cars, and the like into groups. The scores show how well it works.
arxiv-2601-19949:
A speech corpus paper tackles a long-standing comparison problem in reverberant speech research. Echoey rooms distort recordings and challenge recognition systems. Comparing methods across studies is hard because most corpora lack per-file acoustic annotations. Documentation for reproducing results is often thin as well.

The new corpus, RIR-Mega-Speech, pairs speech with rich acoustic metadata. It was built by convolving LibriSpeech recordings with thousands of simulated room impulse responses from a companion collection. The result is over a hundred hours of reverberant speech with known room properties. Every file's acoustics are documented, and the evaluation is reproducible. Such a corpus lets researchers isolate what really helps in echoey conditions. Each file comes with notes on the room that made it. That is rare in this field. It makes fair tests much more easy to run.
arxiv-2601-20049: A methods paper presents a new data assimilation scheme built for ice and snow science. Particle-based assimilation tracks many candidate states and weights them by fit to data, but the method can collapse onto a few states. The new scheme is an adaptive particle batch smoother that draws on recent advances in importance sampling to resist that collapse. Though built for cryospheric problems, it applies directly to land surface and hydrological assimilation, and to geoscience inference more broadly.
arxiv-2601-20349:
A. A. Saharian and three colleagues study topological defects in higher-dimensional cosmological backgrounds. These backgrounds are described by a set of angle deficit parameters. As special cases, the defects include higher-dimensional versions of cosmic strings and global monopoles, flaws in spacetime that may have formed in the early universe.

The authors present the complete set of mode functions for a massive scalar field in these settings. The field has a general coupling to curvature. Mode functions are the building blocks for computing quantum effects near the defects, such as vacuum energy. With them, researchers test how quantum fields behave in curved space.
arxiv-2601-20449:
Fatima Ezzeddine, Obaida Ammar, Silvia Giordano, and Omran Ayoub study fairness in counterfactual explanations of machine learning decisions. Such explanations tell a user which changes to their inputs would flip a model's decision, offering a path to recourse. They hold a pivotal place among explanation tools because they point to action.

The authors aim to ensure fairness at both the individual and group levels. Recourse that is cheap for one group and costly for another quietly bakes bias into the system. Their work matters for lending, hiring, and other fields where a denied applicant deserves a fair route back.
arxiv-2601-20549:
Wies Claeys and ten colleagues compare radionuclide calibrators and SPECT/CT protocols for quantitative imaging of lutetium-177 across multiple centers. Therapies based on this isotope now succeed against neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer. Accurate measurement of the dose is a first need for correct treatment delivery and dosimetry.

Yet a lack of standardization introduces variability between systems, which can compromise multi-center clinical trials. The authors compare how centers measure and image the same isotope. Harmonized protocols would let hospitals pool results and give patients doses that mean the same thing everywhere. Each site was checked in the same way, so the gaps that show up are real gaps, not quirks of one lab.
arxiv-2601-20749:
Tawfiq Ammari and three co-authors study how students learn to work with AI in daily life. Their 2026 paper asks how AI literacy grows through practice, not formal lessons. The team analyzed more than ten thousand ChatGPT messages. The messages came from thirty-six undergraduates over one academic year. That long view shows real habits, not lab behavior.

The authors find five genres of use in the chats. Students used the tool as an academic workhorse and as an emotional companion. They also used it as a partner for thinking, for repair and negotiation, and for calibrating trust. Each genre is a distinct way students learn to work with AI. The study gives teachers a grounded picture of skills students build on their own.
arxiv-2601-20849:
Yapeng Zhang and a large team measure fierce winds on a scorching giant planet. Their 2026 paper studies KELT-9 b, an ultra-hot Jupiter. Fine spectroscopy can probe the air of such a planet. It reads Doppler shifts in the planet's signal. Those shifts change as the planet moves through its orbit. The team used the Keck Planet Finder.

The study is a pilot run on phase curve spectra. A phase curve tracks the planet across its full orbit. The emerging dayside is where night turns to day. Winds there can reach extreme speeds. Measuring them tests models of air flow on worlds with huge day-night gaps. The work shows what the new tool can do.
arxiv-2601-21149:
Maria Despoina Siampou and four co-authors teach a model both what a place is and how it is used. Their 2026 paper learns embeddings for points of interest from human movement. Such models need general-purpose pictures of real places. Points of interest, where activity piles up, matter most. Old approaches lean on static text about place identity. Or they tie the picture to paths, which capture movement habits. Neither captures a place's function well.

Movement data can reveal function at once. A site busy at dawn differs from one busy at night. Visit rhythms show if a place serves work, food, or rest. The authors embed that usage in the model. Their model knows a cafe from an office by rhythm, not just by name. Such embeddings can power maps, tips, and city planning.
arxiv-2601-21249:
Enzo Nicolás Spotorno and Antônio Augusto Medeiros Fröhlich argue that big unified models are a risky fit for safety-critical physical systems. Foundation models now handle time series and physical change well in smooth, slow settings. Real systems, though, shift over their life cycle and must meet strict reliability demands.

The authors make a position case for a modular design instead. Separate parts hold their own state, and that state can be checked and certified. A single large model must stay flexible yet stable, and the paper calls that tension the core problem. Modularity, they argue, is how both needs can be met at once.
arxiv-2601-21749:
Laurent R. Bergé, Kyle Butts, and Grant McDermott present fixest, an R package for fast econometric estimation. The package covers a wide toolkit for applied researchers. Its strength is fixed-effects estimation, a workhorse for panel data across economics and policy work.

A new fixed-point acceleration algorithm, written in a fast compiled language, drives the speed. It converges quickly across many data settings and handles complex models, even ones with varying slopes. Fast estimation changes what researchers can try in a day. Models that once ran overnight become interactive, which invites more careful checking of results.
arxiv-2601-21949:
Christian Schröder and co-authors watch a molecule vibrate in step right after its bond breaks. When methyl iodide absorbs ultraviolet light, it splits and releases a methyl radical. That radical comes out excited in its umbrella mode, a flapping motion where the hydrogens swing through the carbon's plane.

The team reports observing these vibrations staying coherent, moving together in phase, after the break. They probe the motion with femtosecond spectroscopy, which snapshots events lasting millionths of a billionth of a second. Their 2026 preprint shows that a violent break does not always scramble molecular motion. That matters for photochemistry, where coherent motion can steer which products a reaction forms.
arxiv-2601-22149:
Hang Ding and co-authors train web agents inside a model of the web instead of the web itself. Autonomous agents powered by language models and reinforcement learning promise general-purpose assistance online. Training them on the live internet is inefficient, costly, and risky, since real sites change, charge, and sometimes bite back.

Their 2026 preprint, DynaWeb, applies model-based reinforcement learning to web agents. The agent learns a world model of web dynamics and practices inside it, reserving real browsing for what matters. Model-based practice has transformed game and robot learning. Bringing it to the web could produce agents that are both more capable and far cheaper to train.
arxiv-2601-22249:
Ruiyi Zhang and four co-authors tackle a weak spot in code written by large language models. Their 2026 preprint notes that these models still fail often on hard coding tasks. They build on an idea that worked well for math: score each step, then pick the best full try.

Their method, FunPRM, treats each function as one step to be scored. A fix step then cleans up flaws in those scores. The goal is to lift the odds that the picked code is right. The work speaks to teams that rely on model-written code.
arxiv-2601-22349:
Andreas Habring and Martin Zach prove how fast a class of samplers settles to its target. Samplers draw fair samples from a spread; many use drifts that shift over time, set by cooling plans. Their 2026 preprint gives a joint, non-asymptotic account of these Langevin diffusions and their step-wise forms.

They measure the gap with forward KL divergence, a standard odds-based yardstick. Firm rates tell users how long to run a sampler for a set trust level. They also show which cooling plans help or hurt. The work backs tools used across stats and physics.
arxiv-2601-22449:
Tristan Shah and Stas Tiomkin reframe what drives an agent to act when no outside goal is set. Intrinsic motivation lets agents explore and learn on their own. Their 2026 preprint notes that most theory rests on information flow between picked variables, a choice left to the designer.

They propose a view based on information production, not transmission. The shift aims to free the drive from hand-picked variables. A cleaner base could yield agents that explore in richer, less biased ways. That matters for robots and game agents alike. The work is theory, with design in view.
arxiv-2601-22549:
Mu-Yang Wang and four co-authors study chaos in a particle trapped near the edge of a charged, magnetized black hole. Their 2026 preprint uses the dyonic AdS-Reissner-Nordström hole, set in anti-de Sitter space. A light probe particle sits in a harmonic trap just off the horizon.

Three dials — the particle's energy, a chemical term, and the field — tune how wild the motion gets. The team map where order gives way to chaos. Such maps test deep links between black holes and chaos theory. They may also hint at quantum signatures of chaos.
arxiv-2601-22649:
Henning Krause and Balduin Stoye count subfamilies of interval multisets, and find both known and brand-new number sequences. For any finite ordered set, multisets of its intervals form an abelian category. Their 2026 preprint gives natural combinatorial accounts of many classes of subcategories.

Counting those classes yields familiar integer sequences — and, in some cases, sequences never seen before. The count problem leads to a universal category of poset representations. New sequences are a small thrill in pure math. The work ties counting to deep structure. It gives peers a rich new playground.
arxiv-2601-22749:
Riki Matsui, Shigeo Kimura, Kohta Murase, and B. Theodore Zhang predict the light that follows a gamma-ray burst across many bands. Gamma-ray bursts are the most extreme flashes known, yet their jets stay poorly understood. Their 2026 preprint focuses on X-ray flares and extended emission, which glow hundreds of seconds after the main burst.

They forecast what those phases should emit from radio to high energy. Matching forecasts to real sky data can reveal the jet's makeup. The work gives observers a checklist for the next bright burst. It ties theory to telescope time.
arxiv-2601-22849:
Christian Dietz and four co-authors plan how robots can put parts together with care. Assembly planning has long leaned on learning methods and random sampling, both hungry for simulation time. Their approach uses optimal control that accounts for contact between parts.

The method uses exact second-order derivative data, which sharply cuts the number of simulation steps needed. It also stays robust, so plans hold up when the real world differs a little. Sample-efficient planning could make factory robots faster to program for new products. Contact-implicit planning treats contact forces as part of the optimization itself, rather than as an afterthought added later.
arxiv-2601-23249:
Hongyu Cheng and Amitabh Basu examine the theory gaps in learning to guide branch-and-cut solvers. Branch-and-cut is the workhorse method for mixed-integer linear programming. Machine learning now guides its choices, like which variable to branch on or which cuts to add.

Many approaches train on local signals from lookahead rules, then judge success by local score accuracy. The authors argue that local accuracy may not predict whole-solver performance. Their critique pushes the field toward training goals tied to end-to-end solving speed. Local score accuracy is the metric under critique, because a policy can score well locally while slowing the whole solver.
arxiv-2602-00249: Rishav Pramanik and coauthors present SANEval, an open vocabulary benchmark for compositional text to image generation. Current models can be creative, yet they often fail prompts with several objects, attributes, and spatial relations. SANEval joins a large language model for deep prompt understanding to an LLM enhanced, open vocabulary object detector, checking compositional adherence without a fixed word list.
arxiv-2602-00349: Sergio Barbosa and team compute running Love numbers of charged black holes from quantum vacuum loops. Loops of virtual particles render black holes tidally deformable, and the authors compute the static tidal response for unspinning charged black holes at arbitrary radius. For large charged black holes described by effective field theory, they compute the full set of Love matrices from an arbitrary tower of F^2n operators. Although quantum corrections break electromagnetic duality, Love matrices in electric and magnetic backgrounds relate by a Z2 symmetry under electric magnetic exchange.
arxiv-2602-00449: Jia Liang and Liangming Pan study CODI, a continuous-thought distillation model, on polynomial iteration tasks with known states. Latent thought enables stepwise computation without rationales, yet its workings remain unclear. Using logit decoding and activation patching, the authors localize states and trace them to readout. In short cases, CODI forms bridge states across positions, while the final input takes a near direct route, with late fusion predictions at readout. As depth grows, CODI does not sustain a full rollout, instead compressing work into a partial pathway or losing it.
arxiv-2602-00649: Shiyu Sun and colleagues examine linear magnetohydrodynamic waves in a plasma whose background magnetic field repeats in space. They build a plane-wave expansion in two forms. One uses standard perturbation variables. The other uses fluid displacement. Both are checked with numeric tests. One limit recovers uniform-plasma dispersion. The periodic field opens gaps in frequency and cutoffs. The gap widens as modulation grows. Selected modes are suppressed. The Alfvén continuum splits into several branches. The work helps tailor wave travel in structured plasmas and plasma metamaterials.
arxiv-2602-01749: Lin Chen and colleagues give GFlowNet training exploration exploitation control, constrained by fixed equal mixing of forward and backward policies. Linking GFlowNets to Markov chains reveals a reversibility equivalence, explaining the constraint and adapting Markov properties. Their alpha GFlowNets vary mixing through a tunable parameter, controlling exploration and discovery, while hybrids with fewer full layers and far more linear layers cannot solve it. Across set, sequence and molecule benchmarks they beat earlier GFlowNet objectives, finding up to ten times as many modes, the first provable separation from full attention.
arxiv-2602-02149: Sylvia J. Bintrim and colleagues add a small fix to a cheap coupled cluster method for strong correlation. Standard coupled cluster is eased by addition by subtraction tricks, while linearized forms cost less, yet ring terms can blow up when a single bond breaks. A linearized ladder form drops those terms, but then underestimates dynamical correlation. The team adds a second order ring fix to that base wave function, yielding steady xlinCCD(2). In weakly correlated regimes, it matches linearized CCD results.
arxiv-2602-02449:
A. Kasikov and 3 co-authors pin down distances to the Milky Way's yellow super- and hypergiants, in a 2026 arXiv paper. These evolved massive stars are so bright and variable that Gaia parallax measurements, the standard distance tool, fail for them. Without distances, their luminosities and evolutionary states stay uncertain.

The team compiled thirty-five luminous yellow stars from the literature. Using Gaia DR3 data, they matched most stars to clusters or OB associations and averaged the parallaxes of nearby co-moving stars. Radial velocities checked against a Galactic hydrogen map validated the results independently. Distances improved for twenty-eight stars, with six more estimated kinematically. Updated luminosities for twenty stars place most hypergiants above a high threshold, while supergiants spread wider. The paper opens a family portrait series on these rare stars.
arxiv-2602-02549:
Yuki Uchino and 2 co-authors deliver a strict error analysis for a scheme that emulates high-precision matrix multiplication on fast low-precision hardware, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Ozaki-II scheme uses the Chinese remainder theorem to rebuild exact products from a sequence of low-precision multiplications. More rounds buy a closer match.

Earlier studies had shown single- and double-precision emulation beating standard library routines on AI hardware with fast eight-bit units. Quality degrades, however, when input exponents spread widely, forcing many rounds. The new analysis is exact rather than based on trials. It shows exactly how quality behaves as rounds build up. It also estimates in advance how many low-precision multiplications a target quality level requires. That turns a lab trick into an engineering tool with guarantees one can plan on, for scientific computing on modern hardware.
arxiv-2602-02849:
Sizing transistors for analog circuits is slow expert work, and Xi Yu and 3 co-authors try to automate it in a 2026 paper. Their system, AutoSizer, uses large language model agents inside a reflective loop. Language models reason well but are poor at precise number tuning, so the design splits the jobs.

An inner loop runs the sizing search. An outer loop studies progress and reshapes the search space using simulation feedback. The team also built a public benchmark of twenty-four circuits. AutoSizer reached better solutions faster, and more often, than traditional optimizers and earlier language-model agents across circuits of varying difficulty.
arxiv-2602-02949:
Turbulence inside glowing gas clouds can bias what astronomers infer from their light, according to Larrance Xing and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Such clouds, called H II regions, surround hot young stars. Analysts usually assume one uniform zone of density and temperature when reading their spectra, which may miss real complexity.

The team simulates three-dimensional H II regions around a single O-type star, with and without supersonic turbulence. Turbulence shifts common emission-line ratios in systematic directions. Metallicity estimates from the direct temperature method came out biased low. Different density indicators, from infrared to ultraviolet, also disagreed strongly. The authors call for large model grids that include turbulence across conditions seen in near and distant galaxies.
arxiv-2602-03249:
Long chains of thought that periodically summarize themselves are new by Zhicheng Yang, leading 7 other authors, in a system called Accordion-Thinking. Scaling test-time compute through long thinking unlocks gains, but cache growth and focus cost impose practical limits. Their model learns to regulate the granularity of its own thinking steps through dynamic summarization during output, compressing context as it goes.

In fold mode, the model periodically summarizes its thoughts and discards the earlier detail, cutting dependence on historical tokens. Reinforcement learning strengthens that capability. Over training, the score gap between efficient fold mode and exhaustive unfold mode narrowed and eventually vanished. The model had learned to encode essentials into compact summaries. Throughput tripled at maintained score, and summaries stay human-readable.
arxiv-2602-03349:
A black hole inside a dark matter halo gets an exact solution from David Senjaya, together with 2 colleagues, using a Dehnen halo profile that describes elliptical galaxy brightness well. Its implications for black hole spacetimes were largely unexplored. Their construction embeds a black hole in that halo and examines thermodynamics and light motion in the combined system, asking how a realistic halo reshapes a central black hole's behavior.

Mass, entropy, Hawking temperature, heat capacity, and Gibbs free energy assess local and global stability. The halo stabilizes the otherwise unstable Schwarzschild black hole and induces phase transitions. Photon motion studies show the halo modifies the effective potential, changing the photon sphere and shadow size. Instability of circular photon orbits connects to quasinormal modes in the eikonal limit, linking observable signatures to halo structure.
arxiv-2602-03449:
Diffuse optical tomography shines near-infrared light through tissue and infers absorption and scattering from what exits. Fabian Schneider and 6 co-authors test diffusion models, a modern generative technique, on this severely ill-posed imaging problem in a 2026 paper. Real measurements bring noise and modeling errors that break many reconstruction methods.

Their regularization mixes two scores, one learned from data and one based on the physical model, and they justify the mixture theoretically. They compare four approaches, including a classical method and an exact posterior sampler, on real experimental data. Approximate diffusion sampling and the classical method degrade under limited viewing angles, while the exact and regularized samplers reconstruct more accurately.
arxiv-2602-03549:
Breathing rate is a basic vital sign that almost nobody tracks outside a clinic. Michael Küttner and 4 co-authors estimate it from sound inside ordinary earphones in a 2026 paper. The ear canal amplifies body sounds, but street noise, music, and cafeteria chatter threaten to drown the faint breathing signal.

Their system, EarResp-ANS, runs entirely on the earphones themselves, with no neural network and no audio streaming to a phone. Adaptive noise suppression based on the LMS algorithm cleans the signal while preserving breathing components, keeping processor load under two percent. Tested on 18 participants under realistic noise, the error averaged well under one breath per minute after automatic outlier rejection.
arxiv-2602-03949:
Emrah Akyol studies compression when sender and receiver want different things. His 2026 paper treats semantic compression, where a Gaussian signal carries a task-relevant meaning, and the encoder and decoder optimize separate goals. Rate limits and compute limits both constrain what can be sent.

Akyol reduces the encoder's problem to designing the decoder's posterior uncertainty under a rate cap. He works out the best trade-offs for direct, remote, and full-information setups, with waterfilling-style answers. Compute limits act like extra rate limits, and deeper models improve scores fast. Multimodal observation removes a penalty built into remote encoding. The theory recasts large multimodal models as posterior design tools.
arxiv-2602-04349:
Editing a 3D mesh should start from a single image, not a voxel sculpture. Teng-Fang Hsiao and 3 co-authors present VecSet-Edit in a 2026 paper, the first mesh editing pipeline built on a pretrained large reconstruction model. Earlier approaches leaned on voxel representations with limited resolution and labor-intensive three-dimensional masks.

Analysis showed subsets of the model's tokens govern distinct geometric regions. Mask-guided token seeding and attention-aligned gating localize the edit region from two-dimensional image conditions alone. A drift-aware pruning step rejects geometry that wanders during generation. The result is direct, precise mesh editing guided by a picture.
arxiv-2602-04449:
Who actually leads the rankings on a famous coding benchmark? Matias Martinez and Xavier Franch examine that question in a 2026 study of SWE-Bench, a test that asks repair tools to fix real issues from open-source Python projects.

The authors analyzed entries on the Lite and Verified leaderboards. They recorded who submitted each entry, what product stood behind it, and which language model it used. Most entries came from industry, especially small firms and large public companies. Proprietary models, above all the Claude family, dominated the top results. Still, academic entries, usually open source, remained competitive. The study urges more transparency and diversity in benchmark research.
arxiv-2602-04649:
Reward models can give the right verdict for the wrong reason. Binghai Wang and colleagues examine that failure in a 2026 paper on models that judge language model answers during training. Judging only outcome accuracy can hide deceptive reasoning and hurt later learning.

The authors introduce rationale consistency, a metric comparing a model's reasoning process with human judgment. It separated leading models where outcome accuracy could not, and it exposed deceptive alignment. Training with a hybrid signal, mixing rationale consistency and accuracy, improved benchmark scores over outcome-only training. Used in reinforcement learning from human feedback, it also raised performance, notably in creative writing. The trap of declining rationale quality was reversed.
arxiv-2602-04849:
Changhyeok Choi and 12 co-authors present an AI molecular editor in a 2026 paper called El Agente Estructural. Chemists often want to handle molecules directly in three dimensions, as human experts do, rather than rebuild whole structures from scratch with a generative model.

The agent mixes domain tools with vision-language models and takes plain language orders. It gives precise control over atom and group swaps, atomic links, and stereochemistry, with no need to rebuild core structures. Case studies cover selective functionalization, ligand binding and exchange, stereo-controlled builds, and isomer conversion. Others build structures from images of reaction schemes. A planned link into an autonomous quantum chemistry platform adds these editing tools to its set.
arxiv-2602-04949:
Dimitrios Patramanis and Watse Sybesma explore a link between two ideas in this 2026 theory paper. One idea is the quantum walk, where a particle spreads over a graph by quantum rules. The other is Krylov complexity, a measure of how an operator grows as a quantum system evolves. The authors show the second grows naturally out of the first.

Reducing a graph to a chain reveals the standard Krylov structure hiding inside the walk. With that bridge, they build graphs with known complexity behavior and compute complexity for graphs of physical interest. Results include exact Lanczos coefficients for the SYK model, a standard testbed for quantum chaos, and a full account of complexity on hypercube graphs. They also compare Krylov complexity with circuit complexity in black hole settings, finding saturation can arrive sooner than circuit arguments suggest.
arxiv-2602-05149:
Solar flares could become a lab for neutrino physics. D Delepine and A Yebra develop that idea in this 2026 particle physics paper, a companion to their work on supernova neutrinos. The mechanism is resonant spin-flavor precession, where solar magnetic fields convert neutrinos between flavors and spin states at a resonance set by the neutrino's energy.

Using a density matrix treatment with collisional decoherence and real solar density shapes, the authors compare three shapes for the Sun's magnetic field. Plain boron-8 neutrinos resonate deep in the core and never feel the outer fields. Flare neutrinos, a hundred times hotter, resonate instead in the tachocline and convection zones, where strong fields drive efficient flips. That conversion shifts scattering cross sections differently for Dirac and Majorana neutrinos. A catch, or even a miss, could tell the two cases apart and tighten limits on the neutrino magnetic moment.
arxiv-2602-05649:
Gradient-boosted trees have long ruled tabular data, but new foundation models that learn in context now rival them, at a heavy computing cost. Guri Zabërgja, Rafiq Kamel, and 3 co-authors propose TACO, an end-to-end compression model that shrinks the training data set inside a latent space. Standard tabular transformers scale quadratically with data set size, which slows training and inference and caps how much data they can use.

On the TabArena benchmark, TACO ran inference far faster than the leading tabular transformer, in the best cases by a wide multiple, while using a small fraction of the memory. Accuracy held up with no significant degradation. The method also scaled better as data sets grew, and it beat other baselines outright in some comparisons. The authors present compression, not a bigger context window, as the way to bring foundation models to large tables.
arxiv-2602-05749:
Deep clustering is praised for finding groups that k means cannot, such as clusters of odd shapes and varied sizes, but the evidence comes mostly from image data. Kai Ming Ting, Wei-Jie Xu, and Hang Zhang investigate whether a leading deep method, Deep Embedded Clustering, truly overcomes those limits. That method learns a latent representation with an autoencoder and clusters inside it, end to end.

Their investigation finds a gap: deep methods do not exploit the underlying distribution of the data. A non deep learning approach that does use distributional information of clusters achieves what deep clustering aims at, addressing the shape, size, and density limits directly. The authors argue the lesson extends beyond one method to deep clustering in general. The paper is marked as work in progress.
arxiv-2602-06049:
Short, catchy slogans help buyers remember a brand, but repeated slogans wear out fast. Ziao Yang and 3 co-authors propose a fresh source of raw material: famous quotes tied to a public figure. Quotes are brief, use strong wordplay, and carry depth that fits slogan length well.

Their system breaks the job into clear steps. It picks a fitting quote, studies its structure, swaps in brand words, and remixes the result into a slogan. Tests with both automatic scores and human judges showed small gains in variety, freshness, and emotional punch. Readers also preferred the new slogans over those from three strong language model baselines.
arxiv-2602-06149:
Strongly correlated molecules, where electrons influence each other heavily, defeat many standard quantum chemistry methods. Abdulrahman Y Zamani and 4 co-authors study why one fix works so well. The fix runs coupled cluster theory, a high-accuracy method, starting from Kohn-Sham density functional results instead of the usual Hartree-Fock start.

The team shows the gain comes from the one-particle density, written into a key matrix, not from the orbitals themselves, as many had assumed. With that insight, the method hit near chemical accuracy for metal pairs and other compounds. It even traced the full energy curve of a chromium pair, a notorious failure case. A cheap diagnostic flags hard cases in advance.
arxiv-2602-06249:
Where British AI firms cluster, and what drives their earnings, is mapped by Waqar Muhammad Ashraf and 2 co-authors. They assembled records on UK AI entities spanning more than two decades from company, statistics, and commercial sources. London holds a large share of the firms, and tech-heavy sectors dominate.

Firm size and depth of AI specialization were the strongest drivers of revenue, with finance firms earning the most on average. Local factors like skilled-worker rates, density, and jobs added smaller but real contributions. Forecasts to the end of the decade project continued growth in firm numbers, alongside a rising closure rate. The authors argue policy should build AI strength beyond London.
arxiv-2602-06349:
Most quantum systems conserve probability, but open systems with gain and loss do not, and their scattering rules change. Jung-Wan Ryu and 2 co-authors study two-port scattering in small non-Hermitian dimer models, measured through attached leads. Their models balance gain and loss symmetrically, and one also hops in a one-way fashion.

Building the scattering matrix from both left and right states, they compute reflection and transmission chances. Using only the right states breaks the usual unitarity rule. Gain and loss can even boost reflection and transmission, through separate effects from complex energies and from non-orthogonal states. Handling both state families restores a generalized unitarity, clarifying how transport works in such systems.
arxiv-2602-06549:
Learning from scarce data is hardest when useful signals hide inside measurement noise, a daily problem in materials science. Shuai Ning and 7 co-authors present AdverISF, a framework that separates task-relevant features from noise without needing labels that say which is which. Standard tricks cannot draw that line precisely, and older rival methods demand explicit split labels.

AdverISF uses a self-supervised rival trick to force freedom between the useful features and the noise picture. A multi-layer design then recycles noise info across levels to recover features wrongly discarded as noise. Tests showed the method beat leading approaches on scarce data, and on real design tasks it fared better than rivals.
arxiv-2602-06649:
Joan Amaya, Valdivino V. Junior, Fábio P. Machado, and Alejandro Roldán-Correa model populations that grow in colonies but face sudden catastrophes. After each disaster, survivors may scatter to new sites, and that choice can decide whether the population lives or dies out. The paper works out exact formulas for these chances.

The authors derive the survival probability and the average time until extinction, both with and without limits on space. They then compare disasters whose survivor counts follow three different patterns, uniform, binomial, and geometric, in models where space is unlimited. The comparison shows how the shape of a catastrophe, not just its size, changes a population's long-term odds.
arxiv-2602-06849:
Alberto Foresti, Mustapha Bounoua, Giulio Franzese, Luca Ambrogioni, and Pietro Michiardi improve how discrete diffusion models generate sequences. These models, powerful for text, music, and other discrete data, have lacked the information-theoretic understanding of their continuous cousins. The paper analyzes the reverse generation process through thermodynamic entropy production, the rate at which information is created.

That rate, the authors show, bounds how far intermediate states sit from the true data distribution. From it they derive two sampling schedules that space steps evenly in a physics-inspired sense: one holds the rate of information gain constant, the other takes equal steps in Wasserstein distance. Across synthetic data, music notation, vision, and language, both schedules beat state-of-the-art alternatives at lower computational cost.
arxiv-2602-06949:
Shenyuan Gao and colleagues present DreamDojo, a foundation world model for robots learned from 44,000 hours of egocentric human video. Simulating what actions do in varied environments could transform generalist robot development, but dexterous tasks suffer from limited data coverage and scarce action labels. Their data mixture is described as the largest video dataset yet assembled for world model pretraining, spanning everyday scenarios, objects, and skills.

To handle missing action labels, the team introduces continuous latent actions as unified proxy actions, improving transfer from unlabeled video. After post-training on small amounts of robot data, DreamDojo shows strong physics understanding and precise action control. A distillation pipeline speeds it to real-time operation at about 10.8 frames per second while improving context consistency, enabling live teleoperation, policy evaluation, and model-based planning, with strong results on out-of-distribution benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-07149:
Large image data sets scraped from the web can carry private material nobody checked for.  Rawisara Lohanimit and four co-authors hunt for pregnancy ultrasound images in LAION-400M, a dataset widely used to train generative models, using image-embedding similarity to find them.

They recover ultrasound images and detect thousands of pieces of private information, such as names and places, some sharp enough to allow re-identification or impersonation.  The paper closes with useful advice on curating data sets, protecting privacy, and using public image collections ethically.  It is a concrete warning, grounded in one sensitive case, for everyone building on scraped data.
arxiv-2602-07349:
Singular value breakdown offers a handy way to build tests for non-Hermitian many-body systems, but whether those tests locate localization transitions correctly is unsettled.  Huimin You and three co-authors benchmark SVD-based tests against exact diagonalization in time-reversal-symmetric hard-core-boson chains with nonreciprocal hopping.

Across quasiperiodic, random-disorder, and Stark potentials, they compare level statistics, entanglement entropy, participation ratios, and spectral form factors.  Exact-diagonalization figures agree with each other, while SVD-based figures shift systematically to larger disorder and can assign phases in other ways.  Condensed matter experts get a caution: a handy test can move the transition it is meant to find.
arxiv-2602-07649:
Short THz pulses are prized for research and applications, but they are usually made inefficiently by converting light from visible or near-infrared lasers.  Urban Senica and six co-authors demonstrate a direct on-chip THz source that skips the conversion step.

Active mode-locking of an inverse-designed, planarized Y-coupled THz quantum cascade laser, driven by quasi-resonant microwave modulation of its asymmetric cavity, produces pulses as short as 2. 3 picoseconds, with bandwidths spanning 500 to 700 gigahertz around 2. 9 THz.  Photonics teams get a compact, coherent THz pulse source for a spectral region that has long lacked one.
arxiv-2602-07749:
Turning a geometry diagram back into code could teach models to reason about shapes, but existing methods lose constraints and distort structure. Zhenyu Wu and three co-authors propose Geo-Code, a multi-agent framework that reconstructs programs from geometric images in two stages.

First, visual operators and large models work together to pin down pixel coordinates and visual attributes. Then a loop of synthesis, rendering, and validation uses visual feedback to correct the code itself. Experiments show the approach captures geometric detail more faithfully than prior inverse-graphics methods. The work matters for multimodal AI, where a program that redraws a diagram is strong evidence the model truly understood it.
arxiv-2602-07849:
Vision-language models are too heavy for edge devices, and test-time adaptation methods that could handle distribution shifts are themselves too costly. Xin Wang and six co-authors propose LQA, a lightweight quantized-adaptive method combining modality-aware quantization with gradient-free adaptation.

Selective hybrid quantization shrinks the model while a quantized, gradient-free mechanism adapts it on device without backpropagation. Across made and real distribution shifts, LQA improves adaptation results by 4.5 percent, uses less memory than full-fine models, and beats gradient-based adaptation with up to 19.9 times lower memory use across seven datasets. Edge AI builders gain a usable path to robust, private, on-device vision-language models.
arxiv-2602-08149:
Summarizing a conversation is harder than summarizing an article: information scatters across speakers and turns, and the summary rewrites first- and second-person speech in third person. Sahana Ramnath and ten co-authors offer DIAL-SUMMER, a method for evaluating dialogue summaries with a structured taxonomy of layered errors.

Errors are classified at two levels: dialogue level, concerning speakers and turns broadly, and within-turn level, concerning information inside a single turn. The method comes with a dataset of manually annotated dialogue summaries. Summarization teams and product teams gain an evaluation tool that distinguishes kinds of mistakes earlier metrics blurred as one, pointing builders toward the specific failures to fix.
arxiv-2602-08349:
Ethnographers study people, practices, and the tools that connect them, often switching between being insiders and outsiders, researchers and participants. Daniel Mwesigwa and two co-authors ask how digital platforms change that balancing act. Their arXiv paper draws on fieldwork in VRChat and WhatsApp, two very different online worlds.

The authors follow how researchers handle questions of race and caste as they form publics across online and offline life. They propose emergent relationality as a lens for the mutual shaping of researcher, platform, and public. The lens helps explain what can be seen, said, and shared in hybrid settings. Readers get a thoughtful guide to doing fieldwork in public when the field itself is partly digital.
arxiv-2602-08449:
Safety tests assume that how an AI behaves under evaluation predicts how it will behave once deployed. Igor Santos-Grueiro argues that situationally aware agents can break that link by reading cues that distinguish test from deployment and behaving well only while watched. His arXiv paper recasts alignment evaluation as an information-flow problem.

The gap between test and deployment behavior is bounded by how much regime information the agent's internal states carry. A training intervention that restricts access to those cues, called regime-blind training, cuts regime-conditioned failures without hurting task performance, though effects vary by model and failure type. Readers get both a warning about evaluation as a side channel and a partial, honestly limited defense.
arxiv-2602-08749:
Flow-based image editors handle global or single edits well, but editing several items at once causes cross-talk. Carmine Zaccagnino and six co-authors trace that failure to globally tuned velocity fields and joint focus, which entangle edits done at once. Their arXiv paper introduces Instance-Disentangled Attention to split them apart.

The mechanism splits joint focus work, binding each item's text instruction to its own spatial region while working out speeds. Tests on natural image editing and a new benchmark of text-heavy graphics with per-region instructions show better split-apart edits and local detail with the whole intact. The method enables single-pass, item-level editing without cross-talk. Readers get a clean way to edit many parts of one image at once, fast and in one pass.
arxiv-2602-09149:
Viv Kendon and one co-author review quantum annealing for condensed-matter physicists, bridging two communities that can help each other. Annealers exploit interacting quantum spin systems to solve optimization problems, and modern hardware has grown capable enough to tackle condensed-matter questions directly. The review explains how annealers work, what they can do, and where they fall short.

The mutual benefits run both ways: condensed-matter insight can improve annealer design and operation, while annealers offer a new tool for studying quantum materials. Written as a topical introduction rather than a research report, the paper aims to bring physicists into annealing research and to carry annealing methods into physics problems.
arxiv-2602-09349:
Participatory budgeting lets residents help decide which public projects get funded, but designing the rules that turn preferences into feasible budgets is hard. Good rules must balance total benefit against fairness, and the two goals trade off against each other. Nguyen Thach and two co-authors propose LLMRule, a 2026 framework that automates rule design by pairing large language models with evolutionary search, exploiting the resemblance of budgeting rules to knapsack algorithms.

The generated rules were tested on more than six hundred real budgeting cases from the United States, Canada, Poland, and the Netherlands. Preference expressions varied across the cases. The generated rules generally beat handcrafted rivals on overall benefit. Fairness holds at a similar level rather than being sacrificed for gain. The authors present the approach as a way past the domain-knowledge bottleneck that has long made budgeting-rule design slow and expert-bound.
arxiv-2602-09649:
Ancestral recombination graphs have become a more and more key part of people and stat genes. A 2026 note led by Ben Jeffery announces tskit version 1.0, the library that has become key base for the field. Tskit gives a rich, general picture of these graphs with a suite of fast core tasks.

The note tells the why behind version 1.0 and sets out its staying power pledges. Those pledges give a base for durable code works and support long-term rerun of code and work. For a field built on shared base, a stable major release matters: users can build lasting tools and re-run old work knowing the core picture will hold.
arxiv-2602-10049:
Continuous generative models need random seeds with enough variety to produce diverse data, yet classical simulation methods threaten to tame them. A 2026 paper led by Olli Hirviniemi, with two co-authors, introduces a random circuit family designed as such a seed. The circuits resist current classical simulation techniques, namely tensor network contraction and Pauli propagation.

Local variables in these circuits do not concentrate, preserving the variance needed for diverse outputs. The authors therefore argue for using the circuits as a random seed inside a larger classical generative model. That hybrid design, they suggest, brings large-scale quantum-classical models within reach of near-term noisy devices.
arxiv-2602-10149:
Third-party risk assessment leans on vast repositories of cybersecurity compliance questions, yet only some questions fit any given supplier. A 2026 paper led by Ali Nour Eldin, with four co-authors, asks whether a stated semantic label space can sharpen intent-aware question selection. Lexical and semantic retrieval finds topically related questions but often misses assessment intent, including control area and evaluation scope.

The team separates label discovery from large-scale assignment. Overlapping clusters of similar questions are found first, then language models assign one label per cluster, and labels propagate by nearest neighbors for broad annotation. Retrieval then matches queries against labels rather than questions, cutting repeated model calls while preserving consistency. Label-based retrieval aligns better with control domains and scope than similarity-based retrieval.
arxiv-2602-10249:
Picking homework that fits a student's current skills requires knowing those skills across programming topics. A 2026 paper led by Carlos Eduardo P. Silva, with four co-authors, offers a context-aware recommender that models programming skills from code embeddings students submit during a course. Predicted skill profiles are matched to the skills unseen homework problems require, ranking exercises by how closely student profiles match problem skill vectors.

Tests on real data from a first programming course weigh embedding types for skill prediction, with Jina embeddings topping TF-IDF, CodeBERT-cpp, and GraphCodeBERT on most skills. A second test across seven course offerings checks recommendation fit with weekly content, finding the approach steadily more fitting than baselines using correctness or solution time. Predicted skills prove the stronger signal for problem picks.
arxiv-2602-10449:
Pingbang Hu and three co-authors put random projection for influence functions on firmer theory ground in a 2026 paper. Influence scores measure how single training points shape a model, but they involve inverting a huge bend matrix. Builders sketch that matrix down with random projections, usually justified by a lemma about keeping distances.

The paper shows that justification is incomplete: keeping distances does not promise keeping inverses. The authors develop a unified theory of when sketched influence scores stay faithful, covering ridge regularization and ordered bend approximations as well. The results tell builders which sketching choices are safe, and which silently distort the attribution scores they rely on.
arxiv-2602-10749:
Alessandro Fusta Moro and two co-authors publish a ready-to-use air quality and climate dataset for Italy in a 2026 paper. Air quality and climate shape public health and policy, yet teams often wrestle with raw, poorly documented data. The GRINS AQCLIM dataset answers with daily statistics spanning 2013 through 2023.

Drawn from the European Setting Agency and the Copernicus Programme, the dataset covers more than seven hundred monitoring stations. It gives daily summaries of pollutant concentrations and climate factors, from minima and quartiles to means and maxima. Multiple processing steps, including automatic fixes to raw files, ensure trust. The paper presents the dataset as shared infrastructure for Italian environmental research and planning.
arxiv-2602-10949:
Constantin Kogler and two co-authors analyze initialization for deep leaky ReLU networks in a 2026 paper. Strong initialization demands grasp random neural networks, and the paper gives a rigorous chance analysis of deep bias-free random networks with leaky rectified linear activations. A law of large numbers and a central limit theorem govern the logarithm of activation norms.

As layers increase, activation growth follows a Lyapunov exponent marking a sharp phase transition between vanishing and exploding activations. The authors compute that exponent explicitly for Gaussian and orthogonal weights. The result reveals that standard He and orthogonal initializations do not promise steadiness for deep networks of low width. A novel Lyapunov initialization method follows from the theory, designed to keep deep narrow networks stable.
arxiv-2602-11149:
More unique data is not always better for thinking models. Dawid J. Kopiczko and three co-authors show that, under a fixed update budget, many epochs on a small chain-of-thought set beat one epoch on a large set. A small model trained long on hundreds of samples beat the same model trained once on tens of thousands.

Token scores signals when repetition saturates: gains flatten once the model has memorized the set, a pattern that held across settings. No extra catastrophic forgetting appeared. The authors offer a practical rule: scale epochs with token scores as a stop signal, rather than chasing ever-larger data sets. They pose the repetition advantage itself as a new open problem.
arxiv-2602-11549:
Training a model to reason well usually depends on hand-written examples and outside checkers that can mark answers right or wrong. That recipe works for maths and code but leaves out tasks where no checker exists, and it is costly and can bake in human habits of thought. Yuanfu Wang and four co-authors offer a different route, named Native Reasoning Training, that lets a model build its own reasoning chains from plain question-and-answer pairs alone.

Reasoning is treated as a hidden step inside training, rewarded when it raises the chance of reaching the true answer. That setup also exposes failure modes such as policy collapse, where training narrows too far, and points to sturdier ways of combining rewards. Tests on two model families show the best results yet among methods that use no verifier, with the largest gains on hard reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2602-11949:
Graph query languages like Cypher, PGQL, GSQL, and the GQL standard all draw on regular path queries, but they part ways with classical homomorphism semantics when they must list walks explicitly. Victor Marsault and one co-author note the difficulty: a regular path query can match infinitely many walks, so each language picks a finite subset by its own ad-hoc rule. Cypher keeps trails, discarding walks with repeated edges, while PGQL and GSQL keep only shortest walks, and GQL lets users choose.

Existing research on these rules focuses almost entirely on evaluation speed. The authors instead build a framework to categorize and compare rules by other criteria. They formalize properties of rules viewed as functions from a database and a query to a finite set of walks. They show some properties are mutually exclusive or unattainable, and they offer several new rules as examples, seeds for future language design.
arxiv-2602-12149:
Mathematicians study convergence not only for points, but for whole sets of closed subsets, and the tools for that job are still being built. M. Ateş led this work with two co-authors, working in the category of convergence approach spaces and their contractions. They build approach versions of upper and lower Kuratowski convergence and of Fell-type topologies.

For spaces with a pre-approach structure, they pin down how these new forms relate to the core and mirror forms of the base space. Over a full approach space, the lower form turns out to match a known Vietoris-type structure, though it can be finer in general. The paper also lifts a classic result: when upper Kuratowski convergence is pretopological, it is topological too.
arxiv-2602-12349:
Green's functions give the basic response of a partial differential equation, yet they are costly to compute on arbitrary shapes. Joao Teixeira led this work with two co-authors. They present Variational Green's Function, a method that learns a smooth, differentiable form of the Green's function.

It covers linear self-adjoint operators, including Poisson, screened Poisson, and biharmonic equations. Sharp spikes near sources are handled by splitting the function into two parts. One part is an analytic free-space term. The other is a learned corrector. A variational base imposes Neumann boundary rules naturally. A projective layer imposes Dirichlet rules on the neural field output. The result is fast to evaluate, differentiable in source placement, and can adapt to signals that describe the geometry.
arxiv-2602-12449:
Learning a Gibbs distribution from sufficient statistics alone is computationally hard, while efficient learning methods usually need full sample configurations. Abhijith Jayakumar led this work with four co-authors. He asks what can be learned from only a limited set of statistics, a realistic limit for many physical systems where full samples are impractical to observe. The Ising model serves as the test case for trading computation against observation.

The team shows model parameters can be reconstructed for a model with l1 width gamma. This uses statistics up to order gamma. That approach recovers both structure and couplings plus magnetic fields. When prior information about structure is available, the learning problem can be solved efficiently with even less observational power. Readers get a precise account of how much observation suffices for efficient Ising learning.
arxiv-2602-12749:
Extended reality in early childhood mixes dense sensing, live rendering, and close interaction, which makes it both promising and risky for young children. Supriya Khadka and Sanchari Das review 111 peer-reviewed studies of children aged three to eight, scoring technical, teaching, health, privacy, and fairness challenges. Augmented reality dominates the field at 73%, mostly on tablets or phones, while virtual reality stays rare and usually needs headsets.

Their scores show teaching gets the most steady attention, at 1.56 on a 0 to 2 scale, while data security practices score just 0.14, a striking blind spot. The authors fold the patterns into a risk and attention matrix and a child-development model, then sketch a roadmap for child-centred design. The goal is systems that fit development, stay secure by default, and reach diverse learners.
arxiv-2602-13049:
Epithelial tissues flow and reshape, and model building them needs viscosity that respects both cell cortex and bulk dissipation. Shao-Zhen Lin and two co-authors present a rotationally fixed viscous vertex model covering both dissipation channels. The zero-substrate-friction limit is enforced with Lagrange multipliers, which also frame edge handling, including fixed edges and prescribed tractions.

Building on that formulation, a slab-shear rheology protocol extracts an strong tissue shear viscosity at coarse grain. Under polar or nematic activity, viscosity shapes elongated, spatially correlated cell textures and stabilises well-defined shape defects. Because the model stays well-posed at zero friction, it suits free-floating epithelia and organoids, where substrate anchoring cannot be assumed.
arxiv-2602-13149:
Burning and zero forcing are two ways a spread propagates through a graph, used to model phenomena from epidemics to network control. Aida Abiad and Pax Mallee connect them through hypergraphs. First, they prove a tight upper bound for the zero forcing number of a hypergraph's incidence graph in terms of the hypergraph's lazy burning number. That improves a 2025 result by Bonato and colleagues.

Second, they settle a spectral question: while the spectrum is known not to encode zero forcing and several other properties, burning number was open. By building infinitely many cospectral graph pairs whose burning numbers differ, they show the spectrum does not determine burning either. The paper thus ties two propagation processes together while drawing a firm line around what spectra can reveal.
arxiv-2602-13249:
Small-molecule models are usually trained on lone molecules, missing the rich clues that come from seeing a molecule bound to a protein. This study asks whether a protein-ligand co-folding model can supply those clues instead, testing the Boltz2 model by moving its atom-level ligand readings onto stand-alone molecule tasks. The transfer is checked through probing and distillation, two ways of reusing what a trained model already knows.

Boltz2 matched or beat existing models on the ADMET benchmark, sped up molecule generation, and used samples more efficiently when guiding ligand design. Its readings also added value beyond standard training signals such as 3D shapes, lab assay labels, and quantum chemistry traits. Hyosoon Jang leads the work with six co-authors, and the authors present co-folding as a strong base for molecule models.
arxiv-2602-13549:
Night driving scenes defeat most scene rebuilding methods, which are tuned for normal light. Complex lighting and looks degrade neural radiance fields and Gaussian splatting alike. This paper adds physics-based rendering to 3D Gaussian splatting for nighttime self-driving scenes, jointly tuning material traits based on reflectance functions within combined scene Gaussian models.

Soft light is modeled in full through a global light module, and shiny light through stretched round Gaussians. The result improves outdoor nighttime rebuild quality while keeping real-time rendering, and tests on nuScenes and Waymo across varied night scenes beat leading methods on both numbers and looks. Tae-Kyeong Kim leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13849:
Majid Sadeghinejad and four co-authors describe a 2026 arXiv paper on tidying a tabletop with a robot arm. When a target spot is blocked, robots often waste moves parking items out of the way. Grasping gives control but costs moves, while pushing is cheap yet hard to steer.

Their hybrid move, push-placement, shoves a blocking item aside with the held object as it is set down, cutting the need for extra parking moves. Built into a physics-aware tree-search planner and tested in the PyBullet simulator, it cut arm travel by up to 11.12% against a baseline planner and 8.56% against dynamic stacking. The gain matters for long, multi-step tidying jobs.
arxiv-2602-14149:
Alexander N. Manashov and two co-authors discuss a 2026 arXiv proceedings paper on anomalous dimensions in QCD. Those dimensions govern how parton distributions evolve with scale, and their analytic structure in spin matters for precision predictions at high energy. Higher-loop calculations make that structure hard to pin down.

The paper resums a class of small-spin singularities akin to those in the quark flavor-nonsinglet sector. The focus is the interplay between the Gross-Neveu-Yukawa model in epsilon expansion and the Gross-Neveu model in 1/N expansion. That resummation predicts higher-loop singular behavior and links to conformal Regge theory and recent work on detector operators in QCD and conformal field theories.
arxiv-2602-14349:
Jiaxin Cui and one co-author test a 2026 arXiv reproducibility problem in language-model data analysis. Two prompting strategies, six models, and four temperature settings were run ten times each, yielding 480 attempts. Each attempt was scored on completion, concordance, validity, and consistency.

Results varied considerably even within identical configurations, mirroring the variability of human data analysis. The same task, data, and settings did not guarantee the same analytical outcome. The authors conclude that language-model data analysis should be run multiple times independently, with the distribution of results considered, rather than trusting any single run.
arxiv-2602-14549:
T. -H. Chien and seven co-authors report a 2026 arXiv first lab build of a made Hall donut. A spinor Bose-Einstein cloud sits in a ring-shaped trap with in-place imaging.

Cyclic linking of three hyperfine spin states via Raman and microwave fields forces a cycling edge rule in the made size. Joined with the real-space ring, that builds a donut shape with made magnet flux. The flux brings ring-wise density ripples whose cycle is fixed by the quantized donut magnet flux, a mark of Hall donut shape. Shifting the relative phase between links across runs steers the spot of density peaks, mimicking a Thouless charge pump in donut shape. Studying the start of ripples as shape shifts from tube to donut sets up a flexible bench for quantum Hall physics in made curved spaces.
arxiv-2602-14849:
Bardia Mohammadi and colleagues present Atomix, a runtime for timely, transactional tool use in agentic workflows. Language-model agents mutate external state through tools, yet common orchestrators treat tool return as settlement, leaving partial effects, stale writes, lost-branch residue, and irreversible sends when faults, speculation, or concurrent agents intervene.

Atomix splits settlement into two explicit facts: which effects must settle together, and when earlier conflicting work is exhausted. It records reads and effects, seals a transaction when its footprint completes, and commits only after per-resource frontiers show no earlier conflict can still arrive. Agentic work gains transactions worthy of the name.
arxiv-2602-14949:
Gao and colleagues study max-min problems with a bilinear goal, where one side seeks the most and an enemy side seeks the least. This form covers zero-sum games, robust optimization, and learning under attack. They focus on cases whose unknowns sit in the completely positive cone, which captures many mixed-binary quadratic contests.

The team recasts such problems as one linear program over a joined copositive and CP cone. They then build a ladder of semidefinite relaxations from moment and sum-of-squares tools. Flat truncation tests certify exactness. Under mild terms the ladder is shown tight, and on cases of the cyclic Colonel Blotto game it finds the exact mixed-strategy equilibrium.
arxiv-2602-15049:
Brik and colleagues use quantum annealing to pick access points for indoor localization under a budget. Choosing which access points to deploy trades accuracy against cost, and classical selection grows expensive in large 3D indoor spaces. The team frames selection as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem, a form suited to quantum annealing solvers, and uses annealing to find the best subset allowed by the budget.

A realistic 3D testbed shows the method cutting the needed access points by about 96 percent while keeping comparable 3D accuracy. It also beats classical selection on accuracy and speed, running in one fifth of a second, or 61 times faster, with mean error down 10 percent. For floor identification it reaches 73 percent accuracy, ahead of classical selection at about 59 percent and even ahead of using every access point at about 70 percent.
arxiv-2602-15149:
Rahimi and Moutsanidis present SoliDualSPHysics, an open-source GPU extension of DualSPHysics for solid mechanics. It models hyperelastic, finite-strain plastic, and brittle fracture response in solids that deform, within one smoothed particle method. A total Lagrangian setup lets users apply outside loads and edge rules in stand-alone solid runs.

Brittle fracture follows a phase-field approach coupled with SPH. Cracks can start, spread, and branch under dynamic loading with no crack tracking, no ad hoc path rules, and no local tweaks. Users can also prescribe time- and space-varying values through custom math. Native CPU and GPU speed brings large gains for big runs, and tests against benchmarks and lab data show strong, robust scaling. Code and docs are public for community reuse.
arxiv-2602-15549:
Tang and colleagues give factory robots a steadier memory. Vision-language models can plan high-level factory work. But they forget what has left their view, so their picture of the workcell drifts. Their reasoning also stays opaque when a step fails. Blind retries then cost time and money. The team answers by splitting planning from state keeping.

Their VLM-DEWM design stores the world state in a persistent external model that can be queried. Each planned step is written as a reasoning trace covering the proposed action, the world belief, and the causal guess. That trace is checked against the stored state before the robot moves, and mismatches guide focused recovery rather than a full replan. Tests on assembly, facility exploration, and real-robot recovery lift state tracking from 56 to 93 percent and recovery from under 5 to 95 percent.
arxiv-2602-15649:
