The notice is a correction only. In the original version, one author's given and family names, Marco Morelli Coppola, were wrongly ordered, though the name was right in all versions when published. The original article has now been corrected. Its results and conclusions stand.
pmc-13222049:
Zirong Liu and colleagues survey patients with venous thromboembolism about long-term blood thinner use, in a 2026 cross-sectional study at a Shandong hospital. Three hundred eighty-nine patients completed a questionnaire covering knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice around anticoagulation. Younger patients made up a large share, with a mean age near forty-six.

About half of respondents met the preset bar for adequate knowledge, while majorities showed positive attitudes and proactive habits. Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores all rose together in correlation analysis. Patients under forty-five scored higher on knowledge and attitude than older groups. The gaps suggest education should target older patients, whose understanding lagged despite years of potential treatment ahead.
pmc-13223349:
Sarah Søgaard Jakobsen and co-authors run a post hoc quality-of-life analysis of fecal microbiota transplantation for chronic pouchitis, in a 2026 report from the MicroPouch trial. Pouchitis inflames the surgical pouch built after colon removal for ulcerative colitis, and antibiotics often fail in chronic cases. Thirty patients were randomized evenly to transplant enemas or placebo over four weeks, then followed for a year.

At thirty days, transplant patients reported significantly worse quality of life on an inflammatory bowel questionnaire than at baseline. Placebo patients scored higher on a general health survey at both checks. No questionnaire showed improvement from the transplant. The authors conclude fecal transfer may temporarily worsen symptoms in this setting, a caution against assuming benefit.
pmc-13223949:
Manish J Barvaliya and co-authors publish a protocol for testing an Ayurvedic preparation alongside iron tablets for anemia in women, in a 2026 trial protocol. Drakshavaleha, a grape-based formulation, may help the body absorb iron better than supplements alone. The parallel-group, open-label trial will enroll women aged eighteen to forty-nine with mild to moderate iron-deficiency anemia from community settings.

Half receive standard iron and folic acid tablets twice daily for three months. The other half add six grams of Drakshavaleha twice daily before food. Monthly visits will track blood counts and iron profiles, with kidney, liver, and blood sugar checks at the end. The registered trial will judge whether the integrative pairing raises hemoglobin safely.
pmc-13228849:
Ebraheam Aljazei reviews a 2026 literature on AI as a diagnostic aid for benign prostatic hyperplasia, the non-cancerous prostate growth that burdens many ageing men. Standard tools such as PSA blood tests and scans suffer from false alarms and reader disputes, especially when separating benign growth from cancer. Ten studies published between 2021 and 2025 met the review's criteria.

Models applied to MRI and ultrasound images, tissue slides, and biomarker data generally improved accuracy and reduced disagreement between readers. Several also helped distinguish benign growth from prostate cancer, supporting treatment decisions. Persistent problems temper the promise: small and varied datasets, scarce testing outside the development setting, possible bias in the models, and no shared standard for judging performance.
pmc-13232849:
Elisa Moraga and colleagues report in 2026 a rare case where a multiple sclerosis drug appeared to hold HIV at bay inside one patient. The drug, fingolimod, traps immune cells in lymph nodes and changes the surface of the helper T cells HIV targets. The team compared this patient with untreated-HIV controls, healthy donors, and sclerosis patients on the same drug.

At diagnosis the patient carried a far lower viral load than controls caught at a similar stage. After a year of virus therapy, the hidden reservoir of intact virus ran many times smaller, and after three years none was detectable. Lab infections of the patient cells also took hold poorly. A chance drug overlap has outlined a possible route toward shrinking the reservoir.
pmc-13232949:
Yaojun Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 computer vision study on spotting rice diseases in field images. Finding diseased patches early protects harvests, yet older detection software is slow, misses small lesions, and struggles when light or leaf overlap varies. The group rebuilt a detection model called RT-DETR into a leaner version named ECL-RTDETR.

Their design pairs a lightweight EfficientViT backbone with an upsampling step that preserves fine detail and a dynamic convolution that adapts to changing conditions. Against the original model, the new version raised detection accuracy slightly while running faster and using far fewer parameters and computations. The authors present the model as a practical tool for smart farming equipment.
pmc-13233349:
Yingtong Chen and colleagues reported a 2026 study of retinoblastoma, the most common eye cancer in children. Using single-cell gene data from 189,431 cells across 13 tumors and three normal fetal retina samples, the team mapped the cell types inside these tumors. They focused on a fast-dividing cell group whose cell-cycle genes ran unusually hot.

A gene called BIRC5, which makes the protein survivin, was switched on in nearly all of those aggressive cells and barely present elsewhere. Raising BIRC5 in cultured tumor cells sped growth, invasion, and movement, while silencing it stalled the cell cycle and increased cell death. The authors propose survivin as a drug target aimed squarely at the tumor's most dangerous cell state.
pmc-13233649:
Michael W. Wrucke and colleagues published a 2026 feedback study on a psychosocial screening tool for young adults with cancer. The clinic involved mainly treats blood cancers, including transplant and cellular therapy patients, whose emotional and social needs can be missed in busy adult services. Screening questionnaires were given to patients, and twenty eligible providers were invited to judge the tool, with fourteen responding.

Nearly every responding provider had discussed the screener with a young patient during a visit. Overall views ranged from neutral to positive, suggesting the tool fits clinic workflow acceptably. The authors say provider buy-in is the hinge for routine screening. With that support, they argue, clinics can address young adults' unmet psychosocial needs more consistently.
pmc-13233749:
Habib Hassan, Salman Waheeduddin, and William Macdonald published a 2026 case report of gout appearing in an unexpected place, the larynx. Long-standing, poorly controlled gout deposits urate crystals as chalky lumps called tophi, usually in joints. In this patient, a large tophus grew silently between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage at the front of the neck.

Scans first suggested the lump was stray thyroid tissue. Laryngeal tophi can also cause hoarseness, trouble swallowing, breathing distress, or infection, though this one caused no symptoms. Treatment usually centers on urate-lowering therapy and cutting alcohol and red meat, with surgery reserved for blockages. The authors remind clinicians to consider gout when patients with uncontrolled uric acid develop neck masses.
pmc-13235049:
Ziang Li and colleagues built in 2026 a machine learning system that classifies the taste category of traditional Chinese medicine materials. The five-flavor system, covering sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, and salty, guides drug quality control in that tradition. Human tasting is subjective, so the team used an electronic tongue that records sensor responses. Eighty-four processed herbal slices supplied the training material.

Two model ensembles worked in parallel, one naming the flavor and one grading its intensity. An explanation method showed which sensor channels drove each decision the models made. Performance was moderate overall and differed by flavor, with bitter and sweet recognized best. Two sensor features mattered most across the full analysis. The authors present a data-driven route to digitizing flavor assessment, while calling for larger samples and chemical checks before routine deployment.
pmc-13235149:
Aleksandra Flok and co-authors reviewed in 2026 machine learning studies that predict death, hospital return, or patient subgroups in heart failure. Heart failure is common, deadly, and costly, so early warning of decline could improve care. The team searched a major database for studies from 2014 to 2024 using hospital or health record data. More than one hundred studies entered the synthesis.

Age and several kidney and blood measures appeared most often as important inputs for death prediction. Other illnesses, a kidney waste measure, and age led the list for readmission prediction. Random forest was the algorithm most often recommended across outcome groups, followed by support vector machines. The authors derived nine implications for future work, stressing data quality, wider testing across settings, and clearer explanations of model decisions. Reporting gaps were logged openly rather than hidden.
pmc-13235249:
Anri Hattingh, Jacques Joubert, and Michelle Viljoen reviewed in 2026 South Africa's shift to a new health products regulator in 2018. The old Medicines Control Council had suffered long delays, thin resources, and a growing backlog. The review compared organization, governance, and procedures before and after the change. Public reports, academic papers, and official websites supplied the data.

Median approval time fell from more than two thousand days in 2018 to under eight hundred days in 2020. Registrations of new chemical entities rose sharply across the same period in the figures gathered. The inherited backlog of more than eight thousand applications was cleared by 2022. Greater financial independence and reliance-based review routes helped speed decisions, the authors argue. Priorities ahead include digital reform, staff capacity, and stronger monitoring after products reach the market.
pmc-13239049:
Chuhong Ouyang and colleagues reported in 2026 an eight-year-old girl with a rare facial talon cusp, a small triangular extra bump on the outer face of her right upper front tooth. Such cusps usually grow on the tongue side, and the facial form can invite decay, clash with the bite, and spoil appearance. Hers was classed as the mildest stage under the Mayes system.

Treatment stayed minimally invasive: gentle grinding of the cusp plus a flowable resin restoration, keeping the tooth's pulp alive. Eighteen months later the tooth was developing well with a satisfactory look. The authors also gathered twenty published cases covering twenty-six labial talon cusps to propose a treatment strategy by stage. Prevention and restraint, they argue, beat aggressive reshaping in children.
pmc-13239149:
Aliza Paudyal, Parbatraj Regmi, and Sudha Agrawal reported in 2026 a seventeen-year-old boy whose scalp lesion was operated on as a bacterial infection. Only later did anyone recognize a kerion, the boggy inflammatory form of ringworm of the scalp. He had arrived at surgery with a month of hair loss, scaling, and swelling at the back of the head. Incision and drainage plus two weeks of two antibiotics changed nothing.

Dermatology referral changed the picture: an angry red plaque with ulceration where the cut had been, yellow crusting, scaling, and hair loss. Dermoscopy showed the comma hairs, black dots, and broken hairs typical of fungal infection. The authors warn that kerion mimics surgical disease convincingly. Early recognition, they argue, spares teenagers useless operations, antibiotics, scarring hair loss, and bills.
pmc-13240149:
Iffat Islam Mayesha and co-authors review fuel sources beyond sugar burning in brain tumours in a 2026 narrative article. Gliomas are famous for fermenting glucose, yet their flexibility to run on fats, amino acids, and their own power plants may be what lets them survive treatment.

The synthesis gathers preclinical work showing fat oxidation keeps energy and chemical balance going when oxygen is scarce. Breakdown of glutamine and of serine-family amino acids maintains building blocks for growth, while shifting mitochondrial shapes and mutations tune respiration. One pathway from tryptophan helps tumours hide from immunity. Blocking these routes alongside standard therapy shrank tumours and reversed resistance in models.
pmc-13240549:
Tomohiro Takebe and colleagues report a 2026 case of hookworm infection found during hospital care in Japan. The patient was a 59-year-old man from the Philippines with long-standing iron-deficiency anemia that had no clear cause. He arrived with upper abdominal pain linked to bile duct stones.

After the bile duct problem improved, his pain continued, so doctors examined the full digestive tract. Standard scopes and a swallowable camera capsule revealed many parasites spread through the gut. Special light-based imaging made the worms easier to see and remove. Genetic testing confirmed the species, and drug treatment cleared his symptoms and anemia. The case supports checking for hookworm when anemia stays unexplained.
pmc-13240949:
Tingting Xie and co-authors report a 2026 mixed-methods study of newborn RSV immunization attitudes in Lanzhou, western China. RSV is a leading cause of serious chest infections in infants. The team surveyed pregnant and postpartum women and also interviewed some in depth.

Knowledge of the virus was low, and more than half of respondents had never heard of it. Only a minority said they would accept immunization. Most who were willing preferred a protective antibody injection for the baby after birth over vaccination during pregnancy. Safety worries, cost, and national policy shaped views. Education level and past vaccine experience also mattered. The authors recommend health education, subsidies, and clearer communication.
pmc-13242449:
Luise Pickenhan and Amy L Milton report a 2026 rat study of compulsive-like checking behavior relevant to obsessive-compulsive disorder. Rats performed a task where a special lever lit a cue showing which reward lever was currently correct. Extra presses on that lever served no purpose and modeled dysfunctional checking.

Rats prone to chasing cues, called sign-trackers, showed more useless checking than other rats. Their checking persisted even when the link between checking and the cue was weakened, suggesting habit-driven behavior. When checking was punished with shocks, most rats stopped, yet a minority of sign-trackers kept going. The authors compare that persistence to severe human cases where checking continues despite bad consequences.
pmc-13242749:
Abigail Sara Affoo and co-authors report a 2026 study of adding glaucoma checks to diabetic eye screening in Trinidad and Tobago. Glaucoma is very common among Caribbean people and steals sight silently. Diabetic screening already photographs the back of the eye, so the same images might flag glaucoma suspects.

Over seventeen hundred adults with diabetes were screened in community settings. About one in ten met the photo criteria for glaucoma suspicion and were invited for a full check-up. Only a quarter of those invited attended, which limited confirmed counts. Among those examined, most referrals proved correct. The math suggests much hidden glaucoma in this population. The authors judge the combined screening feasible and worthwhile.
pmc-13242849:
Jeffrey A Bair and co-authors publish a 2026 study of time-of-day effects in dry eye disease from a large Norwegian clinic cohort. Patients often say symptoms swing across the day, yet earlier research disagreed. Over a thousand patients had symptom scores and tear film tests recorded with their appointment times.

Symptoms peaked in the morning and evening. Objective tear measures, however, shifted only trivially with clock time, and rhythm analysis found no meaningful daily cycle in them. The gap between felt symptoms and measured signs persisted across the day. The authors suggest time of day matters little for scheduling objective testing. They add that symptom swings likely come from factors standard tests do not capture.
pmc-13243249:
Chi-Hsin Chen and colleagues compare breathing help for cardiac arrest patients outside the hospital in a 2026 study. Crews can squeeze a bag by hand or use an automatic transport ventilator with a set pressure limit. How much air each method delivers to the lungs was not well known.

The team reviewed 178 adults treated in Hsinchu County, Taiwan, during 2023 after advanced airway placement. One ventilator group used a lower pressure limit, one a higher limit, and one group got bag ventilation. The lower-limit group received somewhat larger breaths than the higher-limit group. No method linked to better rates of restored circulation. The results suggest ventilators match bag breathing on air delivery in this setting.
pmc-13243849:
Lu Wang and a large team compare two clot-busting drugs for major stroke in a 2026 study. After vein treatment, a clot in a large brain artery can dissolve, move downstream, or stay put. Whether the newer drug tenecteplase moves clots more than alteplase was unknown.

The team reviewed patients treated from 2022 to 2024 and matched 373 patients per drug. Clots moved more often after tenecteplase, and the edge was clear only when vessel opening began within an hour. Patients whose clots moved also regained independence more often at three months. Tenecteplase users likewise did better overall. The findings link early clot movement to better recovery.
pmc-13244249:
Fatma Elnaggar and colleagues describe a nurse whose eye was infected by a splash of stomach-tube fluid at work. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Infectious Diseases in 2026. The forty-year-old, a contact lens wearer, was caring for a critically ill child when the exposure happened. Cultures from her lens and live microscopy revealed a four-way infection: the amoeba Acanthamoeba plus three bacteria.

Her cornea developed the ring-shaped marks and haze of advanced keratitis, and its inner layer began to fail. Strong anti-amoeba drugs and targeted antibiotics brought the infection under control. The price was heavy scarring, and a partial corneal transplant is now planned to restore her sight. The germs involved normally live in guts and hospitals, not eyes. The authors flag the case as a warning for eye protection and infection control among healthcare staff.
pmc-13244949:
Satoru Munakata and co-authors survey how mice carrying human immune systems have become central tools for studying immune disease. Their review appeared in Inflammation and Regeneration in 2026. Humanized mice are immune-deficient animals engrafted with human immune cells, liver cells, or thymus tissue, building an approximation of human immunity that ordinary lab mice cannot offer. The review traces progress in rebuilding a diverse human immune system inside the mouse.

Recent work layers in patient-specific elements, such as the self-attacking antibodies and T cells behind autoimmune disease, and pairs the animals with single-cell analyses of human tissue. Applications span modeling autoimmune conditions, testing drug candidates, and probing why therapies fail. The authors call these models foundational for both research and drug discovery. Their caveats are practical: reconstitution is still incomplete and variable. The trajectory, though, is toward models that fail less often for mouse-specific reasons.
pmc-13247249:
Bidard, Barrios, and Bianchini interpret a major breast cancer trial in this 2026 letter in NPJ Breast Cancer. The SERENA-6 trial tested switching treatment at the first molecular sign of resistance. When a blood test detected an emerging ESR1 mutation, patients moved early. They left an aromatase inhibitor for camizestrant, an oral drug that degrades the estrogen receptor, before scans showed progression.

The authors defend and explain that design. They argue it is proactive evolutionary oncology: strike a resistant clone while it is still small, rather than waiting for it to dominate. They address doubts about letting circulating tumor DNA guide treatment decisions. They also place the trial among recent setbacks for similar drugs used without targeting. Their reading aims to guide clinicians weighing the switch.
pmc-13247549:
Kun Zhu and co-authors train learning models to predict death in hospital after bypass surgery in a 2026 cohort study. Bypass grafting stays the main surgery for blocked heart arteries. Older risk scores miss some of what modern data can catch.

The study drew 21,443 patients from a national Chinese surgery registry covering 2017 to 2020. Fifteen algorithms were built and checked against two standard risk scores. A boosting model won, beating both scores on the held-back test group. Death in hospital ran near two in every hundred patients. Better forecasts can guide consent talks and focus watchful care on the frailest patients.
pmc-13248349: Yang and colleagues issued this correction in Cancer Cell International in 2026 for their paper on silencing the uracil-DNA glycosylase gene in colorectal cancer. One citation in the reference list was printed in the wrong form. The notice replaces it with the correct reference, a 2025 article analyzing the 2022 global cancer statistics report and comparing cancer burden in China with the rest of the world. No results or conclusions of the original paper change.
pmc-13249049:
Qi and colleagues followed a treat-and-extend injection plan for wet macular degeneration, in a 2026 Chinese study. Thirty-seven eyes received aflibercept shots, with intervals stretched or shortened by response, over twenty-four months. This approach aims to keep vision gains while cutting clinic visits, and the team also hunted for scan features that forecast success.

Vision improved significantly by three months and held through the study period, while the macula's central thickness fell. Two baseline features, that thickness and fluid under the retina, best predicted who responded well. The authors support using the starting scan to tailor how aggressively each patient is scheduled.
pmc-13249749:
da Silva Martins and colleagues tested semi-wild horses for leptospirosis exposure in Brazil's Roraima state, in a 2026 study. Lavradeiro horses roam Indigenous community lands in the northern Amazon, and leptospirosis, a waterborne bacterial disease, passes between animals and people. Blood from three hundred eighty-seven horses was checked against eighteen bacterial variants with the standard agglutination test.

About sixteen percent of horses carried antibodies, the first documented exposure in this horse population. Adults tested positive more than foals, and horses in flood-prone areas showed the highest rates, near a quarter. Strong reactions clustered in one municipality. The authors urge joint animal and human surveillance and protection of the Lavradeiro as a heritage breed.
pmc-13250549:
Harada and a large team trace how sesame seeds rebuild their protective lignan chemicals as they sprout. Their 2026 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences paper covers compounds such as sesamin and sesamolin, long studied in seeds. During germination the oily lignans are fully converted into sugar-tagged forms, and the enzymes behind that switch were unknown.

The team found a family of oxygenase enzymes that rework sesamin and sesamolin into new oxidized forms during sprouting. Sugar-adding enzymes then tag those products in a set order, creating the final variety of glycosides. One oxygenase also proved central to making a key sesame lignan during seed formation itself. The work shows how plants reuse and reshuffle their enzyme toolkits as seeds develop and wake.
pmc-13252949:
Donato Morena and colleagues systematically review micro- and nanoplastic exposure as a possible driver of depressive-like behavior in a 2026 paper. Tiny plastic particles are now everywhere in the environment, and they can cross into the brain. Their effects on mood-related behavior had never been gathered in one place.

Ten studies met the team's criteria: nine in animals and one cross-sectional study in people. Rodents exposed to plastic particles, mostly polystyrene, consistently developed depressive-like behaviors, and fish and other aquatic animals showed compatible changes. Effects grew with dose and shifted with particle size, exposure timing, and sex. The single human study linked higher estimated environmental exposure with more depressive symptoms. The authors caution that the evidence is thin and uneven. They call for standardized behavior tests, realistic exposure levels, and long-term human studies with direct exposure measurement.
pmc-13253249:
Shuang Yang, Chen Tian, and Ding Peng compare gut microbes in Parkinson's disease against constipation alone in a 2026 controlled study. Constipation affects most Parkinson's patients and itself reshapes gut bacteria, which has muddied efforts to find disease-linked changes. To strip out that overlap, the team compared twenty constipated Parkinson's patients against fifteen people with functional constipation only.

Sequencing fecal bacteria showed the Parkinson's group carried richer microbe communities. Beneath broad similarity, distinct shifts stood out: higher shares of Paraprevotella, Akkermansia, a Ruminococcaceae group, and Campylobacter. Predicted microbe functions were weaker in the Parkinson's group for making tyrosine, a building block of dopamine, and for glutathione pathways, a core defense system. The authors read the pattern as Parkinson's-linked damage separate from slow transit. They say it supports the idea that the disease can begin in the gut, with particular microbes and a leaky barrier involved.
pmc-13253849:
Annika Schulte and colleagues study how cell junctions are built in a 2026 paper. Tight junctions seal the gaps between surface cells, forming a barrier and passing signals. The team asked how one junction protein, JAM-C, connects to ZO-2, a scaffold protein that links junctions to the cell's inner frame.

Cell tests and lab experiments showed JAM-C binds ZO-2 directly, needing two parts of ZO-2 working as one unit. JAM-C sat only at tight junctions in sorted surface cells. A sister protein, JAM-A, also lowered JAM-C gene activity, a finding the authors link to how junctions sense force.
pmc-13254149:
Trinari and co-authors pool trials of SSRI drugs for children with autism. Their 2026 review searches seven databases for controlled trials against placebo. Parents often face these drugs for anxiety, repeated behavior, or obsessive symptoms, with unclear payoff.

Seven trials with six hundred six children took part. Evidence was too weak to judge effects on repeated behaviors or anxiety, and weak data hinted at little effect on obsessive or disruptive behavior. Overall daily function likely barely changed, while side effects rose slightly. No trial tracked mood outcomes in this group. The authors conclude current evidence shows no benefit and urge case-by-case risk weighing until better trials arrive.
pmc-13254549:
Arpapan Prakobkarn and colleagues describe two new lizard species from Thailand in a 2026 systematic study of the Calotes irawadi complex. Calotes are day-active agamid lizards spread across South and Southeast Asia, and the irawadi group had been carved out of a catch-all species only in recent revisions. The new species are named Calotes thailandensis and Calotes maehongsonensis.

The case rests on three kinds of evidence: mitochondrial DNA sequences from two genes, detailed body measurements, and bone structure. Both new species sit closest to C. irawadi and C. wangi on the family tree. Males of the new species combine a wider pelvis with a smaller head than true irawadi. Each also carries a signature trait, one a longer spine above the ear, the other a distinctly longer hindlimb. The authors credit combined molecular and anatomical work for untangling look-alike populations.
pmc-13254749:
Hannah Biemans, Astrid de Vries, and Reinoud Brouwer study cold therapy after partial knee replacement in a 2026 trial analysis. Patients used a cryo-compression brace, which applies cold and pressure, five times daily for six weeks, or got standard care. Pain, function, life quality, and oxycodone use were tracked.

At six weeks, pain at rest did not differ between groups. The cold group used 46 percent less oxycodone, though the absolute gap was small, at a median of 3.5 five-milligram tablets total. Work and life quality scores improved more with cold therapy but fell short of the meaningful-change threshold.
pmc-13255149:
Jose Alfonso Ontiveros and colleagues report four cases linking a depression drug to new symptoms in a 2026 case series. Bupropion is an antidepressant also used to help people stop smoking. Four patients with mood disorders, none with past obsessive symptoms, developed obsessive-compulsive symptoms after starting the drug.

Symptoms grew in intensity over time on the drug. After bupropion was stopped, symptoms eased notably and fully remitted over time. Standard scales tracked the symptoms and their course. The authors say the brain basis is not yet understood and urge clinicians to watch for this effect when prescribing.
pmc-13255749:
Valfré and colleagues tested how nursery enrichment shapes resilience in more than six hundred piglets on a commercial farm. Litters received a single chain, chains plus a weekly rotated extra object, or several objects at once. A subsample later faced an attentional bias test, while the team also scored behavior qualitatively and measured hair cortisol and a brain growth factor in blood.

Attention measures barely separated the groups, but coping behavior did: each treatment showed a distinct pattern of excretion, standing, or escape attempts. Piglets with several objects looked calmer and less tense, while the single-chain group carried higher cortisol and lower growth factor. Enrichment style, the authors argue, tunes stress biology.
pmc-13256349:
Xin Hu and co-authors present a 2026 food-engineering study of 3D-printed meat substitutes built from wine-cap mushroom mycelium and pea protein. Mycelium grows fast and forms natural fibers like muscle, yet its weak gel makes printing messy. The team tested curdlan, a gelling polysaccharide, as the structural fix across several ink recipes.

Chopping the mycelium for twenty seconds dispersed clumps while keeping its fiber network. Adding curdlan steadily improved extrusion smoothness, printed shape accuracy, water holding, and heat stability. Cooked products grew harder, springier, and chewier as curdlan rose. One formula, half mycelium with five percent pea protein and six percent curdlan, balanced printability and texture best, landing closest to boiled chicken breast. The authors offer the recipe as a practical route to realistic mushroom-based meats.
pmc-13257149:
Kevin Ghavalas and colleagues review in 2026 how aroma compounds in milk are measured. Aroma drives flavor, and long-life milk often tastes different from fresh milk in ways buyers notice. Dairy studies, the authors argue, too often run chemical tests apart from sensory tests.

Sample preparation, volatile extraction, and chromatographic profiling are each examined, alongside sensory methods. No single approach wins for every milk type or research goal. Multidimensional chromatography resolved complex flavor mixtures better in several cases. Joining instrument data with trained tasting gave the clearest picture of processing effects. Inconsistent designs across studies limit what can be concluded today. Dairy scientists are urged to adopt standard, matrix-fitting methods so results can finally be compared across laboratories.
pmc-13258349:
Violeta Nour leads a 2026 study optimizing ultrasound extraction of phenolics from pear pomace, the press residue of juice making. A statistical design varied alcohol strength, extraction time, and ultrasonic power to maximize phenolic yield and antioxidant activity from the dried powder.

Ultrasonic power showed the strongest curved effect, helping up to a point and hurting beyond it. The best recipe used moderate alcohol for about an hour at a mid-high power setting. Chlorogenic acid, rutin, and epicatechin led the phenolic profile in the extracts. Fruit processors gain a valorization route for a bulky by-product stream. Turning pomace into antioxidant ingredients could lift pear economics while cutting waste, provided drying and solvent recovery costs pencil out at scale.
pmc-13258749:
Mehmet Yildiz and coauthors link depression with chronic disease load in a 2026 primary care records study. Just over three thousand adults at a Turkish family health center were included. Depression status came from psychiatrist diagnoses recorded within the past year.

About one in eight patients carried a depression diagnosis. Those patients were older, more often female, and carried more chronic conditions. One blood inflammation ratio ran higher in the depression group, while another ran lower. Three other ratios showed no clear group difference. Family doctors see support for treating mood and long term disease as connected problems.
pmc-13259049:
Xinpeng Chen and colleagues sharpen body screening images from passive millimeter waves in a 2026 paper. The imaging method protects privacy while revealing hidden objects on people. Single polarization processing often creates stray false pixels or misses real objects.

Their method splits images from several polarizations into three structural layers. Each layer is fused with rules matched to its scale, preserving edges throughout. Tests showed stronger hidden object contrast and better detection accuracy than mainstream methods. False alarms and missed detections both fell in their experiments. Airport and venue security teams gain a processing framework that uses polarization information far more fully.
pmc-13259249:
Asma Komal and Shuaiyong Li survey intrusion detection for connected device networks in a 2026 review. Literature from twenty twenty one to early twenty twenty six was sorted by detection style, learning method, placement, and evaluation practice. Tiny devices limit how heavy protection can be.

Classic signature and anomaly methods stand beside modern learning approaches in the taxonomy. Newer options include shared learning across devices, explainable models, tiny on device models, and language model aids. Public test datasets and scoring methods receive detailed comparison. Open problems span realistic data, attack robustness, privacy, and scale. Security architects gain selection guidelines for the next generation of device defenses.
pmc-13259349:
Soroush Ahmadi and Azizollah Khormali study a polymer scale inhibitor inside carbonate rock cores in a 2026 paper. Calcium sulfate scale chokes oil flow in such reservoirs. Flooding tests plus jar and tube checks set the working dose and tracked how the inhibitor washes back out.

Forty parts per million gave over ninety percent inhibition at high heat. Return concentration fell as more fluid passed, heat rose, or flow sped up. Two statistical models predicted return behavior across early and late flow ranges with excellent fit. Flow volume and injection rate mattered most, while acidity mattered least. Field engineers gain dosing models that keep protection above the effective line.
pmc-13259849:
Euntaek Hong and colleagues surveyed in 2026 the mental health of forensic investigators after the Jeju Air crash in South Korea. The December 2024 crash killed 179 people, and investigators had to identify victims at the crash site. Their survey covered 735 investigators, including 224 who had worked at that site nine months earlier.

Standard scales measured trauma symptoms, depression, anxiety, alcohol use, and suicide risk across the group. Probable post-traumatic stress disorder appeared in about one in ten of all respondents and was more common among those sent to the site. Distress during victim identification, harsh site conditions, and heavy traumatic exposure were linked with trauma symptoms. The authors call for trauma-aware mental health support for staff who do this work.
pmc-13262049:
Andrew J Furlong and colleagues reported in 2026 first tests of fixed bed chemical looping for cleaning up variable industrial waste gases. Chemical looping uses a metal oxide carrier to hand oxygen to fuel gas, keeping the exhaust ready for carbon capture without dilution by air. Their case study was the electric arc furnace, whose off-gas swings wildly in flow and makeup.

Copper and iron-based carriers burned bottled furnace-like gas in a bench reactor with high use of the carrier before breakthrough. Signs of uneven flow and surface resistance appeared at bench scale, which the authors expect larger units to avoid. The iron carrier collected some coke and lost a little activity, fixable by heat control and a touch of steam. The team proposes a reactor with outside heat removal to smooth load swings.
pmc-13263449:
Timothy Lee and colleagues synthesized in 2026 recent North American experience with isolated tricuspid valve surgery, an operation once considered forbiddingly dangerous. Their systematic review and meta-analysis covered twelve studies published between 2020 and mid-2025. Outcomes included operative death, volume trends, and repair versus replacement results.

Operative mortality ran five to eight percent in national cohorts but only about two percent at reference centers, and it has trended downward. Pooled across studies, mortality sat near six percent. Repair carried clearly lower death odds than replacement and far fewer new pacemakers. Case volumes peaked around 2017 and then leveled off as catheter therapies spread. One high-volume hospital reported mortality under two percent across more than a hundred cases. The authors conclude the surgery grows safer with selection and experience.
pmc-13263849:
Jun-Wei Pan and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a panel of familiar blood tumor markers can help tell upper urinary tract cancer from look-alike conditions. Their retrospective study held 140 patients: sixty with the tract cancer, forty-four with a common kidney cancer, and thirty-six with benign urinary blockage. Seven classic markers were measured and compared across groups.

Three markers ran clearly higher in the tract cancer group than in either comparison group. Marker levels also moved with the disease itself, falling after surgery and rising again when cancer progressed. The team combined six markers into a testing strategy that held up across every comparison they ran. In surgical specimens, the number of marker shifts tracked tumor load closely. Tissue staining supported the blood findings. The authors conclude group testing beats any single marker for this elusive cancer.
pmc-13264249:
Alba Tomás-Sitjes and colleagues map how brain vessel cells recycle surface proteins in a 2026 proteomics study. The blood-brain barrier depends on specialized endothelial cells whose membrane proteins control nutrient entry, signaling and immune traffic. The team measured turnover for roughly one thousand proteins in rat cells. Turnover means how fast proteins are taken in, recycled and broken down. Rates were taken under healthy and inflamed conditions, comparing brain cells with vessel cells from elsewhere in the body.

Brain cells showed a turnover fingerprint distinct from peripheral cells, beyond simple protein lists. Inflammation shifted that fingerprint toward the peripheral pattern. Abundance changes flagged immune proteins, while turnover changes highlighted vessel remodeling proteins. Turnover itself emerges as a dynamic regulator of barrier identity and of its failure during inflammation.
pmc-13264549:
Irmand Leblond Mikiela Ndzoumbou and co-authors present a 2026 maths paper on networks of evolution equations, the rules that describe how quantities change over space and time. Older models often assumed every node in a network was the same shape and size. Their framework allows nodes that differ and links at edges as well as inside.

For the single-value case, they prove that flow is conserved and that one positive solution exists. For the multi-value case, they prove like results and show the total mass stays bounded when the system conserves mass. They test the theory on a predator-prey model with two nodes. Computer runs match the theory, and the authors offer the framework for spread and transport problems.
pmc-13264849:
Dimple Sushma Alluri and Felix M Pabon-Rodriguez apply machine learning to intensive care outcomes for viral hepatitis patients in a 2026 retrospective study. A large United States critical care database with tens of thousands of admissions supplied social, clinical and resource data. Models including random forest, logistic regression and gradient boosting were compared on three linked predictions. One was how long intensive care would last. The others were the hospital discharge outcome and where the patient would go at discharge.

Hepatitis drives over a million deaths yearly worldwide, and its intensive care course is resource heavy. Disease-specific prediction has lagged behind general intensive care analytics. Accurate forecasts could guide bed planning, family counseling and discharge arrangements. Performance differences among algorithms are the core result readers should weigh, alongside fairness across patient subgroups.
pmc-13264949:
Karoline Louise Imingen Selvik and co-authors wrote a 2026 Norwegian study on family money worries and teen mental distress. They compared what teens feel about family finances with official records of parent income and education. Data came from two waves of the Young-HUNT surveys, in 2006 to 2008 and 2017 to 2019, linked with parent data.

Each wave held more than 8,000 teens aged 13 to 19. Teens who felt their family was worse off than others reported more anxiety and depression symptoms, with the gap a bit larger in girls. Official parent income and education showed little or no link to teen symptoms. Counting parent mental health did not change the pattern, and results were much the same in both waves. The authors say felt financial stress, not recorded wealth, is what tracks teen distress.
pmc-13265649:
Meng Tian and colleagues design bacterial partnerships that fight ginseng root rot while boosting growth, in a 2026 study. The disease, caused by a soil fungus, is the most severe threat to ginseng farming. Helpful bacteria from roots and soil were combined into synthetic communities. Their joint effects and mechanisms were clarified.

Most combined groups inhibited the fungus more strongly than single strains. Several mixes also promoted plant growth. In field tests, six mixes controlled disease by more than half, with the best near two-thirds. Treated roots carried far less fungus, and colonisation exceeded single strains. Soil and defence enzymes also rose.
pmc-13266149:
Jeong-Woong Park and colleagues test dog gum microbes for calming inflammation triggered by a gum disease bacterium, published in 2026. Porphyromonas gingivalis drives gum disease partly through a surface toxin that sparks immune responses. A novel microbe community from dog gums was cultured. Mouse immune cells exposed to the toxin received the candidate microbes.

Nitric oxide, an inflammation marker, fell with microbe treatment. Three inflammatory genes were dialled down compared with toxin-only cells. Toxin alone had raised those same genes. The authors say the calming mechanism remains unknown. Further work should clarify how the candidate microbes reduce inflammation.
pmc-13266849:
Agustina A Pontecorvo and Enrique F Elli discuss in 2026 whether removing the esophagus can help selected patients whose esophageal adenocarcinoma has already spread. Surgery for metastatic disease was long ruled out, but stronger drug treatments have reopened the question. They comment on a study of stage IV patients who had surgery after long courses of systemic therapy.

Matched comparisons showed better survival for operated patients with distant spread than for similar patients managed without surgery. Results were best at experienced centers working in close multidisciplinary teams. Oddly, one stage group fared worse than the metastatic group, a pattern the authors link to hidden spread missed by scans. They frame surgery as targeted disease control for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13267549:
Dhathri Priya Bandi and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of gum bacteria in pregnant women with diabetes of pregnancy. Both gestational diabetes and gum disease involve lasting inflammation and may worsen outcomes for mother and baby. The team studied 80 pregnant women, all with gum disease: 40 with diabetes of pregnancy and 40 without.

Samples of plaque from under the gum line were tested for seven known gum pathogens. Women with diabetes carried higher loads of five of them, including Porphyromonas gingivalis. That species tracked closely with deeper gum pockets and loss of gum attachment. Gum measures and blood sugar test results both helped predict pathogen levels. The authors call the link between blood sugar control and gum microbes a two-way street worth clinical attention.
pmc-13267749:
Derrick Bennett and colleagues wrote a 2026 summary of a workshop on statistical reviewing for medical journals. Statistics in medical papers have grown more complex, yet journals struggle to find trained statistical reviewers. A national research group ran an online workshop to close that gap, aimed at people new to the task.

Statistical review checks whether a paper's methods fit its question, were carried out correctly, and are openly reported. The summary shares the workshop's key lessons and practical advice for new reviewers. It covers what to look for, how to write a useful review, and why this work matters for trust in medical research. The authors hope more statisticians and clinicians will take up reviewing.
pmc-13269049:
Natalia Quintero Serrano and Olga Lucía Melo Trujillo published a case report in 2026 about a 76-year-old man with gout. Soon after he gave himself one 75 milligram shot of diclofenac, a pain and swelling drug, he developed a severe skin reaction. The reaction, toxic epidermal necrolysis, makes large areas of skin blister and peel away.

At the hospital, sores covered 40.5 percent of his body surface, with severe mouth and organ damage. His risk score of 5 meant an estimated death rate of about 85 percent. He died soon after arrival despite strong supportive care. A scoring method rated the drug link as only possible, since other drugs were also in his history.
pmc-13269649:
Yair Alvarez-Ricardo and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on three new vanadium compounds built with ring-shaped partner molecules, tested against cancer cells. Their structures were checked with standard lab methods, and one was mapped exactly by X-ray crystallography, a method that reveals atomic layout.

Across six human cancer cell lines, the compounds beat the common drug cisplatin in five, needing lower doses to halve cell growth. One compound was strongest against a lung cancer line, and another against a colon cancer line. Unlike cisplatin, they barely harmed healthy fiber cells. One compound pushed lung cancer cells into late-stage programmed death without tissue-rotting death. Computer studies also showed the compounds stick to DNA.
pmc-13269849:
Luisa Di Paola and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on recovering a pigment protein complex from shellfish waste. Shells of European lobster and Atlantic blue crab hold astaxanthin, a pigment with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Computer models examined how the complex could carry the pigment for drug and cosmetic use.

Simulations suggested astaxanthin would compete with a cell defender protein at its binding site. Freeing that defender would switch on the cell's own antioxidant machinery. Early lab evidence supported the modeling. The authors propose shell waste as a source of a bioactive agent for diseases tied to cell stress, including cancer. They stress that animal and human studies must first confirm the promise.
pmc-13270249:

pmc-13270549:

pmc-13270949:

pmc-13271149:

pmc-13271349:

pmc-13271549:
Nakul Verma and coauthors describe in 2026 the features and outcomes of cavitary retinoblastoma, a child eye cancer that forms hollow spaces inside the tumor. pmc-13271949:
Rong-rong Zhang and coauthors follow in 2026 wound healing in people with diabetic kidney disease who take SGLT2 inhibitor drugs. Infection and kidney outcomes at six months also showed no clear difference. The results ease concern about continuing these drugs during wound care.
pmc-13272149:
Heng Chen and coauthors estimate in 2026 how emergency policy changes affected regional emergency logistics capacity across China. Contingency plans are meant to make disaster response faster and better stocked, but hard evidence of their effect is scarce. Provinces whose plans matched the national text closely gained a measurable rise in response capacity, about forty-seven percent on the study's scale. Matching the text alone did not guarantee strength, though; weak alignment reliably went with weak capacity.
pmc-13272249:
Lena Marie Süß is lead author of a 2026 journal article on blocking P2Y6 receptors to slow kidney fibrosis. Fibrosis is the scarring that drives chronic kidney disease. pmc-13272349:
Chen Yuhang and coauthors sort in 2026 older adults in two Chengdu districts by how well their basic mental needs are met or blocked. Life satisfaction, distress scores, and social support helped explain who fell in each group. The authors use the groups to guide local mental health work with older adults.
pmc-13272449:
Ran Meng and coauthors review in 2026 hydrogel therapies that deliver healing cargo directly into heart muscle damaged by heart attack. About seven million heart attacks occur yearly, and surviving muscle often scars into heart failure that drugs and devices cannot reverse. Injectable gels suit the heart because they are water-rich, body-friendly, and can carry living cargo.

The review traces the path from blocked artery to scarred, failing heart, then compares gels loaded with drugs, bioactive molecules, cells, or exosomes. Each cargo class attacks a different step, from calming inflammation to growing vessels. The authors judge hydrogels a promising repair platform still proving itself clinically.
pmc-13272549:
Ellis Eikenboom, Helena van Doorn, and Anja Wagner wrote a 2026 authors' reply about womb surveillance in Lynch syndrome in the Netherlands. Lynch syndrome raises cancer risk, and their earlier paper questioned whether regular checks of the womb lining help Dutch carriers. The reply answers comments on that paper.

They explain why the subtype of overgrown womb lining did not change their advice, since surgery is advised for any such growth. They note that more growths and cancers were found in the checked group, yet cancers were not less advanced in a way that cut later treatment or improved survival. A much larger study is needed, they argue.
pmc-13272749:
Fang Zhang leads a 2026 study of a protein called SEMA6A in colorectal cancer, cancer of the colon and rectum. The protein was lower in cancer tissue than normal, and low levels linked to more aggressive tumors and a poorer outlook. The team tested what raising SEMA6A does in cells and in animals.

It acted by lowering a protein called ISG15, which otherwise helps stabilize TGF-beta, a signal that shields tumors. Patients with high SEMA6A and low ISG15 responded better to immunotherapy, and raising SEMA6A improved anti-PD-1 treatment in mice.
pmc-13273349:
Santi Poungcharean and colleagues described early life development in seven wild mouth-brooding fighting fish in a 2026 study from Thailand. These small air breathing fish hold eggs and young in the father's mouth for protection. Knowing how each species grows helps tell them apart while young.

The team bred fish gathered from type localities and followed their young through larval and juvenile stages. Most species released their young at a set stage about eleven days after fertilization, though one took up to twenty days. Young then reached the juvenile stage within a month of release. Counts of body segments and fin rays differed by species, as did pigment bands on the head and stripes along the body. A step by step identification key with illustrations sums up the differences.
pmc-13274549:
Xiaocui Ma and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on what shapes bird diversity in a small Chinese nature reserve. Louzishan, in Liaoning Province, offers a test of how plant productivity and habitat variety affect birds across seasons. The team surveyed bird communities in summer breeding season and in winter, scoring greenness from satellites as a stand-in for productivity.

In summer, greener sites held more bird species and more varied bird traits, and species replacement along the greenness gradient drove community differences. Winter flipped the pattern: habitat variety related negatively to species counts, and distance between sites drove differences instead. The authors read this as environment filtering birds in summer but limited movement ruling in winter.
pmc-13274849:
Madisen S Mason and co-authors present a 2026 protocol article for growing a deadly childhood brainstem tumor in mouse embryos. pmc-13275249:
Andrea Nana Ofori-Boadu and Rabiatu Bonku built a theory of professional identity in women studying architecture, engineering, and construction in a 2026 study. These fields are male dominated, and women must negotiate clashing expectations as they become professionals. Earlier work mostly took snapshots rather than following the process over time.

The team interviewed 78 undergraduates at five United States institutions across seven rounds, comparing accounts as they built their theory. Women moved gradually from isolating clashing parts of themselves to blending them into one professional identity. A shared coping pattern also emerged, which they name with a new term: women drew on collective resilience, aiming at influential, helpful roles that widen inclusion. The framework ties identity content, process, and setting together.
pmc-13275349:
Hend M. Al-Atif and co-authors surveyed body art knowledge and practice among young adults in Saudi Arabia in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Piercing and tattooing have moved from tradition to mainstream self expression, yet safety habits lag. Their online questionnaire reached people who already had body art across all regions of the country.

The final group held 1,472 participants. More than three quarters knew body art carries health risks, but only about a third recognized non-infectious complications. Most doubted the hygiene standards of the procedures they had used. Ear piercing was by far the most common practice, while tattoos were rarer, and interest among newcomers was low. Age and gender shaped risk views. The authors call for public teaching and stricter regulation of practitioners.
pmc-13275449:
Efrah Ahmed Ibrahim offers a 2026 systematic review of radionuclide therapy across 54 African nations. The review measures availability, travel access, staffing, and cost in one combined analysis.

The author screened thousands of records and kept 47 studies, alongside data from global cancer and atomic energy sources. Radioactive iodine for thyroid cancer existed in only about half of the countries. A newer prostate treatment was present in just seven, and specialist doctors were far scarcer than in Europe. Local production cut drug costs by more than ninety percent, which supports regional hub investment.
pmc-13276049:
Giorgia Picci and a large team report a 2026 brain study of how cortical structure and activity stay linked across life. They used magnetoencephalography, which records magnetic signals from brain activity, in one of the largest lifespan samples of its kind. Participants numbered 388 and ranged from age six to eighty-four.

Coupling between local rhythms and cortical thickness changed with age in distinct frequency bands. Sensory and motor networks showed strong, steady coupling, while higher association networks showed weaker and more variable links. The pattern followed a gradient from basic sensory areas toward complex association areas. The authors frame the results as a baseline map for healthy brain ageing.
pmc-13276349:
Yuchen Ping and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on why a prized Chinese medicinal herb tastes of place. Atractylodes macrocephala, one of the famous Zhejiang herbs, varies in potency by region. Traditional thinking credits local soil, but the microbes living around roots may matter more.

Their abundance tracked with root growth and active compound levels. The authors say soil nutrients, microbe-driven carbon and nitrogen cycling, and plant resource shifts together create the herb's regional authenticity.
pmc-13276449:
Dian Kusuma and Hario Megatsari present a 2026 journal article on whether local tobacco laws can cut teen smoking where national action lags. Indonesia has some of the world's highest smoking rates, especially among boys and men. Bogor City tightened its local tobacco rules from 2014 while national enforcement stayed weak.

The team compared Bogor with a synthetic control, a blend of similar districts among nearly five hundred nationwide, over a decade of data. The gaps grew over time, suggesting lasting impact. Adult men showed smaller gains, and their current smoking stayed above the control. The authors back local action plus stronger national measures.
pmc-13276749:
SM Tawhid and colleagues publish a 2026 dataset of budgerigar flight filmed in stereo for collision-avoidance research. Small birds dodge each other in flight with ease that robots still struggle to copy. Frame-level three-dimensional tracks of real flocks can teach engineers how they do it.

Every bird was hand-labelled in both views with a body box and four key points. Reconstructed three-dimensional trajectories, calibration files, and processing scripts are included, with quality checks such as reprojection error reported.
pmc-13277249:
Nevra Koç leads a 2026 study of appetite hormones and body weight in children with inherited metabolic diseases. The authors link the shifts to diet, toxic buildup, and organ strain. They urge regular hormone checks and personal diet plans for long-term care of these children.
pmc-13277749:

pmc-13278449:

pmc-13279149:

pmc-13279749:

pmc-13280649:

pmc-13281949:

pmc-13282049:

pmc-13282549:

pmc-13282849:

pmc-13283449:

pmc-13284049:

pmc-13284749:

pmc-13284849:

pmc-13285549:

pmc-13285649:

pmc-13285749:

pmc-13286549:

pmc-13286849:

pmc-13287149:

pmc-13287349:

pmc-13287549:

pmc-13287749:

The authors offer the method for targeted cooling programmes worldwide.
pmc-13288549:

pmc-13290449:

pmc-13291349:

pmc-13293449:

pmc-13295049:

pmc-13297049:

pmc-13305949:

pmc-13306949:

The 50 nm beads drove strongest oxidative stress and lasting self-cleaning activity, slowing growth. Mid-size beads caused moderate effects, while 200 nm beads triggered sharp early cell harm with weaker self-cleaning. The clear size split in harm gives strong grounds for tight rules on the smallest bits.
pmc-13307849:
Ahmet Ali Berber and co-authors gather in 2026 what is known about microplastic harm to amphibians and reptiles, groups already in steep decline worldwide. Tiny plastic bits under 5 millimetres now show up in fresh water, soil, and remote springs, and they have been found in every major group studied so far.

Bits can reach sea turtle embryos before they hatch, and they seem to weaken defence against deadly fungal and viral disease in these animals. Most work so far covers frogs and sea turtles in rich regions, while snakes, lizards, and caecilians stay poorly known. The authors urge that plastic loads count in formal risk checks for these species.
pmc-13308549:
Yanda Zhang and co-authors survey in 2026 what patients with high blood pressure plus aortic tear or swelling know, feel, and do about tear prevention. At Henan Chest Hospital, 619 patients took part from September to December 2023, and scores for each of the three areas were tallied.

Knowledge scores sat very low, while stance scores were warm and self told habits sat in the middle range for this group. In their model, knowledge shaped stance, and stance in turn shaped daily habits for prevention. Knowledge also reached habits through stance as a middle step. Teaching must thus build true grasp, not just good will, if habits are to shift for good.
pmc-13308649:
Forrest Bohler and co-authors report in 2026 surgery for a rare chest wall sarcoma, CIC-DUX4, at a small rural hospital in Montana. A woman aged 40 years came in with a fast growing, weeping mass on the left front chest that had grown for six weeks.

Scans showed a local soft tissue lump with no sign of spread to far sites in her body. Wide cut out took the mass plus the deep sheet beneath it in one block at the rural site. Tests confirmed the rare sarcoma type, and she healed with no snags after surgery. Scans two years on showed no return or spread, which backs surgery first care for local cases.
pmc-13308849:
Million Phiri and co-authors break down in 2026 why modern contraceptive use rose among sexually active women in Lesotho from 2004 to 2023, and how fair that rise was. Four survey rounds gave 22,325 women aged 15 to 49 years, and a split method parted makeup shifts from behaviour shifts.

Use rose from 36.1 percent to 62.7 percent over the span in the survey data for those years. Near nine tenths of the rise came from changed behaviour, not from a changed mix of women in the pool. More women with higher schooling drove the top share of the makeup part. Rich poor gaps shrank and then closed by 2023.
pmc-13308949:
Yuki Makizawa and co-authors report in 2026 two cases of acute aortic tear found during transcatheter valve work, spotted by a throat ultrasound probe while surgery ran. The patients, a woman aged 87 years and a man aged 90 years, each had hard device passage or a valve pop up during the fix.

The probe showed a flap and a false channel in the rising aorta before blood pressure crashed in either case. Both went at once to open surgery for valve and aorta repair, and both left hospital walking with no nerve harm. Hard passage alone should prompt a probe check, since other scans give only snaps in time.
pmc-13309549:
Mahmoud Abdelmagied and co-authors test a heat exchanger with a twisted coil tube in a 2026 lab study. Heat exchangers move heat between fluids, and twisting the inner coil should stir the flow and lift heat transfer. The team compared the twisted design against a smooth-coil version of the same shell layout.

Three twisted coils of differing widths were built and run under opposing flows across a range of flow rates. Heat performance and wasted-energy measures were tracked as coil width and flow speeds changed. Swirl from the twist added flow disturbance beyond the smooth design. The authors report where the twisted layout gains and where it costs, giving engineers data for sizing such units.
pmc-13310649:
Francesco Chierigo and co-authors survey world expert practice on urine leakage during orgasm after prostate removal in a 2026 study. The condition, climacturia, is under-recognized and unevenly checked, even as more men live long after prostate cancer surgery. Its toll on life quality and sexual recovery can outlast other surgical effects.

Experts mapped their checks and treatments across 24 clinical situations, the first such world overview. Care hinged mainly on symptom severity and on whether leakage or erection problems coexisted. Mild cases drew conservative steps, while complex cases drew surgery. Routine screening stayed inconsistent despite wide awareness. The authors propose a starter assessment tool and call for prospective testing of it.
pmc-13310949: A short 2026 correction notice fixes one detail in a trial of online therapy for pelvic pain in endometriosis. Weekly group yoga sessions given by video call were first listed as lasting 120 minutes for 8 weeks in total. The length should read 60 minutes for 8 weeks in total. Authors state the typing error changes no results, conclusions, or other content. The notice itself holds no new data, methods, or findings beyond that single fix.
pmc-13311149:
Márcio Fellipe Menezes Viana writes a 2026 letter on crusted scabies in a healthy baby. A girl aged 3 months came in with a month of itchy rash that spread into whole body redness with thick crusts, mainly on the back and upper arms. Crusted scabies is a heavy mite infestation usually tied to weak immunity, so a healthy infant case is rare.

Blood tests showed high white cells, eosinophils, and swelling markers, with normal immune protein levels and no bacterial infection. Bedside skin scope sped diagnosis and helped control a household outbreak. Early suspicion matters, since heavy mite loads spread fast to contacts.
pmc-13311249:
Abdullah Jajan and Michiel van Nieuwenhoven report a 2026 Swedish cohort study on colonoscopy results inside a fast-track pathway for suspected bowel cancer. They ask how results and referral clues differ by age.

The study covers 3258 patients sent through the pathway from 2016 to 2023 who had a colonoscopy. No cancer was found in patients aged 18 to 40, while the share rose with age to 21.2 percent past age 80 in this cohort. Scan findings, rectal exam findings, anemia, and visible blood each linked to cancer on their own. Stool test results added strong signal where available.
pmc-13311749:
Elizabeth LA Cross and colleagues report a 2026 interview study on the unmet needs in diagnosing cellulitis, a skin infection often confused with other leg problems. Wrong calls lead to wasted antibiotics and missed illness.

Twenty-five British clinicians, from nurses and paramedics to hospital doctors, spoke about hard cases between January and September 2023. Odd or repeat presentations, wounds, darker skin tones, and prior antibiotics made calls harder. Clinicians admitted cellulitis becomes a default label, helped by thin skin training and fear of not treating. They also judged early test ideas and sketched what a good test must do.
pmc-13311949:
Tian Zhou and Fangqing Zhao review, in a 2025 article, how AI is reshaping human microbiome research. High-throughput profiling now produces enormous data sets on microbes. Their sheer size strains older statistics. The authors survey the AI toolkit applied so far, from clustering and neural networks to large language models. The survey covers how each method family is used in practice.

Across the analysis pipeline, these methods merge data from many omic layers. They clean and compress it, pull out meaningful features, and classify samples. That lets researchers read patterns at several biological scales at once. The review follows the payoff into community dynamics and host and microbe links. It also covers functional genomics. Uses in translation include disease tests, drug development, and precision engineering of microbe communities. The authors weigh current limits candidly. They also chart how AI could speed tailored medicine grounded in the microbiome.
pmc-13312249:
Wing Hong Seto and co-authors report, in a 2026 article, the work of the Asia Safe Surgical Implant Consortium to set one standard for how implants are sterilized across the Asia Pacific. A survey of sites in ten countries in the region had found wide gaps between actual practice and world sterilization guidelines, plus uneven infrastructure for infection prevention.

Regional trade groups formed the consortium, which met in Tokyo to build agreed recommendations from expert views and current evidence. The group produced three documents on quality checks in sterilization, standard handling of loaner and implantable devices, and a solid recall policy for sterilization failures. They stress combined physical, chemical, and biological checks, careful records, and fast communication. The authors call for ongoing regional cooperation, investment, and training so sterile supply teams can hold the standard.
pmc-13312349:
Henry Bair writes a 2026 essay on Michel de Montaigne as the first reader of his own body. Montaigne began passing kidney stones in 1578 at age 45, the same affliction that had killed his father. He returned to that inherited pain across his essays, wondering what it means to carry a parent's suffering dormant inside oneself for decades.

Bair contrasts Montaigne's way of attending to his body with clinical attention. Medicine scans for patterns and narrows toward a diagnosis, while Montaigne watched his condition without trying to solve it, aiming to know it rather than classify it. That stance, the essay argues, is close to impossible for trained clinicians, who feel idle without a hypothesis. Bair presents this tolerance for non-diagnostic attention as a discipline modern care has yet to learn.
pmc-13313149:
Ângela Graciela Deliga Schröder and colleagues hunt, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, for gene variants that predispose orthodontic patients to severe root resorption. That is the permanent shortening of tooth roots that braces and jaw surgery can provoke. The complication's uneven toll suggests inherited susceptibility, so the team tested seven variants in four bone-related genes, BMP2, BMP4, RUNX2, and SMAD6.

The study covered 158 patients treated with fixed appliances plus jaw surgery, grading root loss on panoramic X-rays and genotyping cheek-cell DNA. Six of the seven variants showed no link to severe resorption. One stood out: the CC genotype of a SMAD6 variant, rs3934908, appeared significantly more often in patients with severe damage. The authors present the finding as a first susceptibility lead, cautioning that bigger samples and gene-environment work must confirm it before it guides treatment choices.
pmc-13313749:
Yuting Bai and co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 study, an early lung rehab nursing programme for stroke-associated pneumonia. Pneumonia after stroke worsens prognosis, and rehab helps, but shared protocols were lacking. The team first distilled domestic and international evidence into a structured protocol. They then compared 35 patients admitted early in the study window, who received standard care, with 35 admitted later who received standard care plus the programme.

The groups started alike on every measure. Afterward, both improved. The programme group, though, finished well ahead on all five outcomes: breathing capacity, breathing muscle strength, a clinical infection score, limb motor function, and self-care in daily life. Each gap held up in the comparison. The authors judge the programme practical and portable. They recommend wider uptake for stroke units managing this common complication.
pmc-13314449:
Anqi Ren and co-workers ask whether the result of a fresh embryo transfer foretells later frozen transfer success, in work published in 2026. The work matters for couples who bank embryos and want a clear sense of their odds on the next try.

The team studied 6491 women who had single blastocyst frozen transfers at a large academic center between January 2016 and June 2024. Women were grouped by their fresh transfer outcome. The groups held 3711 with no pregnancy, 701 with a chemical pregnancy only, 1066 with miscarriage, and 1013 with a live birth, as the counts in the report show. Against the live birth group, the other three groups had lower odds of even a chemical pregnancy next time, with ratios such as 0.58 kept mid-sentence as reported. A good fresh result bodes well for frozen tries.
pmc-13315449:
Artur J Jakimiuk and Marcin Januszewski comment in 2026 on what a landmark Polish trial means for cervical cancer screening. The HIPPO trial was the first large randomized test in Eastern Europe of primary HPV testing against standard cytology inside a national screening program.

HPV testing nearly doubled detection of CIN2 or worse lesions and raised detection of CIN3 or worse as well. That matches wider evidence that DNA testing is more sensitive, at a small cost in specificity. Earlier trials abroad link a strong first-round catch to lower disease in later rounds. The authors weigh whether health systems can handle the follow-on care this shift brings.
pmc-13315649:
Lachlan Coff, Ujala Bashir, and Daniel Bojar review in 2026 how artificial intelligence is changing the study of glycans, the complex sugar chains on proteins and cells. Glycan work has lagged behind gene and protein computing, in part because good training data are scarce and the sugars branch in complex ways.

Deep learning can now read glycan structures from mass spectra. Models fitted to glycomics data can flag likely disease states, and machine learning can forecast how proteins and glycans interact. The review weighs what these tools can do for understanding glycan structure and function, a field long seen as a hard computing problem.
pmc-13315849:
Argyri Chroni and co-authors present a step-by-step protocol in 2026 for pulling out mitochondrial DNA and measuring its overall methylation with liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry. Methylation also acts on the mitochondrial genome, which lacks histones, but studies are often muddied by technical and biological confounders.

The workflow starts with blood and marrow single-cell samples, concentrates mitochondria on a sucrose gradient, then extracts the DNA. Purity checks guard against nuclear DNA contamination before the quantitative methylation read. Clear steps should make results easier to compare across labs studying cancer and cell biology questions.
pmc-13316649:
Michelle Semonella leads a 2026 Italian pilot trial of MobACT, a guided online therapy based on acceptance and commitment methods for adults with chronic pain. Italy had no such online program before, and clinic access to pain psychology stays scarce.

Forty adults were split evenly between the seven-week program and a waiting list. Pain acceptance rose over time in the group as a whole, but the change did not differ between arms during the short pilot window in the reported analysis. The team gathered rich feasibility data: sign-up, staying power, ease of use, satisfaction, and interviews about the experience. Those lessons shape a fuller trial and show how digital care might widen reach.
pmc-13316749:
BangXun Mao and co-authors compare, in 2026, two versions of a cornea-stiffening procedure for keratoconus, a disease that thins and bulges the cornea. Cross-linking uses light and a vitamin solution to strengthen the tissue. One version removes the surface layer first, while the other leaves it in place.

Records covered 77 eyes, with 45 treated through the intact surface and 32 with the surface removed. Measurements came from two imaging devices before surgery and at one and six months. By six months, stiffness rose in all corneal regions only when the surface had been removed, and central flattening was also stronger. A newer stiffness index changed more than curvature measures, suggesting it detects treatment effects more sensitively.
pmc-13317449:
Wei-Jie Sun and a large team report, in 2026, a nanoparticle platform that mimics many enzymes at once to kill tumour cells. Tumour tissue is acidic, low in oxygen and rich in protective molecules, features that resist chemotherapy but also offer targets. A metal-organic framework called MOF-818 sits at the centre of the design.

The particles showed six enzyme-like activities and could run a self-feeding cycle of reactions that remodels the tumour environment. They also activated the common drug acetaminophen into a more reactive form, raising harmful oxygen species further. Cell death followed through three programmed routes at once. Coated particles carrying an added immune protein and an autophagy blocker targeted tumours in the authors' tests, with good safety reported.
pmc-13317549:
Fen Zhang and colleagues frame, in a 2026 review, how extracellular vesicles, the tiny parcels cells send each other, could become medicines. Sources range from stem cells and immune cells to plants, milk, and microbes, and each source loads different cargo and behaves differently in the body.

The review weighs delivery routes, from veins to nose, mouth, lungs, and local shots, against diseases in repair, immunity, cancer, brain, and metabolism. Quality rules and world regulations remain patchy, slowing products despite a growing trial pipeline counted to April 2026. Their five-part matching frame links source, route, disease, quality marks, and rules into one planning tool for developers.
pmc-13318249:
Shengyuan Hua and co-authors describe a 2026 genetic study of two Chinese children suspected of having congenital hypotrichosis, a rare inherited condition marked by sparse hair from early childhood. Both children were six years old, and blood samples came from them and from their parents.

Whole-exome sequencing found four different compound heterozygous variants in the LSS gene across the two patients, confirming hypotrichosis simplex 14. Two variants had been reported before, and two were new, widening the known range of changes in that gene. Protein modelling and prediction tools were used to judge the new changes, and poor teeth development in one child may also belong to the condition.
pmc-13318749:
Øyvind Sandbakk and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of sex differences in sprint cross-country skiing. Thirty elite skiers, fifteen women and fifteen men, raced a classical time trial. The qualification run covered 1.3 km on snow. Satellite and motion sensors tracked speed, technique choice, and cycle features.

Men averaged about 14 percent faster than the performance-matched women. The gap was largest uphill, at 19 to 20 percent on those sections. It shrank to 6 to 9 percent downhill in the same race. Men spent more time double poling, about 61 percent against 53 percent for women. Women used diagonal stride more often. Men's cycles ran 9 to 11 percent longer, while rates were similar. The authors say equal distances pose distinct demands by sex.
pmc-13319649:
Gülnihal Eren and co-authors study vitamin D and gum disease in people with well managed type 2 diabetes in a 2026 article. Low vitamin D is common, and gum harm runs high when blood sugar illness and gum illness meet. Whether low blood vitamin D tracks with worse gums, and what gum fluid shows, were the twin questions.

Two groups were compared, 26 people with low vitamin D and 15 with enough, all with gum disease and steady sugar control. The low vitamin D group showed deeper gum harm and more bleeding on checks. Gum fluid levels of vitamin forms and defense bits did not track blood levels, though two fluid measures moved together. Blood shortfall still marked worse gums.
pmc-13320449:
Phaedra Henley and Maria Albin Qambayot wrote a commentary in 2026 on planetary health teaching in Africa and its older sibling framework. Fresh calls urge schools to teach health and planet as one system as climate strain grows. The piece, written in reply to an article by Filho and co-authors, argues that much of that ground was already built across Africa under the One Health banner.
