The team searched PubMed, Scopus, SportDiscus, and Web of Science following PRISMA guidance, covering programs from early childhood through secondary school.

Sixteen studies met their criteria and were quality-checked. Most programs took a technical, utilitarian approach, drilling specific strokes and skills with little connection to the wider curriculum. Research clustered in infant and primary years and thinned out sharply at secondary level. Program length, session frequency, content, and assessment tools varied so widely that comparisons were difficult. The authors conclude that school swimming has progressed but still lacks systematic implementation. They call for stronger backing, better teacher training, and stage-appropriate teaching.
pmc-13399749:
Ayu Hidaka and co-authors evaluated a shortcut test for lupus anticoagulant, a clotting-related antibody central to diagnosing antiphospholipid syndrome, in a 2026 laboratory study. Their proposed method takes one ratio: clotting time with a high-sensitivity reagent divided by clotting time with a low-sensitivity reagent, both from the familiar APTT test family.

The team checked the ratio against guideline-based testing in plasma from 57 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and 74 patients with prolonged clotting times. They also used samples deliberately spiked with anticoagulant drugs. Agreement with the standard pathway was good overall. Five patients whom the guideline route called negative showed elevated ratios, a discrepancy the authors flag for cautious follow-up rather than dismissal. They position the method as a screening sieve: a negative result makes lupus anticoagulant unlikely, while positives still require the full confirmatory workup.
pmc-13400249:
Ran Svirsky and colleagues mapped germline genetic findings among men with prostate cancer in a real-world, multicenter study. Their 2026 paper asks whether broad next-generation sequencing adds value beyond testing for known founder variants, inherited changes common in a population. Genetic results can guide treatment and family screening, yet testing patterns in routine care had been unclear.

Among 293 tested men, 39, or 13.3 percent, carried a positive finding, including 18 with high-penetrance genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, and ATM, and 21 with risk variants. One third of disease-causing variants found by sequencing were unique rather than founder variants. Family history of cancer was the only demographic or clinical factor tied to positive results. The authors argue for broad sequencing regardless of ethnicity or stage.
pmc-13400549:
João Victor dos Anjos Almeida and co-authors review, in 2026, prebiotics and probiotics in animal nutrition and what they mean for food safety and greener farming. Prebiotics feed helpful gut microbes, while probiotics supply live beneficial microbes directly. Interest has grown as producers seek alternatives to routine antibiotics.

Across poultry, pigs, cattle, fish and shrimp, these additives can improve digestion, gut wall health and immune strength while suppressing harmful germs such as E coli and Salmonella. Trials link them to better growth, feed efficiency and carcass quality, plus less reliance on antibiotics. The review also highlights turning farm waste streams, like fruit pomace and cereal bran, into useful feed substrates within circular production systems.
pmc-13400649:
Anthony W Sali and colleagues issue, in 2026, a correction to their 2025 study of how sustained attention affects readiness to move the eyes. A stimulus error had cut the last trial of each run short for some people. For others, the response was not recorded. A few worked-out measures also held mistakes.

The team cut the faulty trials and fixed the counts, then ran the tests again. One key interaction, between shift likelihood and attention state, kept the same direction but weakened. It no longer cleared the usual threshold for a firm finding. The results and discussion text was softened to match. The authors say the overall pattern and conclusions stand.
pmc-13400749:
Calvo-Sánchez and colleagues studied liver cancer risk after hepatitis C cure in a multicentre cohort study published in 2026. Clearing the virus lowers risk, but some patients still develop hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. The team asked whether longer use of metformin, a common diabetes drug, was linked to lower risk after cure.

They followed 1,531 patients who had cleared the virus with direct-acting antiviral drugs, and 50 developed liver cancer over a median follow-up of about six years. With models that track metformin use as it builds up, each extra year of use was linked to about half the cancer risk. The pattern held in patients with type 2 diabetes. Portal hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and a high fibrosis score each raised risk. The findings support trials of metformin as a cheap preventive after hepatitis C cure.
pmc-13401649:
Davis Ngarashi and co-authors carried out a 2026 cross-sectional study of noncontact infrared thermometers in healthy Black African adults, asking how much the body site and room temperature shift the readings. These forehead-style devices screen quickly at a distance, a virtue during infectious emergencies, but their accuracy varies and evidence from African populations was thin.

In an environmental chamber, 216 adults were measured at the forehead, neck, temple, and wrist. Readings came first at a cooler setting and then at a warmer one, in a fixed order. Statistical tests compared sites and conditions, while Bland-Altman plots and kappa statistics judged agreement between readings. The repeated-measures design isolates how much of a thermometer's answer comes from where it points and how warm the room is, rather than from the person being measured.
pmc-13401749: Andrés Fernando Montalvo Vásquez and co-authors are named in a 2026 correction notice in AIDS Research and Treatment for their 2025 article. It covers how migration movements shape the epidemiology and clinical profile of HIV infection in Quito, Ecuador. The notice is a correction only: the article was first published with the wrong article type, labelled a Review Article when it should have been a Research Article. The first author's name was stated incompletely. The article has been updated and the publisher apologises.
pmc-13401949:
Ram B Basany and colleagues describe making silicone finger prostheses for people who have lost fingers, in a 2026 case series. The team presents their work designing and fabricating custom hand prostheses tailored to each patient. A well-made silicone prosthesis restores appearance convincingly and can support some function, though it cannot fully replace a natural hand. Their reported gains centre on aesthetics, confidence, independence, and reintegration into daily and social life. Success, they argue, rests on clinical expertise, careful treatment planning, and a compassionate approach as much as on materials. The series documents their fabrication efforts and what the devices meant to the patients fitted with them.
pmc-13402249:
Akhilesh M Wodeyar and co-authors review how glowing dyes could sharpen robot surgery done through the mouth for head and neck cancers. Fluorescence imaging, where tissue lights up under special light, offers real-time sight of the tumor instead.

The review weighs a general dye, indocyanine green, against tumor-targeted agents such as panitumumab-IRDye800CW, checking fit with the da Vinci Firefly camera system. Targeted tracers gave the strongest contrast in the sensitive imaging mode, but results hinged on settings: camera angle, light output, field evenness, and autoscaling all mattered. The authors add lessons from their own operating rooms and call for shared protocols and stronger trials before the method becomes routine.
pmc-13402649:
Pritam Bera, Rajesh Raju, and Debodipta Das compare lung tumors with the lung cancer cell lines labs use to model them, working at pathway level rather than gene by gene. They set 513 lung adenocarcinoma tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas against 45 cell lines from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia. Each sample was scored across hallmark gene sets, and a penalized model hunted for separating patterns.

Five pathways split the two groups cleanly: E2F targets, interferon-gamma response, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, coagulation, and the G2M checkpoint. Cell lines ran hot on growth pathways and carried higher mutation loads, with more TP53 and STK11 changes, while true tumors kept immune and surrounding-tissue programs that lines have lost. The same split held in lung squamous cancer. The authors offer the five-pathway test as a yardstick for picking cell models honestly.
pmc-13402849:
Muhammad Usman and co-authors report a 20-year-old Marshallese man whose tuberculosis had spread body-wide, striking skin, brain vessels, and clotting at once despite a healthy immune system. He arrived with trouble swallowing, weight loss, and confusion after a fall, and imaging found disease in lungs, pleura, and the skin by his left ear. He tested negative for HIV, and clotting workups found no inherited cause.

His course worsened with a large stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory, with mild bleeding into it, plus a pulmonary embolism in the left lung. Pleural fluid markers strongly supported tuberculous pleuritis, yet PCR tests on lung washings and blood stayed negative, deepening the puzzle. The authors blame a tuberculosis-driven clotting state and urge suspicion for spread disease in young patients from high-burden regions.
pmc-13403149:
Vishwadeepak Rajput, Vishavdeep Kaur, and Ankalayya Bobbara compare heart rate variability at rest and after step exercise in 200 young adults split evenly between normal weight and overweight. Extra fat in youth can tilt the autonomic balance before heart disease declares itself, and variability in beat timing reads that balance noninvasively. Volunteers aged 17 to 25 stepped on a 23 centimeter stool at 40 steps a minute for up to five minutes.

At rest the overweight group already showed lower variability across time-domain measures and higher heart rate, all with p values below 0.001 in the reported tests. After exercise their recovery values, including SDNN, RMSSD, and high-frequency power, stayed lower, and adjusted models tied overweight status to lower fitness index scores too. The authors read early autonomic strain in overweight youth, detectable with a stool, a stopwatch, and an ECG.
pmc-13404149:
Anna Szlachcic and Nadinath B. Nillegoda probed in 2026 how mixed helper proteins team up to dissolve toxic protein clumps in animal cells. Clumps threaten cell health and build up with age and disease. The clearing machine pairs a workhorse protein, Hsp70, with helper proteins from two classes.

The team muted each helper's grip on the workhorse in turn, while keeping the helpers paired. Teamwork gains vanished when either partner could not engage the workhorse. Size-sorted tests showed the mixed pair handled clump types that neither class managed alone. Both helpers thus pull workhorses in together, widening what the machine can clear.
pmc-13404249:
Shiinoki and colleagues teach a model to read lung function from moving chest X-rays. The aim is patients who cannot do the forced breathing tests demand. Spirometry, the reference test, fails with children, frail elders, and people with poor cognition. Their 2026 study reuses chest radiography, a low dose image sequence taken while a patient breathes, in 151 patients. It extracts image features at breath phases and from a motion map. Models are trained to predict standard lung values.

Models built on the multiphase images and motion map beat the formula that estimates lung function from age, sex, and height alone. The approach predicted both breathing volumes and sorted patients by the ratio used to flag high risk obstruction. Because the study is one center and looks backward, the authors call for validation elsewhere before clinics trust it. An X-ray that reports function could reach patients spirometry leaves untested.
pmc-13404849:
Huayue Zeng and colleagues built a single test that finds three chicken viruses at once, reporting in 2026. Avian leukosis virus, chicken infectious anaemia virus and fowl adenovirus cause tumours, weak immunity and heavy losses on poultry farms. Testing for each separately costs time during outbreaks.

After tuning reaction settings, the test showed strong specificity, sensitivity and repeatability. On 1,211 farm samples it agreed with reference methods in at least 98.18 percent of cases in the reported checks. The team offers the assay for routine flock screening where the three viruses circulate.
pmc-13405449:
Ali Ijaz, Kin Mun Lau and Andrew CF Hui write in 2026 with two objections to a recent study of dermatomyositis diagnosis in 14 patients. The original authors concluded that electromyography, a test of electrical activity in muscle, can exclude the disease. They also proposed that every suspected patient should receive the test.

A test that misses real cases cannot rule the disease out. The correspondents ask for the conclusions to be softened to match the small, real-world series.
pmc-13405649:

Ultrasound-guided drainage through a metal stent serves people with gallbladder inflammation or blocked bile ducts from cancer. The scope can pass through the stomach wall or the duodenum, and which is better is debated.

Seventy consecutive patients treated between 2020 and 2026 were reviewed, with an average age of 77. Technical success reached 98.5 percent in the reported results. The stomach route was used in 48.5 percent of cases. Success, complications, readmissions and repeat procedures are compared between the two routes to guide route choice.
pmc-13407349:
Zhaoxi Wang and co-authors survey, in 2026, heat shock proteins and protein housekeeping in worn spinal discs, a leading source of low back pain. The review tracks members such as HSP70, HSP90, and HSP27 across the disc. They appear in its gel-like centre and its fibrous outer ring. The authors tie them to inflammation, cell death, and matrix turnover. Tuning these chaperones could pair with biomaterials, physical stimulation, or regenerative approaches. Direct disc-specific evidence for some family members is still scarce, a gap the authors flag for future work.
pmc-13407449:
Laura Valentina Klüner and co-authors, in 2026, scanned child-sized head models to compare two CT detector technologies for children's brain imaging. Signal clarity ran higher for both brain tissue and bone, by up to roughly 20 and 50 percent across the full range tested, and image noise was lower in the younger models. pmc-13407849:
Yan Wei and co-authors report, in 2026, turning a water pollutant into a recoverable polymer without gumming up the catalyst. Oxidation-driven linking can convert pollutants into useful products. Reactions on solid surfaces coat catalysts with polymer and stall, though. The team moved the key bond-forming steps out into the water itself. A record 73 percent of polymer product stayed in the aqueous phase for recovery. Fouling-resistant cleanup coupled to resource recovery is the promise.
pmc-13408049:

Combining them aims to restore partial biomechanics and soothe pain through the biological interposition graft. Joint replacement is avoided. Portal placement, graft rolling for insertion, and anchor choice by bone quality are covered as key technical points.
pmc-13408149:
Simone Nascimento Santos Ribeiro and co-authors build, in 2026, a camera-based system that counts newborn breathing without touching the baby. It then extracted the breathing signal from motion between frames, counting peaks only while a pose tracker judged the infant still.

Twenty-three recordings of spontaneously breathing newborns, three to fifteen days old, supplied 3,387 hand-labelled frames. Segmentation precision exceeded 94 percent on the reported metric, and estimated breathing rate missed the simultaneous clinical reference by an average of 2.1 breaths per minute. The single-centre sample was small, so the authors present technical feasibility and call for multicentre prospective validation.
pmc-13408349:
Seenivasan Subramani and Muthu Chidambaram discuss in 2026 why everyday care for bronchiolitis, a viral chest infection of infants, still drifts away from published guidance. The illness fills paediatric wards every season, respiratory syncytial virus causes most cases, and care is supportive only: fluids and oxygen, with no drug proven to help much.

Premature babies face several times the risk of severe disease, which may encourage intervention. Readers get a clear map of the gap between guidance and habit, and a reference point for audits aiming to standardise supportive care in busy children's hospitals.
pmc-13408949:

pmc-13410549:
Ping Han, Yiwei Wu, and Lin Cai survey in 2026 why flooded phone users sometimes step back from their screens on purpose. Endless feeds tire the mind, yet fear of missing news keeps people scrolling. That push and pull sits at the heart of the study.

Questionnaires from 2,508 people in Sichuan Province, China, fed the analysis. Feeling overloaded tied directly to more reflective breaks from phone use. Social media fatigue carried much of that link, passing the effect along. Confidence in handling threats changed the pattern, with links weaker among the highly confident. Students low in confidence leaned hardest on stepping back as a shield against overload.
pmc-13411149:

Small shifts in a tool's claims, users, or automation can slide it from casual wellness help into regulated medical territory. Green, yellow, and red coding uses strict aggregation, so one bad dimension cannot be averaged away. Three raters applying the rules to seven made-up scenarios agreed completely. A governance checklist and lifecycle path round out the package.
pmc-13411349:

pmc-13411749:

Matching antibiotic choice to microbiome cost is the authors' central plea.
pmc-13412149:

In the body, fewer than one in ten thousand sperm reach the egg, filtered by junctions, a storage reservoir in the oviduct, and guided swimming.

Bench methods such as swim-up and density gradients capture only part of that filtering. Newer tools, including microfluidic chips and systems lined with oviduct cells, mimic the tract more faithfully and have lifted embryo yields in trials. Throughput and standardisation still limit routine use, the authors note.
pmc-13412549:
Huixiao Yuan and colleagues follow a large Chinese cohort in 2026 to test whether two blood-and-vessel markers jointly predict death. One marker blends inflammation and insulin resistance into a single index; the other estimates artery stiffness from age and blood pressure. During follow-up, 906 deaths occurred in the main cohort. Each unit rise in the combined index came with 56 percent higher mortality risk, and stiffer estimated arteries added risk of their own accord. People high on both markers faced the greatest danger, with risk about 73 percent above the low group. Each marker explained a small slice of the other's effect.
pmc-13412649:

The authors present the hybrid model, mixing office visits with technology-supported contact, as a workable route for similar clinics.
pmc-13416149:

Pain scores fell from a median of 4 to 2 and behavior severity eased, while memory test scores held steady and caregiver burden trended down without reaching significance. pmc-13416749:

Traps sat under logs or at random floor spots across three seasons from 2021 to 2023. Of 524 droppings, about three quarters fell near logs, and about four fifths of all seeds landed there too. Total seed input was low, yet logs clearly guided where new plants could start.
pmc-13417649:

pmc-13418049:

pmc-13418249:

pmc-13418549:
Cari R Levy and co-authors evaluate a programme to improve life sustaining treatment documentation for veterans in home based primary care, published in 2026. pmc-13418749:

pmc-13418849:

pmc-13420549:

pmc-13421249:

pmc-13421349:

pmc-13421549:

pmc-13421749:

pmc-13422349:

pmc-13423049:

pmc-13423149:

pmc-13423449:

pmc-13424449:

pmc-13424649:

pmc-13424949:

pmc-13426349:

pmc-13426449:

pmc-13426949:

pmc-13427049:

pmc-13427249:

pmc-13427649:

pmc-13427749:

pmc-13428249:

pmc-13428549:

pmc-13430749:

pmc-13431349:

pmc-13432849:

pmc-13433749:

pmc-13434149:

pmc-13434249:

pmc-13434449:

pmc-13434749:

pmc-13435149:

pmc-13435849:

pmc-13436949: Flávio Pereira-Costa and co-authors are named on a 2026 correction that concerns only the funding note of their earlier study on gut bacteria and digested wheat gliadin. pmc-13437149:

pmc-13437549:

pmc-13439149:

pmc-13446349:

pmc-13449649:

pmc-13453049:

Their 2026 study pools 1,499 patients from 12 centers treated between 2020 and 2024.

A simple score split them further: those with better albumin and bilirubin grades and no spread beyond the liver did best. About 31 percent improved to the stronger liver class, often after their underlying liver disease was treated. Response on scans and better liver function each linked to lower death risk.
pmc-13454049:
Tyler Lo and seven co-authors argue that glioblastoma should be read as a disorder of a whole neuro immune network, not a lone tumor. This brain cancer resists treatment fiercely, and immune therapies help only briefly. Their 2026 review maps how the tumor's surroundings, nerve circuits included, shield it from attack.

Changes in that microenvironment block immune cells at the blood brain barrier and wear out the ones that get in. Nearby neurons feed the fire: signals such as glutamate and neuroligin-3 push tumor growth while calming immune attack. Immune looks vary by brain region, which may explain uneven patient outcomes. The authors call for combined plans that join nerve signaling, immune tuning, and maps of the tumor's terrain. Such a systems view, they hold, fits the disease better than tumor only thinking.
pmc-13454149:

A support-vector model beat other smart models for clean-up guesses, with top hit rates and good reach past the test range. Water teams gain a pull-back bead plus a tune model for its use.
pmc-13454349:
Jhommara Bautista and Andrés López-Cortés review, in 2026, how gut and body microbes shape cancer through whole-body signaling. Cancer growth and treatment response vary widely, and tumor genes alone do not explain the spread. Microbes gone off balance link to lasting inflammation, DNA damage, and changes in gene control.

These chemicals feed into immune, metabolic, nerve, and hormone pathways inside the body. Many routes merge on shared switches such as NF-kB and STAT3, which steer tumor growth and drug response. Microbe profiles may one day guide prognosis and treatment choice. The authors caution that mixed methods and small, varied patient groups still block firm clinical use.
pmc-13454449:
J. M. Sowerby leads a large team reporting, in 2026, a drug-screening route to stronger vaccine memory. Vaccines protect by training immune memory, yet memory fades in older people who need it most. The team matched gene patterns of memory T cells against patterns from known drugs, hunting for compounds that push cells toward a lasting memory state.

Deep molecular profiling showed the drugs boost glutamine breakdown inside T cells, and blocking that step erased the benefit. A common drug from the family, sodium valproate, improved memory in four mouse infection and vaccine models. In a human flu challenge study, vaccine protection markers rose about tenfold. The authors call such drugs immune-metabolic adjuvants, meaning helpers that work through cell fuel use.
pmc-13455249:
Atikom Eidbur and Thiti Atjimakul checked prediction models for severe cervical lesions in Thai women in 2026, to test if they travel across health-care settings. Predictive models for CIN2+ and HSIL built in varied folk need outside checks before clinic use. The team studied Thai women set for colposcopy from 2022 to 2024 at a tertiary referral centre.

Five hundred thirty-six women made the cut, with twenty-eight point seven percent diagnosed with CIN2+ or HSIL. Two past published models were run with no tweaks, with scores judged by discrimination via AUROC, calibration via plots and Brier scores, and clinic value via decision curve checks. In spite of demographic, HPV type, cytology, and colposcopy gaps from build cohorts, both models did well in the Thai group. Doctors gain checked models for cervical lesion triage in Thailand.
pmc-13456849:
Tang, Yuan, and Pan test whether gut microbes help cause five common mouth problems: loose or aching teeth, bleeding or sore gums, and mouth ulcers. Their 2026 study uses Mendelian randomization, which treats gene variants as natural proxies, with gut microbe data from the MiBioGen consortium and mouth outcome data from two large gene banks. The team also ran the test in reverse, to check whether mouth problems might reshape the gut instead.

The main method found 42 possible links between microbe groups and mouth conditions. Two broad groups, Mollicutes and Tenericutes, tied to lower odds of loose teeth, while a genus called Slackia tied to higher odds of toothache. Repeat analyses confirmed these links, and they held after adjusting for standard risk factors such as smoking and diabetes traits. The authors frame the gut mouth axis as a real causal path and a possible target for prevention.
pmc-13457149:
Mingyuan Pan and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study of whether an immune balance measure can predict short-term death in sepsis. Their index divides interferon-gamma, a signal that drives inflammation, by interleukin-10, a signal that calms it. The team drew records for 411 sepsis patients treated in one intensive care unit at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University between December 2023 and January 2026.

Patients were grouped by their first ratio value within a day of admission, and survival was tracked at 14 and 28 days. Higher ratios went with clearly lower death rates at both points, and the link held after adjustment for other factors, with hazard ratios near 0.48 and a similar 0.62 for the highest group. The relationship was curved rather than straight, with turning points near 0.07. The authors suggest the ratio could help flag which sepsis patients face the greatest early risk.
pmc-13457449:
Luiz Gustavo de Quadros and colleagues pool the studies on pairing stomach-shrinking endoscopy with weight-loss drugs. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty reshapes the stomach from inside, and clinics increasingly add anti-obesity medications, yet the extra benefit was unproven. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered comparative studies of the combination against the procedure alone in adults with overweight or obesity.

Ten studies with 578 participants qualified. At roughly seven months, the combination held a small edge in total weight loss, a mean difference of 1.9 percentage points, but the gap was not statistically significant and the studies disagreed sharply with one another. Blood sugar results were essentially a wash, with a pooled HbA1c difference of minus 0.04 percent and inconsistent findings across individual reports. The authors suggest combined therapy may suit selected patients rather than everyone, and they call for multicenter randomized trials with standard drug protocols and longer follow-up.
pmc-13457649:
Chunyan Wang and Congli Yuan propose a fresh lens for how bacterial weapons plug into human cell signaling. Many pathogens inject effector proteins carrying EPIYA motifs; host enzymes phosphorylate them, and host SH2-domain proteins then dock and reroute the cell. Their 2026 perspective builds a sequence-informed, three-layer convergence model comparing the bacterial motifs with the host's braking signals, ITIM and ITSM.

Convergence, they argue, happens at three levels: the sequence grammar around the tyrosine, compatibility with host kinases writing the mark, and recognition by SH2 readers interpreting it. Effectors such as Helicobacter's CagA, Bartonella's BepD, and E. coli's Tir show pathogens installing look-alike docking sites without copying host motifs; a logo-based comparison makes the pattern visible. The authors stress this is analogy, not homology. Their framework shifts attention to whether host machinery can write and read a motif, a prediction tool for new effectors.
pmc-13458249:
Yi W. Their 2026 single-center retrospective study includes 61 adults carrying at least one F508del mutation: 23 with cystic fibrosis-related diabetes and 38 without, followed for a year on treatment.

In the diabetes group, HbA1c drifted from 6.6 to 6.1 percent and insulin doses eased, neither change reaching statistical significance. The non-diabetic group showed clearer movement. Glucose at one and two hours after a glucose drink fell significantly, 13 of 38 people improved their tolerance category, and nobody progressed to diabetes during follow-up. Lung function improved in both groups, as expected. The authors read the pattern as a favorable metabolic bonus atop the known respiratory gains, supporting more dynamic, individualized management of blood sugar in cystic fibrosis clinics.
pmc-13458349:
Jane Koerner and colleagues try to bring order to Australia's thicket of digital mental health navigation tools, the apps and sites meant to guide people to the right service. Proliferation without shared definitions has produced confusion, with navigation and navigator swapped freely. As part of building the MChart tool for planners, their 2026 study convened 28 experts, from psychiatrists and GPs to funders, community groups, and consumers, for two structured co-design sessions.

The panel agreed a consensus definition of what these tools are, whom they target, and what falls inside their scope. It then listed 157 traits, sorted into five domains: type, management, content, design, and quality. Working within an implementation-science readiness framework, the group produced a typology meant to serve as a shared frame. The authors argue the definition and list lay the groundwork for quality standards, letting developers, users, and officials judge competing tools on common terms.
pmc-13458549:
Jack H DeLap and colleagues track birds across 12 years of edge building near Puget Sound in a 2026 study. Fringe building reshapes habitat, yet whether low-intensity green layouts beat dense planned estates for birds was untested at group scale. Presence models for single birds and whole bird groups compared green developments with planned estates in the central Puget Sound region of Washington.

More of the overall bird group, plus forest-shy birds and flexible birds, lived in green developments than planned estates, matching forecasts. Built-area birds showed no overall building effect and varied on their own. Guild best forecast single-bird results for shy birds at 87 percent, then flexible birds at 63 percent and built-area birds at only 44 percent. Planners gain proof that building layout, not just density, shapes bird groups, above all for fragile birds.
pmc-13459249:
Osman Faruk Bayramlar and Selma Karabey price device-linked bugs in a Turkish ICU in a 2026 matched study. Care-linked bugs lengthen stays and drain budgets, yet clean cost figures need careful matching for patient differences. Data from 700 stays between 2016 and 2018 at an Istanbul ICU were studied, with 81 bug cases matched to controls.

Bugs hit 14.1 percent of stays. Extra costs ran to 6,781 dollars for ventilator-linked pneumonia, 2,037 dollars for central line blood bug, 5,320 dollars for tube bladder bug, and 4,213 dollars for all bugs combined. Bug rates ranked highest by US NHSN rules. Hospital leaders gain matched, per-device cost figures to justify spending on stopping them, above all against breathing-machine pneumonia.
pmc-13459749:
Bourdeau-Brien and colleagues modeled in 2026 how to shape Canada's new flood cover plan so the public gains the most from it. Flood cover in high risk zones fights two pulls: bills must stay fair, yet only the most at risk sign up. The team set three aims: fair bills, full pay outs, and wide take up. A fresh loss bank, built from seven hundred thousand fake flood scenes, fed the tests. Fee parts were mixed and matched: aid, caps, first loss sums, top pay lines, and shut outs.

One blend won the trade offs. Aid that grows as means shrink did the heavy lift on fair bills. Fee caps and a mid first loss sum held costs in check. A top pay line kept the plan sound, and shut outs for the worst risk homes kept take up broad. The team holds the blend up for peer lands too.
pmc-13460649:
Amit R. T. Joshi, Adrian Anthony, Dara O'Keeffe, April Roslani, and David O'Regan argue in a 2026 essay that surgical education needs a genuinely global structure. Workforce shortages, competency-based training, tangled regulation, and fast-moving technology now cross every border, yet training governance stays national or local. Colleges, specialty societies, and certifying bodies each contribute strengths, the authors concede, although none was built as a worldwide platform.

They present ICOSET, an international collaborative begun in the mid-2000s by surgical educators from major colleges, as the vehicle for that shared venture.
pmc-13461349:

When the light's energy sat near the material's bandgap, the bands inverted, the signature move that creates topological behavior, and the band shapes warped in ways revealing the light-dressed states themselves. pmc-13461849:

Other liver markers and problems, including two key enzymes, fluid in the belly, and a bile enzyme, showed no clear difference. pmc-13461949:

Virtual patients were simulated under steady dosing, then pushed through varied patterns of missed or extra doses. A sampling algorithm estimated each patient's drug traits and dose history, producing an adherence probability. Using both measures beat either alone, above all for missed doses. pmc-13462049:

pmc-13463249:

pmc-13463649:

pmc-13465049:

Trimming to a few key signals helped acidity and moisture forecasts, while lycopene scored best with the full cleaned signal. pmc-13465149:

pmc-13465349:

pmc-13465549:

pmc-13465649:

pmc-13465749:

pmc-13466149:

pmc-13466449:

pmc-13466549:

pmc-13467049:

pmc-13467549:

pmc-13468449:

pmc-13468749:

pmc-13469249:

They argue the cases offer decolonial lessons for climate strategy in diverse, damaged regions.
pmc-13470349:

pmc-13470449:

Electron microscope images revealed a roomy client holding cavity formed with Hsp90. Cells missing FKBP8, or carrying its disease linked mutations, trapped the test proteins for destruction instead. A rebuilt mixture of purified parts restored correct folding, defining a minimal folding machine.
pmc-13470649:

Both sides improved significantly, and the degree of improvement never differed significantly between protocols at any checkpoint. At six months the low-energy side actually showed the higher improvement rate, about twenty-four percent against fifteen on their reported figures. Pain separated the protocols clearly: mild on the low-energy side, moderate on the high-energy side. Redness and swelling settled within six hours, and no scarring or pigmentation problems occurred.
pmc-13470849:

They trapped the extract, made with a natural solvent blend, inside a double emulsion, meaning droplets nested inside droplets, before adding it to the film.

Films carrying it held about 47 percent less moisture and let about half as much water vapor through as plain films. Microscopy and X-ray checks showed the emulsion changed the film's internal structure without stopping it from forming, supporting biodegradable active packaging uses.
pmc-13470949:

pmc-13471249:

pmc-13471449:

pmc-13471549:

pmc-13472149:

pmc-13472849:

pmc-13473449:

pmc-13473549:

pmc-13474249:

Lab checks first confirmed the coating wrapped the core well.

pmc-13474549:

pmc-13474849:

pmc-13475349:
Fengqing Chao and co-authors estimate teen birth rates in 2026 for 201 states and areas from 1950 to 2023. Girls aged ten to fourteen and fifteen to nineteen were modeled apart. pmc-13475549:
María José Ferreira Díaz maps the global health workforce shortfall toward 2030 in a 2026 review. Literature, global data sets, and policy papers from 2014 to 2024 were screened and blended. pmc-13476449:
Gowhar Iqbal and co-authors build gene-editing tools in 2026 for the myostatin gene in rohu, a major farmed carp. Myostatin brakes muscle growth, so editing it could raise yields. pmc-13478049:

Data were collected over about three weeks in mid-2025 at one nursing college, using the DASS-21 symptom screening scale.

Symptoms rated mild or worse were reported by about 75 percent for depression, about 78 percent for anxiety, and about 53 percent for stress. Female sex, poor peer relationships, lack of rest chances, and dissatisfaction with staff nurse behavior were tied to worse scores. The authors stress that the scale screens symptoms rather than diagnosing illness, and they point to rest and ward culture as practical targets.
pmc-13478749: Harkins and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their 2020 methods study on reading the native ends of broken DNA strands. The fix swaps back the color codes in two figures, which had been flipped in revision: blue marks the three prime overhangs, and red marks the five prime ones. Fresh copies of both figures are printed with their full captions. The authors state plainly that the slip touched the legends alone. No result, claim, or finding of the study changes.
pmc-13479449:

pmc-13479549:
Hongrui Cui, Qingli Tan, and Xiaoshan Liu published a 2026 numbers-based study of gaps in health care across China's regions. Large gaps appeared, with the lowest service levels in poorer regions and the west and center of China shortest on supplies. pmc-13480049:

The main gripe was that the help ended too soon, with many wanting more sessions. Findings fed into a new feedback tool built for this type of support.
pmc-13480249:

Caregivers rated their own unmet support needs and quality of life, while patients rated theirs, and a chained model traced how each side shaped the other.

pmc-13480749:

pmc-13481949:

pmc-13482149:

pmc-13482549:

pmc-13483249:

pmc-13483349:

pmc-13483849:

pmc-13483949:

pmc-13487949:

pmc-13489949:

pmc-13490449:

pmc-13490749:

pmc-13491749:

pmc-13491849:

pmc-13493449:

pmc-13493849:

pmc-13494549:

pmc-13495149:

pmc-13495249:

pmc-13495349:

pmc-13495549:

pmc-13496349:

pmc-13498549:

pmc-13499849:

pmc-13499949:

pmc-13500049:

Records covered patients who underwent below-knee or above-knee amputation between 2010 and 2024, with deaths counted around the operation and broken down by age and sex.

A total of 1,744 patients were identified, and roughly one in five died in the perioperative window in the reported averages. Yearly rates swung widely, peaking in 2021 during the hospital's hardest COVID-19 year. Death shares were similar for women and men, and rates during the pandemic years did not differ significantly from the pre-pandemic decade. Sepsis led the causes, so the authors press for earlier action on diabetic foot infection.
pmc-13500349:
Sidhom and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether vaping changes the human oral microbiome, the community of microbes in the mouth. Vaping has surged while its mouth effects stay murky. Their systematic search of six databases to August 2024 gathered studies comparing sole e-cigarette users with non-smokers or cigarette smokers, and checked study quality with a standard scale.

Eighteen studies qualified, most of them one-time snapshots, covering 1,418 people in all. Most found that e-cigarettes shift the mix and variety of mouth bacteria in ways distinct from both non-use and smoking. Several studies flagged rises in genera tied to gum disease among vapers. The authors caution that most studies trusted self-reported vaping and looked only at broad bacterial groups, so the size and health meaning of the shift remain uncertain. They call for tighter studies that verify sole use.
pmc-13500749:
李林 刘 and others survey infectious disease knowledge among entering university students across Hunan Province, China. In 2026, the one-time study collects 156,185 valid surveys from first-year students at thirty-six universities in autumn 2025, covering AIDS, HPV illness, hepatitis B, and tuberculosis. It models school-level influences with mixed effects models.

Knowledge was highest for tuberculosis at about ninety-one percent and AIDS at about eighty-five percent, lower for hepatitis B at about seventy-seven percent, and lowest for HPV at about fifty-five percent. Schools with higher undergraduate shares showed fairly weaker HPV and hepatitis B knowledge, while schools with medical programs showed stronger HPV knowledge. The authors urge aimed entry-stage health education, mainly on HPV.
pmc-13501649:
Abiola Okunade and Gbemisola Bolanle Ogbeye report a 2026 retrospective study of newborn jaundice across ten years of records from tertiary hospitals in Ondo State, Nigeria. West Africa carries the world's heaviest jaundice burden, and untreated cases can cause brain damage or death. The team extracted perinatal data for 10,182 mother-baby pairs from 2015 to 2024 with a structured form, then used chi-square tests to relate jaundice to social and obstetric characteristics. Eight percent of the babies were preterm and 92 percent were full-term.

Jaundice prevalence split sharply by maturity: 37.4 percent among preterm babies against 5.7 percent among high-risk full-term babies across the decade. Among preterm infants, cases clustered in the first four days of life, and 90.1 percent of jaundiced high-risk full-term cases also fell in that early window. Low birth weight and prematurity amplified risk, as did low maternal education, unemployment, and rural residence.
pmc-13501849:
Peng Liu leads a ten-author team with a 2026 nanorobot design meant to rescue radiation treatment against glioblastoma, the deadliest brain tumour. Radiation struggles twice over: tumour hypoxia blunts it, and dying cells leak potassium ions that then suppress immunity. The train-style robot has a silica head coated with a potassium-selective membrane and decorated with a brain-targeting peptide, plus a palladium tail with enzyme-like activity. At the tumour the tail converts peroxide into oxygen bubbles that propel the robot deeper.

Gold and palladium together amplify X-ray energy and generate hydroxyl radicals, sharpening radiation kill. Meanwhile the head mops up leaked potassium, holding the tumour's ionic environment low. That prevents macrophages from switching to the suppressive M2 state and relieves T cell exhaustion. In mice with brain tumours the robots targeted precisely, boosted radiation response, ignited a strong immune response, and significantly prolonged survival.
pmc-13502649:
Lin Guo leads a sixteen-author team reporting a 2026 enzyme-engineering workflow that pairs causal inference with a few-shot learning model to find mutation combinations. Optimizing an enzyme's catalytic numbers in a test tube is slow. So the team established a shortcut: yield per unit of enzyme expressed in living cells tracks the costly lab measure closely enough to steer by. Single mutations were predicted from binding calculations for intermediates, then tested by that unit-yield readout.

Combinations were predicted by their model, PIFS-PLM, a physics-informed selector over protein language model features that needs only sixty to one hundred combinations to learn from. Applied to a bicyclogermacrene synthase, the workflow stacked twelve mutations into variants giving a 73-fold increase in yield, or a 15 percent gain in selectivity. Crystal structures and biochemistry documented what mutations changed. The authors present unit yield as the target for metabolic engineering.
pmc-13503449:
Martínez-Cadena and Garza-Villafuerte propose a way to rank drug safety signals by stamina. A reaction flagged in every quarter of the year is likelier to be real than one that flashes once. Working with the FDA's 2025 adverse event releases, eight and a half gigabytes of reports, their 2026 workflow screened drug-reaction pairs each quarter using statistical cutoffs. It then sorted the survivors by how many quarters they persisted through.

From an annual pool of over eighty thousand screened pairs, fewer than a quarter appeared in all four quarters, forming a persistent core the authors recommend reviewing first. That core carried higher report counts and stronger statistics than one-quarter pairs, though average effect sizes were similar, and most core pairs stayed stable across the year. The pitch is triage: regulators drowning in signals get an order in which to investigate them.
pmc-13503849:
Sanjay Agal and four colleagues present one machine learning framework that both maps the shape of a data network and forecasts its change, in a 2026 paper. Past tools did one job or the other, which split the insight each task could give the other. Their system, NetStructPred, joins the two.

Parts of the design read the web of links, track how ties evolve over time, and learn both jobs at once with feedback between them. Tests ran on six real data sets, from scholar and social webs to traffic sensors and device security logs. Scores matched or beat twelve specialist tools. In one case the system flagged at-risk device groups well before odd behavior showed. Growth in computing cost stayed near linear as networks grew.
pmc-13503949:
Bixi Tang leads a team showing how weight-loss surgery heals a fatty, inflamed liver through a single metabolic path, in a 2026 study. The liver illness, called MASH, often follows obesity, and sleeve surgery helps some patients but not others. Why results vary was unclear.

In mouse models, sleeve surgery cut liver fat and scarring beyond what weight loss explains. Deep profiling showed the surgery raised an enzyme, MAT1A, that feeds one-carbon metabolism, a hub for chemical tagging in cells. That restored a key fat balance in liver cells and calmed cell stress. Removing the enzyme or its food sources erased the benefit, while a supplement rescued it. Human biopsy and blood data showed the same marker tracked who improved.
pmc-13504349:
Nikolas A Baya leads a team studying people whose bodies defy their polygenic scores, in a 2026 study. Such scores add up many small gene effects to forecast traits like height, yet some people land far from their forecast. Those outliers may carry rare, strong variants that the score misses.

Working in the UK Biobank, the team flagged people far above or below their genetic forecast for seven traits and three diseases. Shorter-than-forecast people carried more damaging rare variants in two growth genes, and lower-bone-density outliers carried them in two bone genes. A wider scan found 74 genes tied to such gaps, some new. In diabetes, patients with rare harmful variants needed less common-variant risk to fall ill, which fits a threshold model.
pmc-13505049:
Haokun Leng, Yuanqi Liu, and Lei Wu review the cancer-driving roles of a gene switch called SOX12, in a 2026 paper. The switch helps build the embryo, but many tumors switch it back on. Past reviews had not mapped its networks across cancer types in one place.

The review finds SOX12 overactive in gut, reproductive, blood, and other tumors, where it tracks with aggressive traits and poor outlook. It works through RNA sponge networks, growth pathways like PI3K/AKT, fuel rewiring, and shaping of the immune setting around tumors. The authors call it a crossroads where tumor metabolism and immunity meet. They discuss blocking its DNA-binding part or its RNA networks as drug ideas, and ask for large clinical trials.
pmc-13505149:
Xiangyang Zhang and colleagues built health profiles from blood proteins measured in 11,900 adults who were free of disease at the start. Unsupervised learning grouped these adults into five proteomic health archetypes, each a pattern across many proteins at once. A classifier based on pairs of protein ratios was trained so the patterns could survive a change of testing platform.

The classifier reproduced the archetypes in an internal group of 3,570 people and in three outside cohorts tested with different technology. Each archetype carried its own reproducible risks across heart and metabolic, immune, brain and blood-vessel, and mental illnesses. People in the highest-risk patterns also lost survival ground faster. Gene analyses lined up with the same disease patterns. The authors present the archetypes as a base for prevention talks and for sorting people into risk groups before illness appears.
pmc-13506249:
Hiroto Koba and Toshio Doi present a 2026 case report about a 66-year-old woman whose severe trunk tilt came mainly from nerve pain, not fixed deformity alone. She had long-standing curved spine disease, low back pain, and left thigh tension that worsened over a year. Drug treatment and epidural blocks had failed to help her.

A selective block of the L4 nerve root briefly eased both pain and tilt, pointing to that root as the main driver. Fusion at a single level, L4/5, then restored upright balance and improved her X-ray measures. The authors argue that finding a focal pain trigger first can spare some older patients a large rebuild operation.
pmc-13507249:
Abu Saeed Baidya leads a 2026 team that identifies common dark igneous rocks as a steady source of reactive phosphorus for life's origin. Phosphorus is essential for DNA, membranes, and energy currency, but its usual mineral form barely dissolves. Reduced and paired forms react far more readily, yet known sources like meteorites seem episodic.

Rock samples from fifteen sites worldwide held phosphite shares up to about a quarter of total phosphorus in some rock types, plus paired pyrophosphate in volcanic rocks. Ocean and lake models suggest released phosphite could reach useful levels, especially in shielded waters. Seafloor weathering of widespread early rocks may have fed prebiotic chemistry for long spans, on Earth and rocky planets alike.
pmc-13507449:
Valeriia Fast and others study swimming patterns of the multi-mode germ Pseudomonas putida in fluid shear flow. In 2026, the work joins auto cell tracking and swimming mode finding with dual-color glow scope work and number models of true-life swimmer shapes. Germ swimming is well known in still uniform liquids, but natural homes involve moving fluids and shear.

Shear-led lining up rested on swimming mode, while swimming and surface nearness fought lining up. Tail wrapping became less good as shear stress rose, holding the pulling mode. Models backed tests with how-it-works detail. The findings clarify how distinct swimmer types move through flow, fitting to root settling and illness spread.
pmc-13508349:
Justyna Gleba, John Copland, and Han Tun review how cancers rewire fat chemistry to survive, and how that wiring could become a drug target, in 2026 work. Cells soften fats by adding double bonds, a step called desaturation, which keeps membranes fluid. Two enzyme routes run this work. Tumors lean on the first route to dodge toxic fat buildup and a form of iron-driven cell death. The second route is a paradox: it feeds growth signals yet loads membranes with fats that make that same cell death easier to trigger.

Drug hunters are now testing blockers of the first enzyme, with one candidate in an early human trial for solid tumors. Tumors fight back through a side shunt that restores soft fats, driving resistance. The review maps combination ideas pairing these blockers with diet changes, other drugs, and smart delivery systems to corner the workaround.
pmc-13508449:
Binta Jallow leads a nine-author team comparing gut bacteria in house-area flies from The Gambia and China, in 2026 work. Non-biting flies that live near people can carry germs on and in their bodies, yet their inner microbes vary by place in ways barely mapped. Four fly species were sampled in a Gambian council area and in Changsha, China, in late 2023. Midguts were pooled into twenty-one samples, and a marker gene census named their bacteria.

Two bacterial groups dominated every sample, together covering about four fifths of the census. Community makeup still differed sharply by country, with diversity scores splitting by location. Gambian flies carried far more of one wound-linked bacterium, while Chinese samples held more Pseudomonas. The survey shows the same fly species can ferry different microbial cargo in different places, a point local disease control should weigh.
pmc-13511549:
Chuhan Shao and colleagues review evidence that a mother's diet in pregnancy can reprogram the energy factories of her children's cells. Those factories, the mitochondria, sit at the hub of cell metabolism and pass effects across generations.

The changes differ by organ rather than failing evenly, the review finds, hitting placenta, liver, muscle, heart, and brain control centres. The review screened studies in two large databases published up to July 2026. Offspring mitochondria shift their growth, copying, and energy output, ending in weaker energy supply, more oxidative stress, and insulin resistance. Fixes under study include diet changes, exercise, drugs, and even transplanting healthy mitochondria. Shao frames organ-specific mitochondrial damage as the key link carrying metabolic syndrome from mother to child.
pmc-13512249:
Christian Spiegel and six co-authors test whether fluid draining after soft tissue sarcoma surgery can warn of an unplanned return to the operating room, in 2026 work. Wound trouble after removing these tumors is common, and standard risk models lean on patient and tumor traits. Records covered 95 patients treated at one center between 2021 and 2025, of whom 23 needed unplanned revision surgery.

Drainage volume after surgery stayed tied to revision risk after other factors were counted, and the volume of fluid given during surgery was the only in-operation factor that held. Among patients without a planned second-stage reconstruction, drainage sorted future revision cases well, and a high cut-off point was rarely crossed by patients who healed cleanly. The authors present drainage watch as a cheap early marker, while calling the single-center findings exploratory.
pmc-13512549:
Wallace Pereira Silva and six co-authors study what shapes the usability of remote assessment for people with interstitial lung disease in Brazil, in 2026 work. Video-based checks can widen access for these patients, yet owning a device does not settle whether remote care works. Thirty-one adults from four regions joined a mixed study pairing a usability questionnaire with semi-structured interviews.

Income, whether patients felt remote checks were clinically fitting, and how strong their access barriers ran each tracked with usability scores. The authors name digital inequity, meaning unequal skill, connection, and means, as a driver of who can use remote care well. Interview material fleshed out the numbers with daily obstacles. Recommendations stress digital literacy support, attention to social conditions, and clear rules for when remote assessment is appropriate in chronic lung care.
pmc-13514549:
Hatice Sevim and colleagues report a retrospective study, published in 2026. It covers pancreatic shrinkage during treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer. The drug is bevacizumab. It blocks blood vessel growth. The team reviewed paired CT scans from 105 patients at one Ankara hospital. Pancreatic volume was measured before and during therapy. The change was related to survival.

Average pancreatic volume fell measurably on treatment. Patients who lost more volume progressed sooner. Their overall survival was also shorter in the main analyses. The link to progression held up more consistently in sensitivity checks. Scan-measured volume loss may be an early warning sign during this therapy, the authors propose.
pmc-13515549:
Yong Jun Choi and seven colleagues test a liver blood marker against heart artery calcium in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The marker, M2BPGi, reflects scarring in the liver and rises in fatty liver disease tied to metabolism. The question was whether it also flags silent coronary disease in the same patients. Records covered 6,514 adults with the liver condition who had health screening between 2020 and 2025, sorted into four marker bands.

Calcium in the coronary arteries grew steadily more common from the lowest marker band to the highest, rising from about thirty-nine percent to about fifty-seven percent. After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, sugar, and fats, the top band still carried clearly higher odds of calcium, and of worse calcium grades, than the bottom band. Choi's team proposes the marker as an extra flag for hidden heart risk in fatty liver patients, alongside standard risk checks.
pmc-13516849:
Giulia D'Alvano and five colleagues report how fast a targeted antibody works in hard-to-treat myasthenia gravis, in a 2026 single-centre study. The drug, eculizumab, blocks a complement protein and is approved for patients whose disease defies standard therapy and who carry a certain antibody type. Eight older patients, averaging seventy-three years, were scored for daily function and muscle strength before treatment, at five weeks, and at three months.

Improvement came quickly. Daily-living scores fell by roughly three-quarters within five weeks, and strength scores fell by about three-fifths, both shifts being large and statistically firm. Gains held at three months. The drug was well tolerated in this small group. D'Alvano's team reads the speed as clinically valuable for frail, elderly patients who need early relief. Eight patients at one centre still make a narrow evidence base.
pmc-13518849:
Ewelina Grochowska and six colleagues test in 2026 whether spraying selenium on spinach leaves can enrich the crop while it grows in salty soil. Salt-affected farmland is spreading worldwide, and selenium is a nutrient many diets lack. Their pot trial under field-like conditions used the Matador spinach variety at two salinity levels.

Leaf spraying raised selenium levels in the plants roughly tenfold without hurting yield, even at the higher salinity. Treated plants carried more phenols and antioxidants, tolerated salt better, and gained dry matter plus sulfur, zinc, and manganese. Selenium uptake tied closely to sulfur metabolism. Grochowska and co-authors see foliar feeding as a workable way to upgrade spinach grown on salty ground.
pmc-13518949:
Hossein Taghizadeh, Davoud Fazeli, and GholamHossein Nazemzadegan test in 2026 whether practice schedules that adapt to a learner's error rate improve soccer instep kicking. Seventy-one novice students aged 18 to 25 were split into blocked, random, two algorithmic, and control groups. Algorithmic groups started with easy blocked practice and earned harder random orders only after clearing accuracy thresholds of either 67 or 56 percent.

Everyone practiced 324 kicks over two days from three distances. During learning itself the groups looked alike, aside from gains in the stricter algorithmic group. At retention testing two days later, both algorithmic groups beat the random and control groups. Under transfer conditions, the looser-threshold group topped everyone, even under added psychological pressure.
pmc-13519449:
S H Bharathi and colleagues surveyed eight hundred dentists on their grasp of artificial intelligence in gum care. Published in 2026, the survey ran from January through June 2024, drawing a stratified random sample and using a tested questionnaire on knowledge, attitude, and daily practice. Gum disease touches about half of adults worldwide, so AI tools for reading X-rays and planning care could matter widely.

Three quarters of dentists knew of AI and four fifths said they would adopt it, yet only one quarter actually used it in clinic. Worries about data privacy and job displacement surfaced in two fifths of replies. The gap between warm views and thin use points to missing training, ethical rules, and access rather than hostility. Readers get a clear case for teaching and guidance that turn interest into routine practice.
pmc-13520149:
Elif Nur Özen and Ali İbrahim Hatemi survey eating habits in 2026 among 50 patients with inflammatory bowel disease at an Istanbul hospital. They link diet patterns to gut symptoms, mood, and quality of life. Thirty patients had Crohn's disease and twenty had ulcerative colitis. Data came from questionnaires, a 24-hour dietary recall, and standard symptom, depression, and quality-of-life scales.

Most patients, 82 percent, named foods that worsened symptoms, led by legumes, milk, and raw vegetables, while yogurt and cooked vegetables helped many. Intakes of fiber, several vitamins, and minerals fell below recommendations. Meal skipping, commoner in Crohn's patients, tied to worse gut symptom scores. Higher depression scores tracked with lower quality of life and stronger symptoms.
pmc-13520449:
Mutita Wongsuwanlert and colleagues assess in 2026 whether non-surgical gum treatment helps people with chronic kidney disease over three months, tracking mouth bacteria, inflammation signals and kidney measures together. Gum disease has been linked with faster kidney decline, so a dental intervention might offer wider benefit.

Forty-five patients with moderate to advanced gum disease received deep cleaning without surgery. After three months, gum pathogen counts fell by roughly one to ten fold, pro-inflammatory signals fell, while a calming signal rose. Kidney markers improved in roughly six to nine of ten patients depending on the measure. Longer trials would be needed to prove lasting kidney benefit.
pmc-13521549:
Brown and colleagues tested whether a viral protein from two tick-borne hemorrhagic fever viruses damages the blood vessel wall by disabling pericytes, the support cells wrapped around tiny vessels. Their 2026 laboratory study used the non-structural protein 1 of the Alkhumra and Kyasanur Forest disease viruses in cultured vessel cells grown alone and together. Both viruses can cause severe bleeding.

Brown found the viral proteins did impair pericytes, weakening their ability to support the endothelial cells that line vessels and maintain the barrier. Yet under the team's conditions, the proteins did not make the vessel layer leaky, whether endothelial cells grew alone or alongside pericytes. The authors conclude that pericyte dysfunction alone seems insufficient to open the barrier. Simultaneous impairment of both cell types is probably needed, pointing future work toward how the two cell types interact during infection.
pmc-13522249:
Divya Bhatia and colleagues survey in 2026 academic bone surgeons at one school on where they seek medical facts. Sources faced peer review checks. Rivals were social media and large language models. Use was split by purpose, for patient care and for self care.

Surgeons marked any past use of each source type. Users then rated ease of grasp and felt help for each source. Paired tests compare sources within the same surgeons. The headline result favours peer-reviewed guides as the top pick. Full shares with error ranges fill the result tables. Teachers gain a base line on pro fact habits as AI tools spread through clinics.
pmc-13522449:
Elif Nur Noyan and Bahar Çiftçi test a bundled support program for people with high blood pressure in a 2026 study conducted in Turkey. Sixty-three patients were split, without random assignment, into an intervention group and a control group. The program combined personal education, a printed manual, home blood pressure checks twice daily, text reminders, and monthly follow-up calls over three months.

After the program, the intervention group reported stronger confidence in taking medication as directed and higher general self-confidence than controls. Blood pressure and body mass index also fell over time in that group, with no comparable change among controls. The authors conclude that combined education and follow-up support may help patients stay with hypertension treatment.
pmc-13522549:
Alemu Chemeda Ifa and Bikila Wedajo Lemi survey a dangerous foodborne bacterium in retail foods in southern Ethiopia in a 2026 study. More than four hundred meat and dairy specimens were collected over about ten months and tested by culture and sequencing. Isolates of Listeria monocytogenes, which causes a rare but often deadly illness, were checked against six antibiotics.

About one specimen in six carried some Listeria species, and just under six percent carried the dangerous species. Cheese showed the highest rate, followed by raw fish and raw meat. Isolates remained sensitive to several antibiotics yet all resisted penicillin. The authors call for better hygiene training for food handlers and tighter control of antibiotic use in food animals.
pmc-13523249:
Zihan Anna Zhang and colleagues engineer immune cells with a drug-controlled switch in a 2026 study of CAR-T therapy. CAR-T cells are patient T cells fitted with a synthetic receptor against cancer, yet constant signaling can exhaust them and endanger healthy tissue. The new design embeds a viral protease module inside the receptor so that an approved drug stabilizes the full receptor on the cell surface.

Without the drug, the cells showed minimal background activity. With it, surface receptor appeared within an hour and neared peak levels by four hours, driving dose-dependent killing and cytokine release. Switching off after tumor clearance reduced attack on healthy target cells in laboratory tests. Under chronic stimulation, switched cells showed fewer exhaustion markers and a more durable memory profile, supporting safer and longer-lasting therapy.
pmc-13523349:
Jung Eun Choi and co-authors link long-term fine particle air pollution to urinary tract infections in children in a 2026 nationwide Korean cohort study. Nearly four hundred thousand children and teenagers from a national insurance sample were followed from 2002 to 2019. Yearly average exposure to fine particles was estimated at fine geographic resolution and assigned to home districts, while infections were identified from diagnosis and prescription records.

More than twenty-eight thousand urinary infections occurred during follow-up. Each standard increase in yearly particle exposure was tied to a modestly higher infection risk, with a slightly stronger link for antibiotic-treated infections. The association was stronger in rural children and held across sensitivity checks, with exposure lagged by a year showing stronger effects. The authors suggest inflammation and immune disturbance as possible pathways.
pmc-13524149:
Chi-Han Huang and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, survival evidence comparing acral melanoma, which arises on palms, soles, or nails, with other skin melanomas. Acral disease is rare and linked with poor survival, yet how much worse its prognosis is remained unclear.

Searches of three databases for studies from 2000 to 2025 produced twenty studies covering 568,346 patients. Five-year overall survival was significantly lower for acral melanoma than for nonacral disease. The gap held for stage II and stage III subgroups. Patients from darker-skinned populations with acral disease also fared worse than White patients with the same subtype. The authors highlight staging and ethnicity as important modifiers and call attention to later detection and access gaps that may drive the disparity.
pmc-13527949:
Serhii Maslennikov and five colleagues report a 2026 rabbit experiment on whether stem cells from fat tissue can heal thigh-bone fractures that refuse to unite. Cells were taken from donor rabbits; some were used as-is and others were first coaxed in the lab toward becoming bone-forming cells over four weeks.

A gap was cut in the thigh bone of each animal and fixed with a plate, then animals received no cells, plain cells, or pre-differentiated cells, five per group. By six weeks both cell groups bridged the gap faster than controls, and the pre-treated cells led slightly on bridging and remodeling measures. Blood markers of bone activity also shifted. The authors see pre-differentiation as a modest advantage worth further study.
pmc-13528149:
Shihan Li and six colleagues review how reliable surface topography is for judging scoliosis in a 2026 paper. The method scans the back's shape without radiation. Nineteen studies with 778 people in total were pooled. Quality was graded with the COSMIN checklist for measurement tools. The team also sorted the many index types into a clear scheme.

Most surface indexes proved steady enough for clinic use. Evidence quality, though, was only low to moderate. Marker dots, age, and having scoliosis did not shift reliability much. Scanning posture did matter. The authors see real promise for screening and follow-up without X-ray dose. They want better studies and smarter algorithms before the method takes a bigger role. Their sorting of index names should help future work speak one language.
pmc-13529849:
Hasler and colleagues present in 2026, in German, the case of a 52-year-old woman whose hearing loss in both ears was the leading sign of an ANCA-associated vasculitis. That condition is an autoimmune inflammation of small blood vessels. Ear symptoms can be its first and only clue.

The woman was first treated with ear drops, nasal spray, and steroids for suspected sudden hearing loss, with only brief improvement. Further workup revealed the systemic disease, a granulomatosis with polyangiitis affecting airways and kidneys. Once doctors started immune-suppressing treatment, steroids followed by rituximab maintenance, her hearing improved steadily. Five months later testing showed nearly normal hearing, with only a slight high-frequency dip remaining on both sides. Her blood markers and chest imaging also normalized. The authors urge clinicians to suspect vasculitis when hearing loss resists standard treatment.
pmc-13530149:
Yan Hao, Yanmei Yuan, and Hui Liu describe a 2026 artificial intelligence system for applying fertilizer with less carbon cost. Ordinary monitoring misses how soil nutrients shift over time, which weakens precision farming. Sensors for soil, weather, and crop growth feed field data into a shared edge and cloud setup.

A memory-based network with attention learns to spot fertilizing events and their timing from noisy field signals. A planning model then picks the lowest-emission schedule that still meets crop nitrogen needs and safety limits. Field tests showed modest forecast error at day 30 and lower emission intensity per unit of fertilizer.
pmc-13530249:
Xiujuan Yao and co-authors map a scar-forming cell type in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease during 2026 work on blood and lung tissue. Fibrocytes travel in blood and settle in airways, where they may drive the wall thickening that blocks airflow. Earlier work counted them without sorting their subtypes.

Blood counts looked similar between 25 patients and 10 controls, yet patient cells more often carried receptors for two airway alarm signals. Inside lung tissue, total and activated fibrocytes clearly rose in both patients and mouse models. The pattern implicates these cells in airway and lung scarring.
pmc-13530649:
Kumar, Sang, David, and Pandya present in 2026, as conference poster 120, an investigation of Achilles tendon ruptures in the National Basketball Association. The 2024-25 season produced seven ruptures, the most ever in one year. They ask whether workload spikes precede the injury.

Reviewing public data from eleven seasons, the team identified 25 ruptures and kept 19 that occurred in basketball play. Position, starting role, and early sport specialization showed no pattern in who tore the tendon or in schedule congestion before it. The signal sat in playing time: minutes played spiked significantly across the ten and fifteen games before the rupture compared with the players' own norms in the analysis reported here. The authors argue that monitoring short-term workload surges matters more than static player traits for prevention.
pmc-13531849:
Rui Liu and co-authors review in 2026 how nurses are trained for combined heart and lung rehabilitation work. Demand grows as cardiopulmonary disease spreads, yet training routes and skill expectations stay scattered. Nine databases in Chinese and English were searched, with formal appraisal of each study.

Only nine studies survived screening, covering specialist trainees, registered nurses, and one student group. Programs formed a tiered yet unstandardized ladder, hampered by weak certification and poor transfer of classroom gains to wards. Curricula stayed broad with vague skill staging. The authors describe a field still early, needing defined roles and lasting competence checks.
pmc-13532949:
Toro and colleagues used a computer model in 2026 to ask how much the veins matter in high blood pressure. Drugs fail to control pressure in many patients, which hints that the standard picture of the disease is incomplete. Their closed-loop model of the whole human circulation let them vary parts of the system one by one, with random variation added to test how shaky the results were.

Toro found that reduced venous compliance, meaning stiffer veins that stretch less, was the second strongest driver of raised arterial pressure, behind higher resistance in small arteries. Stiffer veins alone were enough to push the model into a high-pressure state. Since veins hold most of the blood volume, their stiffness shapes how much blood returns to the heart. The authors propose the venous system as a fresh target for treatments that aim to lower pressure.
pmc-13534449:
Nur Azrah Fazera Mohd Ariffin and colleagues study in 2026 what happens when Notch signalling stays switched on in adult mouse neural stem cells. The signal normally helps keep stem cell pools in balance. A switchable mouse model let the team force lasting activation in stem cell lineages.

Forced activation drove rapid dividing that pushed stem cells to mature instead of renewing, draining pools in two brain zones. New neurons still reached the smell centre, yet they did not improve function. Mice showed weaker spatial and emotional memory plus poorer social recognition, warning against blunt activation.
pmc-13536549:
Majed Mowanes Alruwaili explores in 2026 moral leadership in neonatal intensive care nursing in northern Saudi Arabia. Newborn units face ethically hard choices daily, yet leadership that supports nurse moral agency is poorly understood outside Western settings. Narrative interviews ran with 24 nurses across four top-level units over eight months.

Five themes emerged, including a gap between moral judgement and action tied to hierarchy and low psychological safety. Servant-style behaviours such as listening, mentoring, and role modelling acted as scaffolding for ethical voice. Faith-grounded motivation and sanctioned silence added local texture to the picture.
pmc-13536649:
Chaoqun Ba and colleagues study in 2026 how the reed Phragmites australis spreads underground across shifting sand dunes in the Ulan Buh Desert of China. Sand burial is the main physical stress in these dry dune systems. Field work tracked rhizome growth across burial depths and three dune zones.

Deeper burial came with faster and longer rhizome spread in the seasonal checks. Rhizome shape and new shoot sources shifted by zone, with lowlands favouring rhizome shoots and slopes favouring tillers. Growth funds moved from upright shoots in lowlands toward sideways spread on slopes over the season.
pmc-13536749:
Ahsenullah Qadri, Tania Stafinski, and Devidas Menon interview care staff about giving medical help in dying in Canada in a 2026 interview study. The service has been lawful since 2016, with wider access added in 2021, yet how it runs varies by region. Forty-six doctors, nurses, managers, and officials from seven provinces and one territory told what helps and what hinders the work between mid 2024 and early 2025.

Heavy workloads, weak links with other services, poor teamwork, and thin training and funding were leading barriers. Newer problems included false beliefs about who qualifies, little grief support for families, and trouble getting and moving needed drugs. Central oversight, standard forms, teamwork across jobs, and strong backing from leaders helped. The authors map system fixes ahead of a planned 2027 widening of who qualifies.
pmc-13536849:
Shuhei Miyazaki and colleagues measure movement during breath-hold radiation for stomach lymphoma in a 2026 study of twenty-one patients treated between 2013 and 2023. Holding breath at the end of exhale shrinks motion, yet repeatability within a session was unclear. Each patient had three or four planning scans under the same breath hold. Target volumes and center shifts were compared across scans and by age.

Target volumes stayed stable, changing only slightly across scans. Center shifts stayed within a few millimeters on average, largest along the head-to-foot direction. The first scan shifted notably more than later scans in every direction. Patients aged seventy or older shifted more overall than younger patients. The authors recommend several planning scans and personal judgment for older patients.
pmc-13538549:
Chengchi Xia, Tianshu Rong, and Baoqing Wang grade chemotherapy video quality on two Chinese short-video platforms in a 2026 content analysis. Patients increasingly learn about treatment from clips, yet accuracy there is unchecked. A total of 188 videos were scored for quality and reliability with two standard scales. Uploader identity, clip traits, and engagement counts were modeled within and across platforms.

Overall quality fell short on both platforms. One platform drew far more interaction, while the other scored higher on reliability and quality. Certified cancer doctors supplied the largest share of clips and clearly outscored patient uploads. On the engagement-first platform, better clips drew fewer likes and comments, a pattern absent on the rival service. Platform identity itself predicted reliability after adjustment. The authors urge recommendation systems that weight professional quality over traffic.
pmc-13539549:
Christy R Austin and colleagues confront myths and mistaken beliefs about what dyslexia is and how it should be treated in a review grounded in reading science. Despite solid research, confusion persists in the United States where state laws, school practice, and parent advocacy collide, and fad treatments thrive on misinformation spread by the uninformed or sold for profit. Historical misreadings and shifting definitions receive scrutiny.

Dyslexia is framed as word-reading difficulty on a severity continuum needing the same proven teaching at greater intensity. Structured literacy, meaning explicit systematic teaching of foundational and language skills, carries the strongest evidence. Vision treatments, special fonts, and brain training lack support, and the famed multisensory element of one legacy method adds nothing beyond shared structured parts. The authors urge critical appraisal of treatment claims.
pmc-13540249:
Daniel Mead, Timothy Mallers, Ian Rios, and Emily Ho investigate, in a 2026 records study, new cases of low blood sodium among residents of a skilled nursing facility. Low sodium is common in such homes and is tied to falls, confusion, hospital transfer, and death.
