Data covered 1,256 adults with laboratory results at one suburban facility. About thirty-five percent developed low sodium after admission. Feeding through a tube more than doubled the adjusted risk, while chronic kidney disease and liver disease also raised it independently. Heart failure, age, sex, ethnicity, and risky medicines showed no clear link at the study's strict threshold. Monitoring plans for tube-fed residents are the practical message.
pmc-13540849:
Fangwang Fu leads a 2026 brain imaging study testing whether water movement beside the brain's fluid chambers separates chronic migraine from the episodic form. Chronic migraine brings heavy disability, yet scan markers that distinguish the two patterns remain scarce.

Scans from 289 adults covered healthy controls, episodic migraine, and chronic migraine, all taken between attacks in evening sessions. The marker, periventricular diffusivity, was clearly lower in chronic migraine than in both other groups, which did not differ from each other. Lower values tracked with more frequent headaches, greater disability scores, and several structural brain differences. The authors propose the measure as a candidate signature of chronic migraine.
pmc-13543349:
Mohammad Affendy Mhd Akhir's team published a 2026 scoping review of programmes that try to improve how low-income parents feed young children. Feeding habits formed early shape children's diets and self-control, yet poverty and food insecurity tangle every piece of advice. Using standard scoping methods, the team searched three databases and found sixteen articles on fifteen distinct interventions from 2015 to 2025.

Most centred on parenting support; others came online, at home, or through combined nutrition education. Attuned feeding, meaning spotting and meeting a child's hunger and fullness cues, was the target that grew most often. Schemes built around active skill practice, such as coaching and guided practice, changed behaviour more steadily than information alone. Few designs faced household food insecurity head-on, a gap the authors flag for the next round of interventions.
pmc-13543449:
Arzu Sarialioğlu and Tuğba Oluç published a 2026 randomised trial of a liquid motion bubbler timer. This soothing sensory toy, with slowly falling coloured bubbles, was tested for whether it calms young children during blood sampling. Blood draws frighten many children and can erode trust in healthcare. Ninety children aged four to six were split evenly between a group that played with the toy before and during sampling and a control group. Fear and anxiety were rated on child-appropriate scales.

Children given the toy scored significantly lower on both fear and state anxiety than controls. The authors conclude the inexpensive, reusable toy is a practical distraction for invasive procedures in paediatric units. The intervention needs no drugs, training burden, or screen, so it can be adopted quickly. The trial was formally registered, lending its simple result extra weight for nurses planning kinder blood draws.
pmc-13543549:
Bhiromlak Charoenrat and colleagues reported in 2026 on how smartphone use affects balance and walking in older women with neck pain. Neck pain already disturbs posture and gait, and phones add a second task. Thirty-four women with neck pain and thirty-four without stood on a force plate and walked through motion capture under three conditions each: no phone, and phone tasks including texting, watching, and talking. Dual-task cost measured how much performance fell when the phone was added.

Phone use did not interact with group membership; instead, two separate effects appeared. Women with neck pain swayed more, walked slower with shorter steps, and paid a higher dual-task cost under every condition. Talking on the phone disturbed balance and gait most for everyone. Phone conversations while walking, the authors imply, deserve a specific caution for older women whose necks already compromise their stability.
pmc-13543649:
Michalina Jakimowicz's team ran a 2026 field trial on adding effective microorganisms, bought blends of helpful microbes, to common carp ponds. Over 103 days in twenty-five earthen ponds, two products were dosed into feed and water. Microbial communities were sequenced in water, sediment, and fish intestines, and fish growth was tracked, testing whether the blends take hold or simply pass through.

The dosed families never settled clearly in the pond waters, and the resident communities stayed broadly unchanged. Yet fish under certain treatments grew plainly better. Benefit without colonisation suggests the products act in passing, perhaps during digestion, rather than by reshaping the pond. For farmers seeking growth without antibiotic residues, the authors present that as a hopeful, if puzzling in mechanism, result worth chasing.
pmc-13546549:
Mohammed Y Youssef and co-authors analyzed in 2026 three decades of data on colorectal cancer diagnosed before age 50 in the United States, asking which changeable risks drive its rise. Drawing on the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study, they tracked incidence, deaths, and disability from 1990 to 2023 and projected trends to 2050 under different risk scenarios.

Incidence rose by about 47 percent over the period, and men carried a consistently higher burden than women. By 2023, a diet high in processed meat had become the leading changeable contributor to deaths from the disease, ahead of low whole grain intake, high body mass, and smoking. Their modeling suggests that serious risk reduction could cut projected mortality by more than half by 2050.
pmc-13547349:
Matilde Balbi and a large team studied in 2026 whether the tiny vesicles released by lab-grown stem cells can calm inflammation and oxidative damage in osteoarthritis. The work tests a cell-free alternative to transplanting the cells themselves. Their stem cells came from reprogrammed adult cells, a source meant to be more uniform than donor tissue. The team profiled the vesicles' microRNA cargo at several growth stages and tested six chosen microRNAs in a laboratory joint disease model.

Together the six microRNAs lowered inflammatory messenger levels, cut the buildup of harmful reactive oxygen, and restored the cells' own antioxidant defenses. The authors read the cargo as the active ingredient behind the vesicles' effects and propose vesicle therapy as a minimally invasive route to modify the disease.
pmc-13548549:
Lucas Petit Navarro and colleagues study how well a breathing monitor reading matches true blood carbon dioxide in brain-injured patients before hospital arrival, in a 2026 retrospective study. Crews ventilate these patients by machine and steer by end-tidal carbon dioxide, the gas measured at the airway, yet blood values can drift away from that reading. The team reviewed 100 ventilated adults with moderate to severe brain injury at a major trauma center.

Patients were grouped by how stable their circulation was before arrival. The gap between blood and airway readings widened step by step, from stable patients to those who stayed unstable despite low-dose blood pressure drugs. Agreement between the paired readings fell across the same groups. Shifting targets by circulation group did not fix the mismatch. The authors warn that airway readings alone can mislead ventilation decisions in unstable brain injury.
pmc-13548649:
Jia-Qi Huang and colleagues test a radiation planning strategy that shields the segment of the esophagus nearest the tumor, in a 2026 feasibility study in lung cancer. Swallowing-tube inflammation is a common, painful side effect when the esophagus sits close to the treatment target. Eighty high-risk patients treated between 2023 and 2025 had their most exposed esophageal stretch mapped, with dose caps set by how much that stretch overlapped the target.

About thirty percent developed esophagitis, nearly all mild, with a single severe case and none at the worst grades. A historical comparison group treated before the strategy had suffered inflammation in over three quarters of cases. In ten patients planned both ways, the new approach lowered esophagus dose while keeping tumor coverage broadly intact. The authors call the method feasible and ask for prospective trials.
pmc-13549949:
Inas Rahou and colleagues used citizen science to map fellow problems in endometriosis. Published in 2026, the study drew on the Isala platform in Flanders, setting 95 women with self-noted endometriosis beside 2,279 without. Endometriosis, a chronic swelling-linked condition of childbearing-age women, often brings pelvic pain and baby trouble.

Vaginal microbe mix and variety did not differ between groups, hinting at most a small role for vaginal microbes in the condition. Endometriosis linked strongly to ovary cyst syndrome, migraine, touchy bowel syndrome, and painful sex, with odds ratios from 1.67 to 3.75. The authors present citizen science as a strong partner to clinic research for catching missed fellow problems. Readers get a fellow-problem map with a null microbiome result.
pmc-13550449:
Marcel Bahia Lanza and colleagues ask whether the resting quality of leg muscles explains how quickly younger and older adults shift their weight when stepping, in a 2026 pilot study. Falls often begin with a failed step, and stepping needs fast, efficient weight transfer. Twenty-three volunteers had ultrasound scans of three leg muscles, strength tests for knee and hip muscles, and a reactive stepping test, with statistical compression folding nine muscle measures into four profiles.

The first profile captured good muscle quality with strength, while others captured mismatches between muscle size and force. Yet when the profiles and age group were modeled together, none significantly explained the timing of weight transfer, neither when it began nor how long it took, in either stepping direction. The authors suggest stepping depends on dynamic qualities like reaction speed and coordination, and they call for larger studies.
pmc-13551749:
Mustafa Demir, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 meta-analysis of the link between problematic social media use and social comparison, the habit of judging oneself against others. The team pooled twenty independent studies from 2019 to 2025 covering adolescents, students, and adults in individualistic and collectivist cultures, using a random-effects model.

The overall relationship was modestly positive, and a bias adjustment trimmed it only slightly in the reported analysis. When studies controlled for other variables, the link weakened yet stayed detectable. Effects varied widely, growing with older samples, higher shares of men, and theory-based comparison scales, while adolescent effects stayed small. The authors call the connection real but limited and context-sensitive.
pmc-13551849:
Minxia Hua, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 survey of mpox knowledge among Chinese public health professionals responsible for infectious disease control. Mpox has twice been declared a global health emergency, and these professionals handle reporting and public communication during outbreaks. A nationwide online survey collected 1,568 valid responses from professionals in 28 provincial-level regions, testing 37 knowledge items on cause, features, spread, and prevention.

Most respondents had heard of mpox, yet only about three in five reached the sufficient knowledge threshold in the reported scoring. Knowledge of clinical features ran higher than knowledge of cause or prevention. Working at a disease control center, senior title, frequent attention to mpox, and using more information sources all associated with sufficient knowledge, guiding where training should aim.
pmc-13551949:
Shalin Wan Fei Lee, Li Sze Chai, and Saloma Pawi published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of music interventions for breastfeeding mothers. Stress can block the milk ejection reflex, especially for mothers of infants in intensive care, and music is a drug-free candidate remedy. The team searched four databases for randomized trials published up to 2024, rating quality with standard bias and evidence tools.

Six trials with 696 participants qualified, all carrying some concerns on quality checks. Pooled results showed music significantly raised milk volume, both right after sessions and cumulatively, improved milk fat content, and lowered the stress hormone cortisol in saliva in the reported analyses. Evidence certainty was moderate to low, so the authors advise cautious interpretation alongside the encouraging direction.
pmc-13554449:
Shixi Shang leads a nine-author team testing a ginseng compound for vessel damage in sepsis in a 2026 study. Sepsis makes vessel linings leaky, starving organs of steady blood flow. Mice with severe abdominal infection and human vessel cells dosed with bacterial toxin both modelled the damage. The compound, ginsenoside Rb1, was checked against known pathway blockers to pin down its route.

Treated mice survived better and suffered less lung injury. Inflammatory signals in lung fluid fell, and immune cell balance steadied. In cells, the compound rebuilt the protein seams that seal vessel walls and cut oxidative harm. It steadied the power plants inside cells by blocking a shape-changing pathway. The authors nominate it as a sepsis candidate.
pmc-13555849:
Yixuan Zhong leads a nine-author team studying how family health resources cushion rural Chinese households against the money shock of illness in a 2026 study. Data came from a 2020 national family panel survey. Households rated modestly on health resources on average, and about one in eleven faced high economic risk from disease. Path analysis traced how resources flow into protection.

Richer family health resources predicted clearly lower economic risk. Part of the gain ran through saving up resources and putting them to work early. Another part ran through needing less rescue spending after illness struck. Households with balanced, plentiful resources gained most through the saving and investing paths. The authors urge targeted help to build household reserves before illness hits.
pmc-13555949:
Xili Feng leads a five-author team comparing the fine print of dog and cat parvovirus genomes in a 2026 study. The cat virus likely gave rise to the dog virus, which now devastates puppies worldwide. Both viruses keep their protein-building sites highly conserved, under strong purifying selection. Spare letter pairs called CpG run scarce across all four viral genes, hinting at host pressure.

Silent spelling choices vary more freely, yet still follow nonrandom biases tuned by selection. Coat genes show tighter spelling discipline and better matching to host transfer RNAs than other genes. Dog virus genes oddly fit cat hosts better than dog hosts at the translation level. The authors read this as fine-scale tuning for host jumping.
pmc-13557149:
Piazza and colleagues argued in a 2026 review that voice box cancers reaching different parts of one deep tissue space should not share a single stage. Since 2002, any tumor entering the paraglottic space, a fat-filled route beside the vocal cords, has counted as stage T3 in the international TNM system. Newer surgical evidence splits its lower part into front and back compartments with different outlooks.

Piazza gathered surgical and non-surgical evidence and proposes dividing these tumors into T3a and T3b. Front-compartment tumors, where the vocal fold stops moving but the small arytenoid cartilage still moves normally, carry a better prognosis. Back-compartment tumors, marked by impaired arytenoid movement and spread past a defined anatomical line, fare worse because they involve the joint unit that moves the vocal fold. Adopting the split would refine staging and help match treatment intensity to real risk.
pmc-13558249:
Chenchen Huang and four colleagues reviewed in 2026 why hepatitis B virus genotype C, common across East Asia, earns its high-risk reputation. Infections with this genotype tend to keep replicating, delay a key immune milestone, inflame the liver more, and end in cirrhosis or liver cancer more often. The review assembles the molecular events thought to explain that pattern and weighs what remains uncertain.

Two promoter mutations and a precore mutation change how the virus copies itself. They also change which antigens it shows. A faulty viral X protein pushes toward cancer, as does viral DNA woven into the host genome. Faults in cell damage responses, a weakened tumour suppressor, and disturbed cell recycling may add to the risk. Even when modern antiviral pills suppress the virus, genotype C patients keep a higher residual cancer risk, which the authors say justifies closer surveillance.
pmc-13558549:
Sung Cheol Park and four colleagues built in 2026 a deep learning tool that predicts spinal cord compression in the neck from plain X-rays taken in three head positions. Magnetic resonance imaging confirms this degenerative condition but costs more and is harder to access. Their dataset held nearly eight thousand patients who had both X-rays and MRI at a major centre, labelled by the scan results, plus 575 patients from an independent hospital for outside testing.

Ten proven image networks were trained on single positions, combined positions, and combined images plus patient details. The best pairing, a classic architecture fed all three positions, separated compressed from uncompressed cords well at home and respectably abroad. Heat maps pointed at disc bulges, bone spurs, ligament hardening, and unstable segments as the regions driving decisions. The authors propose the tool as a cheap first screen.
pmc-13558649:
Wen-Jing Zhong and eleven colleagues identified in 2026 a pore-forming protein that neutrophils need in order to cast out their DNA traps during acute lung injury. Those traps, called NETs, help catch germs yet in excess they shred lung tissue in the severe syndrome ARDS. Mining public single-cell data, the team found the protein NINJ1 concentrated in inflammatory neutrophil groups, then tested its role in patient cells and in mice.

The protein must link into clusters before traps can escape, and two specific building blocks in its chain proved essential for that clustering. Mice whose neutrophils lacked the gene released no traps, suffered less lung dysfunction, and died less often from lung injury. Patient neutrophils behaved the same way. The authors nominate NINJ1 as a drug target that might disarm traps without disabling the cells themselves.
pmc-13558749:
Y Ravi and colleagues compared in 2026 Indian genotypes of Nigella sativa, the black seed spice prized in traditional medicine, hunting for lines that combine oil yield with health chemistry. Seeds vary wildly between varieties, and no breeder can improve what has not been measured. The team profiled oil content, fatty acids, the signature compound thymoquinone, antioxidant strength, and nutrition indices across a genotype panel, then used multivariate statistics to rank the lines.

Oil yield spanned a threefold range, from about ten percent to about thirty percent of seed weight. Linoleic acid dominated the fat profile, and unsaturated fats earned favourable nutrition scores in every line. Thymoquinone, the compound behind much of the seed's reputation, varied sharply and peaked in one standout line. Ten genotypes combined high oil, rich unsaturated fat, strong antioxidants, and dense bioactives. Those elite lines are the authors' candidates for functional foods and targeted breeding.
pmc-13560149:
Seda Adamyan and colleagues screen golden jackals in Armenia for tick-borne pathogens, testing whether this expanding wild canid carries infections of human concern. Their 2026 study collected blood from 77 jackals across six regions between August 2024 and March 2026. A PCR and reverse line blot method screened simultaneously for several bacterial and protistan pathogen groups.

Six zoonotic pathogens turned up. Rickettsia helvetica led at 16.9 percent of samples, with Lyme disease bacteria and Babesia canis each found in a small share. Co-infections appeared in 7.8 percent of all samples, including one triple infection. Female jackals carried Rickettsia helvetica far more often than males in the reported comparison. Adults trended toward higher infection rates than juveniles. The authors call the work the first molecular evidence of these pathogens in Transcaucasian jackals and flag the animals as potential reservoir hosts under a One Health lens.
pmc-13560349:
Hongsoo Kim and colleagues develop explainable machine learning to predict which older home care recipients will move into institutions or die, using routine needs-assessment data from Korea's long-term care insurance. Their 2026 study covers 36,526 newly enrolled beneficiaries. Four models vied in a setup treating the two ends as rivals.

Within six months, 10.4 percent of recipients had entered facilities, rising to 18.8 percent by twelve months in the reported figures. A penalized regression model did best overall. Its strongest move-in signals were striking: eating nonfood items, a marker of advanced dementia, suctioning needs, and a dementia label. Death was best flagged by oxygen therapy, cancer pain care, and diabetic foot care. The authors propose embedding the algorithm in assessment workflows so care workers can aim preventive services at those likeliest to lose home care.
pmc-13560649:
Melanie Baires and twenty-six colleagues published this 2026 genome announcement of two bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, isolated from topsoil using the soil bacterium Arthrobacter globiformis as host. PrairieDogTown came from soil at Texas Tech University in Lubbock, and Kinny from the University of Ottawa in Canada. Both were plaque-purified, grown to high titre, and fully sequenced as part of the student-driven phage discovery programme that catalogues actinobacteriophage diversity.

PrairieDogTown carries a compact 36.2-kilobase genome with 52 genes and falls into cluster FO of the actinobacteriophage database, while Kinny is larger at 56.4 kilobases with 93 genes and belongs to cluster AU. Both are lytic, meaning they destroy their host cells rather than integrating quietly. Announcements of this kind steadily expand the reference collection used to study phage evolution, host range and the genetics of bacterial viruses. They give future researchers named, sequenced material from two distinct North American soils.
pmc-13561749:
Yu-Yue Zhou and colleagues review in 2026 how oxidative stress, damage from excess reactive oxygen molecules, drives bladder dysfunction when urine outflow is partly blocked. Such blockage, often from an enlarged prostate, forces the bladder through repeated cycles of oxygen loss and return.

Drawing on studies from 1990 to 2026, the review traces how those cycles spark inflammation, cell death programs, and scarring inside the bladder wall. Key pathways include a master inflammation switch and the body's own antioxidant defense system. Several antioxidant drugs eased damage in animal studies. The authors note that human translation lags, and they urge work on injury markers and combined treatments that restore the bladder's chemical balance.
pmc-13562549:
Guanghui Liu and five colleagues measure how wind forces act on ice-coated power lines, and test a shortcut engineers use to predict dangerous line vibration. Ice building up on one side of a cable gives it a crescent shape that catches the wind unevenly. The 2026 team ran wind tunnel tests at speeds from 10 to 18 metres per second with ice layers 14, 24, and 33 millimetres thick. A swinging model captured how forces change as the cable moves, not just when it sits still.

Fitted formulas linked the steady forces to the wind angle. A neural network trained on the measurements then predicted forces for untested settings with fit values above 0.95. Converting steady values through the standard quasi-static shortcut matched the swinging-model data well in this range. The authors say the shortcut holds here, and the network gives designers a sharper tool for judging galloping risk on overhead lines.
pmc-13562649:
Jing Ma and colleagues traced a chain from fermented feed to richer goat milk. Silage, forage preserved by fermentation, feeds ruminants through winter, and inoculating it with lactic acid bacteria is known to improve its quality. Yet how that feed reshapes the rumen and the udder was unclear. Their 2026 study fed dairy goats silage inoculated with Lactiplantibacillus plantarum BX62 and followed the effects along the gut-to-udder axis.

The inoculated silage carried more flavonoids, plant compounds that reshaped rumen microbes and boosted fibre breakdown. That shift raised acetate, a building block for milk fat, and switched on fat-making genes in the udder. Milk fat synthesis improved as a result. The authors present the work as a mechanistic basis for improving goat lactation by managing silage fermentation.
pmc-13563849:
Ruoyu Li and four colleagues model how MRSA, the drug-resistant staph bacterium, spreads through Alberta's hospitals, including the carriers nobody flags at the door. Patients can carry the germ without symptoms, and arrivals quietly seed wards. Their 2026 study built a Bayesian compartment model of 106 hospitals, splitting patients by where the germ was acquired and whether it merely colonised or infected. Data from Edmonton, Calgary, and rural areas fitted the model, and simulations varied how many carriers slip in per thousand admissions.

Infected patients passed the germ to susceptible contacts more readily than carriers did. Calgary's hospitals showed the highest transmission, rural hospitals sat in the middle, and Edmonton's ran lowest, though the uncertainty ranges overlapped. Assuming more hidden carriers nudged transmission rates up slightly. The authors say the model gives teams a map of where spread pressure concentrates, and a way to test screening policies before paying for them.
pmc-13564149:
Abdul Shadab and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, lipid nanoparticles that hitch a ride on albumin, the common blood protein, to deliver messenger RNA more safely. Standard particles tend to collect in the liver and can harm it, while older fixes such as surface coating have stopped yielding much improvement.

By recruiting the body's own albumin, these particles may dodge the liver and travel through lymph channels, which suits immune-focused treatments. The authors frame the shift as a biological alliance rather than chemical camouflage. Drug developers get a concise tour of a delivery strategy that could widen where mRNA medicines can safely go.
pmc-13568249:
Gabriel Thierry and co-authors test, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether clamping the liver's blood vessels during liver surgery leaves patients with high blood sugar afterward. The clamping step, called the Pringle manoeuvre, limits bleeding. Records covered 163 adults having planned liver removal at one university hospital between 2020 and 2022, with 107 clamped and 56 not.

High blood sugar within a day of surgery struck about fifty-five percent of the clamped group against about twenty-three percent of the others. Clamping stayed linked after other factors were weighed. The study also examined infections and hospital stay. Anesthesia and surgical teams gain a concrete metabolic side effect to anticipate when clamping is used.
pmc-13569849:
Lyu and co-authors evaluate a candidate biomarker in this 2026 pan-cancer study of ITPRIPL1, a protein recently tied to tumor-immune regulation, across four gastrointestinal cancers: stomach, colon, rectal, and esophageal. Integrating bulk tumor sequencing, immune pathway analysis, survival modeling, and single-cell data, they asked where the marker actually carries clinical meaning.

The gene was switched on across all four cancers, yet its prognostic bite was strikingly specific: high expression predicted worse survival consistently only in stomach adenocarcinoma. There it tracked with genomic instability features and immune pathway activity, and its effect shifted with the local balance of killer and helper T cells. Single-cell data placed the protein preferentially in T cells and immune structures beside tumors. Early checks even linked higher levels to better survival in some immunotherapy cohorts and to stronger drug sensitivity in cell lines, sharpening its gastric focus.
pmc-13572549:
Yunyi Chen, with seven colleagues, presents a 2026 design for lithium metal batteries that start with no anode at all. Such cells pack more energy and are simpler to build, since lithium plates onto a bare copper sheet on first charge. The snag is poor reversibility: lithium plates and strips unevenly, grows spikes, and dies fast.

The team added a silver-based starter mix to the electrolyte. Silver ions settle on the copper and make it welcome lithium, while partner ions trigger a skin that forms in place and can heal itself. That skin flips the usual layout, with an organic-rich inner layer and a mineral-rich outer layer. A test cell kept 90 percent of its capacity after 200 cycles. A 2 amp-hour pouch cell reached 467 watt-hours per kilogram.
pmc-13574149:
Batista and colleagues test gene therapy in this 2026 study of Cockayne syndrome, a recessive disorder of failed DNA repair that stunts growth, degenerates the nervous system, and shortens life. About 30 percent of cases trace to the ERCC8 gene, called CSA, and no treatment exists. The team packaged a working human CSA copy into an AAV9 virus vector and injected it into the brain ventricles of newborn mice modeling the disease.

Treated mice lived significantly longer than untreated littermates, and the human protein spread broadly through brain and heart with no sign of vector toxicity. The rescue was incomplete: brain imaging and tissue analysis still showed underdeveloped myelin, reactive glial cells, and inflammation, and liver gene activity at endpoint hinted at life-limiting changes there. The authors present the lifespan gain as proof of principle paving the way toward human trials.
pmc-13576749:
Christopher E Berndsen leads a 2026 teaching paper on bringing real research projects into a large biochemistry lecture course. Course-based research experiences boost student confidence and skills, yet class size and dense content block them in big lectures. The team rebuilt a semester project around protein structure and function using free cloud computing.

Students work through four modules, then study a novel protein variant of their own in a final project. Running the tools in Google Colaboratory removed the barrier of varied student laptops. A science and maths librarian teaches information and data skills alongside. Since autumn 2024 more than 250 students have taken part. Self-assessments show gains in confidence for reading molecular structures, linking gene changes to protein function, and using databases such as UniProt. The authors offer the model to other large courses.
pmc-13578449:
Ichiro Matsuo and a large team of co-authors test how a gum germ toxin harms the mouse heart, in a 2026 study. The germ behind gum disease sheds a toxin that can enter the blood, and gum disease has long tracked with heart trouble. Mice got the toxin daily for a week, and a common beta blocker drug was tested as a shield.

The toxin sped the heart, tilted nerve signals toward the stress branch, and cut the heart's pumping share. Scar tissue, cell death, and DNA damage all climbed several fold in heart muscle. The blocker reversed nearly all of it. Tracing the chain pointed to a stress pathway that leaks calcium inside heart cells. The authors argue stress nerve signals help turn gum infection into heart damage.
pmc-13578749:
Zilin Chen and colleagues built a screening model to flag children with tic disorders who may also have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Tic symptoms can mask attention problems, so the second diagnosis is often delayed. The team studied 1,364 children treated at Guang'anmen Hospital between October 2023 and October 2024, of whom 475 had both conditions.

From twenty-eight clinical features, seven proved most informative, led by learning initiative and guardian type, followed by school performance, allergic rhinitis, irritability, adenoid enlargement, and sleep quality. A random forest model scored best, with an area under the curve of 0.780 on the test set. External validation is still required before any clinical use.
pmc-13579149:
Julio M Pimentel, Jun-Ying Zhou, and Gen Sheng Wu review a new cancer drug for a deadly brain tumor type, in a 2027 paper. The drug, called ONC201 or dordaviprone, recently won fast track approval for tumors carrying a gene fault named H3 K27M, the first such win for that disease. It began life as a compound that coaxes cancer cells to raise a death signal.

The review maps four routes by which the drug kills: the death signal itself, a cell stress program, a switch inside cell powerhouses, and blocking a dopamine sensor. Early trials showed a safe profile with a once weekly pill. Resistance paths are already in view, among them faults in the powerhouse switch and detours through growth pathways. Trials now reach into blood and womb related cancers, alone and in drug pairs.
pmc-13579749:
Xiuli Xu and colleagues lay out a trial plan testing a squeezing cuff therapy for chronic insomnia, in a 2026 protocol paper. The therapy, built for blood vessel disease, inflates cuffs on the limbs in rhythm with the heart to boost circulation. A small pilot from the same team hinted it may also aid sleep, so a full trial was designed to check the claim and hunt the mechanism.

Ninety eight adults with chronic insomnia will be assigned by chance to real or sham sessions, forty five minutes each, five times a week for thirty five sessions. Sleep quality scores lead the outcome list, backed by sleep timing measures, mood and life quality scales, fitness and vessel tests, and blood markers. Checks run through a year of follow up at one center.
pmc-13579849:
Gloris Joseph, Shrivathsa Kulavalli, Sabine Bélard, and Kavitha Saravu review how often leptospirosis arrives with a second infection in India, in a 2026 study. The water borne bacterial disease mimics several local fevers, which can mask a double infection. Four databases were searched for studies from 2010 to mid 2024, and thirty nine papers covering over fifteen hundred cases made the cut.

About one in seven cases in the pooled set carried a second infection. In the stricter set of studies built to hunt coinfections, the share was lower, near one in eleven. Dengue led the partner list by far, ahead of hepatitis E, typhoid, and malaria. New Delhi and Kerala reported the most doubled cases. Shared signs like fever, yellowing, and low platelets blur the picture, and doubled cases died more often.
pmc-13582249:
Burri and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether draining the stomach outlet during a major esophagus operation prevents slow stomach emptying afterward. The Ivor Lewis operation removes part of the esophagus and rebuilds it with a tube made from the stomach. Slow emptying of that tube affects between one and five of every ten patients and can cause lung infection from inhaled food and longer hospital stays.

Burri found only four studies, covering 739 patients, that compared preventive drainage methods such as widening the outlet or injecting botulinum toxin against no drainage. About a third of untreated patients had slow emptying, but study results varied so much that pooled figures were shaky. One method looked strong only after a mismatched study was dropped. The authors judge the proof too thin and uneven to back routine drainage, and they call for shared definitions and larger trials.
pmc-13582349:
Jie Ying Wu and colleagues ask patients how they feel about surgical robots that act partly on their own, in a 2026 interview study. Fifty adults who had surgery in the past three years, by robot or by hand, took part by video call. Most were women, with an average age in the early fifties.

Just over half said they would accept a semi autonomous operation. Willingness swung with which step the robot controlled, peaking when it only handled instruments. Four drivers shaped the answer: a wish for consent that honors self rule, fear of new risks, trust in the surgeon, and belief in the gains. The authors say naming these worries in consent talks could ease the path for surgical robots.
pmc-13584249:
Marie-Soleil Hardy and colleagues ask what helps or blocks new practices in Canadian long-term care homes in this 2026 study. The COVID-19 pandemic hit care home residents hard and showed how slowly proven methods reach these settings. The team used a readiness survey built for that purpose and gave it to staff before and after a new practice was put in place.

Responses came from 256 workers in 55 care homes, split between managers and front-line staff. Readiness scores changed most with the province a home sat in, which reflects how health care is run locally. Homes with a medical director, and homes that belonged to a chain, also scored higher. The authors say leaders should weigh those setting factors before rolling out change.
pmc-13584349:
Mingli Dong and colleagues ask whether embryo screening helps couples who have lost pregnancies again and again. The screening, called PGT-A, checks embryos for the wrong number of chromosomes before transfer during fertility treatment. Their 2026 study reviewed cases at a large hospital in China, comparing patients who used the screening with those who went ahead without it.

Per transfer, the screened group reached a clinical pregnancy in well over half of cases, against about a third in the other group. Live births per transfer also doubled in the screened group, reaching half of transfers. Rates of early chemical pregnancy and later miscarriage, though, did not differ clearly between groups. The authors read their findings as support for screening in this hard-hit group of patients.
pmc-13586649:
L M Guedes and colleagues dissect the tiny galls that mites raise on the leaves of a Chilean tree. The tree, Crinodendron patagua, grows in dry coastal forests and has tough, leathery leaves packed with defense chemicals. Such armor should repel leaf feeders, yet small eriophyid mites settle in and reshape the leaf into a shelter. The team compared galled and clean leaves in structure and chemistry.

Inside the gall, the mites thinned the upper cell walls and stocked the feeding cells with proteins and sugars for their young. Around the gall's mouth, hairs hardened into a guard, outer cells swelled with thicker walls, and bitter polyphenols rose in the tissue. Some tough leaf traits grew stronger under the mites' control while others stayed put. The picture is of a leaf reprogrammed to feed and shield its tiny tenants.
pmc-13587649:
Radu-Ioan Onija and colleagues used quantum calculations to ask why biology chose cobalt for vitamin B12 and nickel for coenzyme F430. Both cofactors stabilize super-reduced metal(I) states, in which the metal holds an extra electron, during catalysis. The team modeled porphyrin, corrin, and corphin rings holding cobalt, rhodium, iron, manganese, or nickel, and checked the available spin states.

Porphyrin rings gave no clear metal(I) picture, instead pairing metal(II) with ring radicals, matching the fact that biology does not use porphyrin for super-reduced chemistry. Corrin yielded a clean cobalt(I) ground state and no clear super-reduced state for neighboring metals. The least conjugated ring, corphin, yielded a clear nickel(I) state, explaining each cofactor's metal choice.
pmc-13589049:
Michael R Williamson and colleagues hunt the brain changes behind memory trouble in childhood sleep apnea. In this condition, the airway collapses repeatedly at night, and the front-line fix, removing tonsils and adenoids, often fails to restore learning. Working in a mouse model that mirrors the illness, the team read gene activity cell by cell in the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub.

Gene programs were disturbed in every cell type, most sharply in glia, the brain's support cells, and in neural stem cells. Six genes showed matching drops at the protein level across four cell types. Insulation of nerve fibers, the myelin wrapping laid by glial cells, was measurably impaired, glial shapes looked abnormal, and stem cell numbers in their nursery zone had thinned. The authors frame glial failure as a core driver and publish the full cell atlas for others to mine.
pmc-13590149:
This 2026 document collects the contributed papers of the Canadian Health Libraries Association conference, a bilingual bundle of short research reports from health librarians across Canada. No single study unites them; together they survey a profession in transition.

Among the contributions, one team studied how closing the British Columbia physicians' college library in 2024 affected doctors. Those doctors lost literature search and document delivery services, and the team interviewed seventeen physicians about the change. Another compared human screeners' key concepts against machine indexing for finding records. A French-language report from a Quebec health network describes reinventing a hospital library around five projects, including embedding a librarian inside clinical services and supporting artificial intelligence use. Other papers cover grey literature publishing at a Quebec occupational health institute and further service redesigns.
pmc-13591749:
Kenneth Boe Krarup and colleagues studied how in situ drills, training in the real ward setting, affect learning versus off-site drills. Cross-training, where staff adopt other jobs' roles, is common but disputed. Their interview-based study in a Danish critical-care unit mixed watching, field notes, and 16 talks with doctors and nurses, read by theme.

Four themes emerged: realism, feel-safe factor, transfer, and cross-training. In situ drills felt more lifelike and gripping than off-site drills, aiding deeper buy-in and learning. Safety grew with known teammates, limited watching, and skilled, polite leading. Transfer to practice seemed stronger, sometimes changing ward routines. Most staff, above all juniors, liked true-role training best, saying cross-training hurt safety and learning. The authors urge setups centred on true roles.
pmc-13592149:
Nigel Sherriff leads a multinational team building a scale to grade how ready health workers are to care well for LGBTQI+ patients. Such patients still meet stigma and thin knowledge in clinics, which delays care and breeds mistrust. Experts first drafted 100 candidate items, then a Delphi panel of specialists trimmed the pool to 39 test items. The survey ran online across three countries: the United Kingdom, Italy, and the United States.

Over 1,300 health workers and trainees finished the survey, alongside two older comparison scales. Analysis began as the protocol paper closed, with results due later. Sherriff and the team expect the PRIDE scale to prove sound in both English and Italian, giving trainers a firm yardstick for teaching and for judging workplace climate.
pmc-13593549:
Xianjin Hu and co-authors present a patient whose early extra heartbeats arose next to the His bundle, the heart's central electrical relay, and kept coming back after radiofrequency ablation. In their 2026 report they turned to focal pulsed-field ablation, which uses brief electric pulses rather than heat, in a spot where burning tissue risks permanent damage to the conduction system.

During energy delivery the patient briefly showed a junctional rhythm and even complete heart block. The authors say such changes may not signal lasting injury. They still warrant an immediate pause and close watching. A right bundle branch block persisted after the procedure, which they attribute to a mix of mechanical trauma from the catheter and the electrical effect of the pulses. Patients should be warned about such risks beforehand, the team concludes.
pmc-13594449:
Marie R Biondi Ryan leads a sixteen-author coalition from universities, industry, and government weighing how to make infant formula more like human milk. Human milk is a living, changing food packed with active components. Those components protect and develop the baby. Formula has gained ingredients over thirty years. It still does not match milk in composition or in outcomes for infants.

New ingredients could come from other species' milk, from precision fermentation, or from cultured mammary cells, the review notes. Getting them into formula is the hard part: doses must track milk's natural variability, safety must be reasonably certain, and researchers need agreed ways to test both safety and real functional benefit. The authors argue the field advances only if academic, industry, and regulatory scientists settle these questions together.
pmc-13595049:
Yi Chieh Chang, Cherng-Shyang Chang, and Chung-Kan Tsao engineered a living wrapper for cartilage scaffolds. The wrapper is a sheet of fibroblast cells. It shields the implant from the host body after surgery. Cartilage engineering often fails because host tissue invades the scaffold and disrupts new cartilage, while sealing the scaffold off completely starves it of exchange with its surroundings.

Implanted in mice, the plain fibroblast sheet did block invasion, yet cartilage matrix inside the scaffold fell, showing the cost of a purely defensive barrier. Adding endothelial progenitor cells, which encourage blood vessel growth, to the sheet changed the balance: matrix formation recovered and vessels grew richer around the scaffold. The authors present the cell sheet as an active interface rather than a mere wall, letting the implant negotiate with host tissue instead of hiding from it.
pmc-13595749:
Maryam Shahdoust, Rosa Aghdam, and Mehdi Sadeghi present SimMapNet, a method for inferring which genes regulate which others. A simple hunch guides it. Genes with similar documented functions are likelier to be wired together. Their 2026 Bayesian framework folds Gene Ontology similarity directly into the statistical prior of a network model.

Tested on a bacterial DNA-repair pathway and on fruit fly data, SimMapNet reconstructed networks more accurately than three established methods on the standard F1 score. It also runs fast enough for large networks. The clearest advantage appeared when samples were few, the setting where purely data-driven inference usually starves. Simulations backed that strength. The authors offer the tool as a principled way to let accumulated biological knowledge steady network building when experiments are small.
pmc-13599249:
Hongjie Jiao leads a twelve-author team studying hydatid infection, caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus, in children in Xinjiang, China. Their 2026 paper reviews cases in children aged 0 to 14 collected between 2007 and 2024 at two hospitals. The infection forms cysts, most often in the liver, and the team also asked whether the infection changes platelet counts, one part of routine blood tests.

After screening, the study covered 316 infected children alongside 496 healthy children. Infections clustered in the Yili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture in the north and were more common in rural areas than in towns. Infected children showed higher platelet counts and higher platelet distribution width than healthy children, with lower mean platelet volume. Sex, age, and ethnic group did not drive the platelet differences. The findings give doctors a fuller picture of how this parasite shows up in children's blood work.
pmc-13600549:
Enze Hu and Yuanfu Qiu planned a meta-analysis of two blood inflammation markers in liver cancer patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Hepatocellular carcinoma, which accounts for ninety percent of primary liver cancers, usually presents too late for curative surgery, making systemic therapy central. Chronic inflammation drives its growth, yet the prognostic value of interleukin-6 and the systemic immune-inflammation index in this treatment setting remains unsettled.

The protocol searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang Data from January 1997 to January 2026 for cohort studies reporting survival outcomes. Hazard ratios for progression-free and overall survival were to be pooled, with subgroup and sensitivity analyses probing heterogeneity. The work aims to test whether simple blood markers can help forecast who benefits from checkpoint immunotherapy.
pmc-13600649:
Shaomeng Sun and colleagues tested whether four blood markers can aid diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome. The syndrome affects five to fifteen percent of women, bringing excess androgens, obesity, and insulin resistance that disrupt ovulation and conception. Vitamin D, Müllerian inhibiting substance, insulin-like growth factor 1, and its binding protein 3 were compared between patients and healthy controls.

Two hundred twelve patients treated between May 2022 and May 2024 were matched against 212 healthy women examined in the same period. Vitamin D ran lower in patients, while the other three markers ran higher, and all four tracked with insulin resistance. Combined, the markers reached an area under the curve of 0.963, beating any single marker alone, suggesting real auxiliary diagnostic value.
pmc-13602449:
Nicholas Gillman and Eric Chung trace in 2026 how two invasive treatments for erectile dysfunction fared in Australia after erection pills arrived. Injections into the penis and surgically implanted prostheses were mainstays before PDE5 inhibitor tablets became first-line therapy in the late 1990s. Using Medicare billing records from 1998 to 2024, the pair counted procedures per 100,000 men and broke trends at key moments such as pill launches and the COVID years.

Across 260,756 procedures, prosthesis implants first plunged after sildenafil appeared, then grew steadily for two decades before COVID slowed elective surgery. Injection therapy collapsed by 97 percent over the period and is now used almost only by men over 55. Both treatments shifted toward older men, especially ages 65 to 84 for implants. Government spending fell sixfold by 2003, then plateaued. Subsidized pill prescriptions climbed from about 440 a year to 25,500, with tadalafil taking the largest share by 2024.
pmc-13602549:
Yongqun He leads a six-author team explaining in 2026 how the Vaccine Ontology sorts what vaccines do to the immune system. Vaccines trigger many responses, from antibodies that block a germ's entry to killer T cells that destroy infected cells, unevenly described across research. The Vaccine Ontology is a shared, community-built language for vaccine science, and the paper shows how it represents responses, biomarkers, and response profiles.

One key move separates 'vaccination', the act of giving a vaccine, from 'vaccine immunization', the immune outcome that follows. Responses are modeled at levels from whole populations, such as herd immunity, down to genes and proteins. Biomarkers like neutralizing antibodies and interferon gamma serve as measurable signs of immune state. Profiles such as Th1- or Th2-biased responses are classed formally, as are correlates of protection. The authors say this structure sharpens classification and should help vaccine design.
pmc-13605749:
Mary F. Wyman leads an eleven-author team surveying caregiver support awareness in a Midwest Tribal Nation in 2026. Family caregivers can draw on training, support groups, and respite, yet few use them, and Indigenous caregivers' views were little known. The team worked under a tribally led research framework. They offered an online survey to all adult Tribal members and affiliates, asking about caregiving, awareness of seven named resources, and cultural fit.

The 481 respondents averaged about 53 years old, and 43 percent were current caregivers, mostly helping an older adult or someone with memory loss. Current caregivers, older adults, and reservation residents knew them best, yet 17 percent knew of none of the seven. Caregivers learned of help mainly through their own research and networks, while non-caregivers cited Tribal communications. Whether a service felt culturally aligned varied by service type. The findings aim at outreach that respects tradition while widening use.
pmc-13612349:
Ferdaus Ibne Aziz leads a six-author team building a brain tumor classifier meant to survive contact with real hospital data. MRI scans vary by scanner and site, tumor classes are imbalanced, and black-box models strain clinician trust. Their NeuroTrustNet framework fuses three views of each scan: convolutional networks, vision transformers, and handcrafted radiomic features. An adaptive attention stacking mechanism blends them, weighting features case by case rather than with fixed rules.

On a large multi-dataset corpus, heavyweight ensembles peaked at 96 percent accuracy externally, while NeuroTrustNet reached 94 percent. The trade was deliberate: the fusion stage cost roughly 80 percent less computation than full ensemble training. Lightweight baseline models filled out the comparison across budgets. A post-hoc layer adds visual attribution maps and plain-language summaries for clinicians. The authors pitch the system as decision support for settings that cannot afford datacenter-scale inference.
pmc-13613249:
Philipp Braun and colleagues test a free-breathing MRI scan for measuring fat in the pancreas, as part of the LION lifestyle study of adults with obesity who were losing weight through diet. Fat stored in the pancreas is tied to diabetes risk, so tracking it matters, yet the standard scan asks patients to hold their breath. The new scan lets people breathe freely and takes just under three minutes, against 16 seconds for the breath-hold version.

Eighteen adults had both scans at 3 tesla field strength. Software first outlined the pancreas, and staff then fixed the outlines by hand to keep out nearby belly fat. The team also checked how well one reader repeated the hand fixes after three months. Their results show whether the more comfortable scan can match the standard one, which would help patients who struggle to hold their breath.
pmc-13613349:
Seon Young Song, Jiyeong Kim, Yu-Mi Kim, and Joo Yeon Ko report a 2026 nationwide study of cutaneous lupus in Korea. This form of lupus affects the skin. It can stay limited there or spread to the whole body. Using national health insurance records from 2005 to 2020, they found 32,337 patients, with an average age near 43 years and women making up 72.5 percent. About 16.6 percent already had body-wide lupus at the same time.

Discoid lupus, the type that leaves round, scarred patches, was the most common form. The authors tracked how many skin-only patients later developed body-wide disease and looked at links with skin growths that can turn cancerous. Readers in a field short on Asian data get firm national rates for how often this skin disease appears and how often it deepens into a wider illness.
pmc-13614049:
Maureen M. Kitheka, Yan Jing, Yan Yao, and Puja Goyal report a 2026 study on predicting how organic molecules pack into crystals, using a fast computer method called density functional tight-binding. Guessing crystal packing matters for drug and farm chemical design, and for battery materials such as quinones, whose charged forms are hard to pin down with X-ray methods. Full quantum calculations are accurate but slow and costly.

The lighter method used here skips the need to rebuild force fields for each new chemical species formed as a battery charges and drains. The authors show their prediction routine succeeding on test cases at a fraction of the computing cost. For labs screening many candidate materials, a cheaper route to reliable crystal guesses can speed the search for better batteries and medicines alike.
pmc-13615249:
Huan Tang and colleagues ask in 2026 whether one scan timing predicts poor recovery after stroke treatment. The treatment successfully reopens a blocked artery. The timing in question is how long contrast dye takes to reach the large veins of the brain during a final scan. This sad outcome, called futile recanalization, means the vessel is open yet the patient still fares badly at three months. The team studied patients whose front-brain artery blockage was cleared by a catheter procedure.

The vein filling time runs from the first dye arrival in the neck artery to the first showing in the brain's veins. It stands in for how well tiny vessels in the brain are flowing. Statistical models tested whether a slow time flagged patients heading for poor function. Such a sign, read during the procedure itself, could warn teams early and guide closer care after the operation.
pmc-13616049:
Junqin Mao leads a team describing in 2026 an artificial membrane for covering the brain after surgery, modelled on the layered build of a dragonfly wing. Real dura, the tough sac around the brain, is hard to replace: patches must be strong, stop tissue sticking, and vanish as healing completes. Their two-layer design pairs a strong polymer sheet outside with a gel fibre layer inside carrying bioactive glass and cerium oxide particles.

In lab tests the best version was gentle on cells, mopped up harmful oxygen waste, and calmed inflammation in a timed sequence. Implanted in animals, it spurred new dura growth and blood vessel growth while limiting scarring and sticking, and it broke down on a schedule that matched natural repair. Neurosurgeons may one day reach for a patch that works with the healing clock instead of fighting it.
pmc-13616849:
Gozde Aydin and four colleagues evaluate a wellbeing questionnaire built for people with disability, called the Disability Wellbeing Index. They compare it with two versions of the Adult Social Care Outcomes Toolkit, a widely used measure of social-care quality of life. Their data come from an online survey of Australian disability insurance participants aged fifteen and older, carried out in 2024.

Nearly nineteen hundred people answered, and the two tools agreed moderately for young respondents and strongly for adults. Agreement was strongest on safety questions and weaker on dignity, and factor analysis showed the tools overlap only partly. Both measures separated groups in expected ways, such as by self-rated health. The authors conclude the new index is valid, while stressing that it leans toward general wellbeing where the toolkit leans toward care outcomes.
pmc-13617749:
Rahul Shah and nine colleagues survey caregivers in a children's hospital emergency department about firearm safety counseling. Firearm injuries are the leading cause of death for American children over age one. The prospective survey, run from November 2020 to May 2022, asked parents whether they remembered receiving safety counseling in the past two years. It also asked whom they trusted to give it, and how they would prefer to receive it.

Eight hundred twenty caregivers answered. Only about a quarter recalled any firearm safety counseling, yet more than half said pediatricians ought to provide it. About one in six reported a firearm at home, and those caregivers were more likely to have received counseling recently. Police departments and pediatricians ranked as the most trusted sources. The authors conclude parents are receptive to counseling from pediatricians and could benefit from learning the American Academy of Pediatrics storage guidelines.
pmc-13618049:
Joshua M. Courtney and Phillip C. Stancil design a quantum computer algorithm that simulates low-energy scattering between two helium atoms in real time. Scattering calculations underpin reaction rates and spectra across chemistry and astrophysics, but classical machines pay steeply rising costs as systems grow. Their product-formula algorithm evolves a Gaussian wavepacket directly, skipping any precomputed energy states, and applies the interatomic potential through closed-form circuits.

From the tracked wavefunction they extract phase shifts and then the deflection function, scattering amplitude, and differential cross section that experiments measure. For identical helium bosons, total cross sections matched trusted classical benchmarks within about six percent, with a small localized discrepancy in the s-wave channel. The design handles any potential built from inverse powers of distance at no extra gate cost, scales toward multichannel problems, and offers a ground-truth operator for testing simpler quantum simulations.
pmc-13618949:
Hawa I. Obaje and a large evaluation team assess Liberia's National Community Health Assistant Program, which posts assistants to serve villages more than five kilometers from any facility. The program rolled out across Grand Bassa County between 2018 and 2022. The staggered rollout enabled a stepped-wedge evaluation. A 2022 census collected birth and death histories from twenty-two thousand mothers covering thirty-three thousand young children.

The headline result: under-five mortality did not differ before and under the program, with an adjusted hazard ratio at one. Care patterns shifted, though. Seeking care from providers for fever, diarrhea, or breathing illness doubled to over half, while drugstore and black-market care collapsed, and facility-based deliveries rose from forty-one to fifty-seven percent. Full vaccination puzzlingly fell. The authors conclude the program improved treatment coverage and care-seeking quality, but more is needed to move mortality itself.
pmc-13620449:
Yakup Ozbay questions predictor directions and outcome definitions in a study linking thyroid ultrasound to low thyroid function after partial thyroid removal. Kang and colleagues built an ultrasound tissue score from routine pre-surgery scans, yet Ozbay finds their tables point opposite ways. His 2026 letter flags three mismatches between group differences and reported odds ratios.

Higher ultrasound scores and lower thyroid-stimulating hormone appeared in the wrong outcome groups relative to odds ratios above one, and larger remnant volume paired with a protective odds ratio below one. Defining low thyroid function by levothyroxine use at two years, rather than by blood hormone levels, may also blur two distinct states. Ozbay calls for clarification before clinical use.
pmc-13620849:
Hallie Arno and seven colleagues asked whether escaped farm salmon are quietly eroding wild salmon's ability to adapt to a warming climate. Farm fish that escape breed with wild Atlantic salmon and pass on domestic genes. The team ran a genome-environment study on more than five thousand wild salmon across North America, using a dense marker chip. They then compared wild fish with aquaculture stock at climate-linked spots in the genome.

Climate adaptation in wild salmon turned out to rest on many genes, including one large flipped chromosome segment already tied to climate response. At those climate spots, wild and farm fish differed about twice as much as they did across the genome overall. Differences also grew with distance from the southern farm source. The authors warn that interbreeding may dilute exactly the variation wild salmon need, compounding climate harm in a way single-threat plans miss.
pmc-13623949:
Garp Linder and colleagues watch single molecules to learn how a chromatin remodeler called INO80 finds its workplaces on DNA. Remodelers are protein machines that slide the DNA spools called nucleosomes into place around gene start sites and replication origins. INO80 places them with unusual precision, and the team asked whether the shape of the DNA itself guides it.

Using a technique that stretches rows of DNA like laundry lines under a microscope, the researchers observed INO80 binding, searching, and remodelling in real time. DNA shape features common at promoters and origins strongly controlled how well the machine bound and worked. INO80 also slid along DNA in one-dimensional searches and hopped between segments, yet it could not slip past nucleosomes or a barrier protein. The authors conclude that roadblocks pen the remodeler into promoter regions, raising its contact with the spools it must position.
pmc-13625349:
Fateme Asadollahi and colleagues tested a phone-health app for promoting healthy habits in pregnancy. Healthy habits matter for mother and baby, yet many pregnant women struggle to adopt them. Their randomised trial enrolled 80 pregnant women in Mashhad, Iran, split evenly between a multimedia app covering responsibility, exercise, nutrition, spirituality, relationships, and stress, and standard prenatal care for four weeks.

App users improved significantly on every healthy-habit subscale, scoring about 30 points higher overall than controls. Gains held across demographic subgroups. Asadollahi and colleagues present phone-health tools as a practical prenatal add-on, pending wider trials.
pmc-13626949:
Guoliang Zhou and colleagues demonstrate, in a 2026 materials paper, a new way to grow indium arsenide quantum dots exactly where wanted on indium phosphide. The dots emit at telecom wavelengths for quantum photonics. Quantum dots can emit single photons on demand, but dots grown the usual way land at random, which blocks scalable devices. Dots on gallium arsenide also emit near 900 nanometers, too lossy for fiber networks, while dots on indium phosphide reach the low-loss C-band near 1,550 nanometers.

The team patterned regular nanohole arrays by electron-beam lithography and etching, regrew indium phosphide, then formed dots by droplet epitaxy, crystallizing indium droplets trapped in the holes. Light measurements on a 14 by 14 array showed single-line telecom emission. Lines were narrow, near the instrument limit, for about sixty percent of dots. Single-dot occupancy reached over eighty percent of holes. The design suits fiber-based communication and chip integration.
pmc-13629049:
Anushka Reddy Marri and five colleagues examined how India's first COVID-19 lockdown, imposed in March 2020, affected nutrition across wealth groups. They drew on the country's fifth National Family Health Survey, conducted across 2019 to 2021, and measured underweight adults, wasting in young children, and anaemia, each broken down by household wealth.

After adjustment, most indicators improved after the lockdown, yet the gains clustered in richer homes, and the poorest gained least. Near-poor men were the exception, showing a rise in underweight. Child wasting fell in every group but least among the poorest, and anaemia declined everywhere while staying highest at the bottom. The authors caution that the design cannot prove cause, and they call for nutrition systems built to protect the vulnerable during crises.
pmc-13633149:
Matteo Aulicino and ten colleagues published this 2026 comparison of robotic versus open surgery for a major pancreas operation. The operation, pancreatoduodenectomy, removes the head of the pancreas together with nearby organs. Robot assistance promises smaller wounds, yet the technique is hard to learn. The team studied patients treated at one busy center from 2020 through 2025. They compared the fifty most recent robotic cases with matched open cases, setting aside the early learning period.

Robotic patients lost less blood and left the hospital about two days sooner. Their operations took far longer, even though times had dropped since the team's first fifty robotic cases. Rates of major complications were similar between the groups. One leak type, involving lymph fluid, occurred less often after robotic surgery. Tracking charts placed the team's turning points just past fifty cases. The authors judge the robotic approach safe and workable in expert hands after the learning curve.
pmc-13634049:
Aleš Maver and a large expert team published this 2026 consensus on genetic testing reports for rare neurological diseases. Modern sequencing can hunt disease genes quickly, yet lab reports vary in quality and completeness. A European quality scheme the authors helped run exposed those gaps. From its findings, the team listed twenty-eight topics that needed shared guidance, grouped under clinical information, interpretation, methodology, and reporting.

Thirty-one experts rated every topic important or very important across two survey rounds. Working groups then drafted recommendations, and the full team approved nearly all of them by consensus vote. The guidance covers which genes panels should include, quality minimums, known blind spots such as repeat expansion disorders, and sharing of variant readings between labs. One topic resisted agreement: who should be offered testing, since national health systems differ. The authors expect the shared standards to make reports easier to compare across laboratories.
pmc-13634649:
Jamie Cowley and colleagues tested brain-penetrant drugs that block a receptor driving inflammation after head injury. Traumatic brain injury kills and disables people worldwide; no drug is approved to treat it. Much of the lasting damage comes from inflamed brain immune cells. A chemical activator made both systems release the inflammatory messengers IL-1β and IL-18 in rising amounts. Clinical-stage blocker drugs stopped that release in a dose-dependent way, at levels relevant to real dosing. Blockers of a partner complex or its enzyme also worked, confirming the pathway. Because the findings come from human cells and tissue, not animal models alone, the authors argue the case for trying these blockers in injured patients strengthens.
pmc-13635249:
Michael Warchol and six colleagues studied how chemical tags re-tune the cell's cargo-hauling motor.
